MURDERED BY A NEGRO.
MURDERED BY A NEGRO.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

St. Louis, Mo., Dec. 25.—The little Town of Franklin, a few miles out from here on the Missouri Pacific Road, was the scene of a murder Christmas-Eve, the victim being Henry Speers, one of the road's locomotive engineers. The whole town seems to have celebrated the night in a lively way, and several fights took place before Speers became involved in an altercation with a negro named Andrew Beal. Speers and the negro had several words together, when suddenly the darky was seen to draw a razor out of his bosom and slash Speers with it. The white man cried out for help, and vainly tried to get a revolver out of his pocket. After staggering for a second or two he fell to the ground. The negro, as soon as he had done the cutting, turned and fed out of town into the brush. As the hour was late, and the night very dark, he easily made his escape. Speers was picked up and carried into a grocery store, where his wounds were found to be of a very serious character. His throat was cut, the jugular vein being severed, and there were two or three bad cuts across the windpipe. At first it was thought that there was some hope for him, but he sank rapidly from loss of blood, and a little after 1 o'clock this morning he died. Parties of citizens are today scouring the woods for Beal, who is supposed to be hiding in the vicinity. If he is caught it is probable that no one will ever find out what became of him. The Chief of Police this morning received a telegram from Franklin describing the fugitive murderer as a negro five feet seven inches tall, smooth face, 20 years of age, and the police will be very apt to capture him if he comes to St. Louis.

CRIME.

JAMES KNOWLES and George Owen were drowned in the canal at Holyoke, Mass., Dec. 28, while drunk.

JONATHAN MOYER has been convicted of participation in the murder of John Kintzler and wife, at Middleburg, Pa.

ANDERWERT, the newly-elected president of the Swiss confederation, shot himself dead on the street at Berne, last week.

Five men who pleaded guilty, in the courts of New York, to sending lottery tickets through the mails have been fined $500 each.

FRANK MICHAEL, who murdered Alice Becker ten days since, was sentenced Dec. 28, at Galveston, Tex., to 99 years in the penitentiary.

PETER VANDERHOOF, one of the gang who attempted to wreck the passenger train on the Wisconsin Central road, last week, was arrested in Fond du Lac Dec. 28.

OFFICER MUNN, of La Salle, Ill., shot and dangerously wounded John McGuire. The officer tried to arrest McGuire, who resisted. The ball entered the man's thigh.

CHIEF HAYES, of the Ansonia, Conn., police, was shot dead Thursday night by a ruffian named "Chip" Smith, whom he attempted to arrest.

A DETROIT book-keeper, named H. D Wright poisoned himself because a Canadian lady to whom he was engaged had changed her mind and refused to marry him.

MASKED burglars entered the residence of John E. Kirby, a deputy sheriff in St. Louis, chloroformed that officer, and held his wife prisoner while they deliberately ransacked the rooms.

A RESTAURANT-KEEPER, of Montreal, named Gustave Cherol, has been arraigned on charge of maintaining a den into which young girls are inveigled, debauched and shipped to the states.

THREE men, named John Shea, Chester Morse and John Bruce, wile attempting to cross the B. & A. railroad track, in a wagon, near Walker's Grove, Mass., were struck by the train and all instantly killed.

The authorities at Sheboygan, Wis., have jailed Mrs. Peter Vanderhoff and her sons and sons-in-law for stealing wheat. A search of their premises revealed a large amount of plunder.

CHARLES WHITTAKER, who has gone to the Massachusetts penitentiary for seven years, for a burglary in which he obtained $1,500 worth of silver plate, was in July last discharged from prison at Joliet, Ill.

After a Christmas eve fight at the railroad town at Franklin, Mo., Andrew Beal, a young negro, killed Henry Speers, an engineer, with a razor. The murderer fled in the direction of St. Louis, followed by a competent lynching party.

EX-GOVERNOR SCOTT, at the close of the coroner's inquest at Napoleon, O., was taken back to jail at Defiance. His counsel will demand a rehearing before an examining court.

The investigation into cruelties practiced at the penitentiary at Syracuse reveals terrible inhumanity toward the inmates. An ex-convict, named Cusick, has sued Superintendent Spaulding for $1,000.

CONGRESSMAN VORHEES, of Hackensack, N. J., was arraigned in Bergen county court Dec. 30, for trial on the charge of embezzlement. The case was set down for the next term of the April court. It is the impression this ends the matter.

UNDER the provisions of the law of Michigan forbidding the sale of liquor on holidays, the temperance agitators of Detroit have secured the arrest of twenty of the most wealthy and influential saloon-keepers, as a practical test.

An unknown fiend fired shots into a smoking-car on the Iron Mountain railway, at Neeleyville, Mo., on Friday night, and escaped into the forest. Dr. J. H. Paine, of Carroll, Tex., was killed, and P. P. Jones and wife, from Pennsylvania, mortally wounded.

TWENTY-EIGHT murders and fifty-seven suicides were committed in St. Louis during the past year. Of the persons murdered, five were women and two were infants. There are now eighteen murderers confined in jail, awaiting trial.
THE Denver Republican's special says that on Saturday night during a drunken row in a dance hall at Robinson's Camp, a man named Meally was shot through the breast. Policeman McElhany, in attempting to arrest the disturbers, was shot in the foot. Several others had bullet-holes in their clothing.

THE mutilated bodies of Jacob Gogle and wife, residing near Bethlehem, Pa., having been found in their bed, on Dec. 29, Joseph Snyder, who boarded in their family, was lynched for the crime by a mob. He made a detailed confession, from which it appeared that he had been refused the hand of their daughter by his victims, and thought to possess her after their death.

A DISPUTE arose on the 24th at a supper table at a boarding house in New Alexandria, Ohio, near Steubenville, and Dr. Henry, a dentist, attacked Dr. Schooley, a prominent young physician of Mount Pleasant. A wealthy farmer named Buckingham took Henry's part, when Schooley drew a revolver and put a ball through Buckingham's head, inflicting a probably fatal wound. Henry seized a shovel and beat Schooley about the head, wounding him so that he cannot recover. They are all of the best citizens of Jefferson county.

THE railroad to the city of Mexico begins to look like a sure thing. A banking house in New York has advertised that it will receive bids for seven and a half millions in bonds and seven and a half in shares for the proposed construction of a railroad from the city of Mexico to Laredo, on the Rio Grande, where it will meet the American system. The distance is 750 miles. The route is generally favorable, and it could be constructed for that sum if there is no stealing on the part of the officers and the contractors.

IN COLD BLOOD.
Henry Yaruell Shot Down While Looking After Inscendiaries—
Fears of Lynching.
Louisville, Ky., January 22.—A special to the Courier-Journal from Chattanooga says: A few nights ago in an adjoining county some one fired a hay rick belonging to Henry Yarnell. While Yarnell, after he had extinguished the flames, was searching for the incendias, assisted by a man named Howe, the report of a gun was heard and Yarnell dropped dead, shot through the brain. Howe was also shot in the mouth and dangerously, perhaps fatally injured. The next day two men named Brooks and Griffey were arrested on suspicion, and being some distance from the jail they were confined in a blacksmith shop, where they were guarded by two men. During the night noise was heard at the windows and almost simultaneously two rifles were fired, the bullets entering the brains of the two prisoners and causing instant death. The greatest excitement provails in the county. Several parties have been arrested and have been removed to another part of the county for fear of lynching. There are no positive proofs of the cause of the murder of Yarnell, but it is believed that it is the result of an old feud. It is believed the two prisoners were killed by friends of Yarnell.

SOUTHERN NEWS.

A town clock is wanted in Columbus, Mississippi.

There are fifteen women in the Arkansas penitentiary.

Cholera has killed a good many hogs in Izard county, Arkansas.

Several sales of town lots were made at Arkansas City, Arkansas, last week.

The bonds of Madison county, Alabama, recently sold for twenty-five per cent. premium.

The new zinc works at Clinton, Tennessee, will soon turn out 5000 pounds of spelter per day.

Over two hundred cases of measles were reported at McMinnville, Tennessee, up to last Saturday.

No smoking will hereafter be allowed in any of the buildings of the Vanderbilt University at Nashville.

Mr. Bell expects soon to revive the Beebe (Ark.) Watchman, the office of which was recently destroyed by fire.

In a row caused by whisky, Coon Brown shot and fatally wounded Bill Bateman at Mineola, Texas, Monday.

A drunken man at Hot Springs, incensed at the severe weather, smashed a thermometer hanging outside of a drug store.

Rev. Mr. Steel will soon begin the publication of a monthly paper at Columbus, Mississippi, to be called the Prohibitionist.

The citizens of Bellville, Tennessee, last week voted down a proposition to petition the present legislature to repeal the charter of the town.

Gallatin will soon have its gas works finished, and the streets and many residences will be lighted up, much to the satisfaction of the citizens.

The Howard Reserves are guarding the jail at Lebanon, Tennessee, fears being entertained that Conner, the murderer of Mr. Alexander, will be lynched.

Henry Yarnell was shot and killed in his own yard, in James county, by a concealed assassin one night last week. A Mr. Lowe also received a severe wound.

Trenton was saved from destruction last Thursday, when the jail was burned down, by the accumulation of snow on the jail roof and a light rain falling at the time.

A shooting affray occurred in East Bernard, Texas, Monday, in which Milton Sparks, Frank Sparks, and a man named Monroe, were all wounded, and Frank will probably die.

Captain William McElwee, says the Roane
Texas, Monday, in which Milton Sparks, Frank Sparks and a man named Monroe, were all wounded, and Frank will probably die.

Captain William McElwee, says the Roan County (Tenn.) Republican, has a contract to deliver 10,000 tons of iron ore in twelve months. He will deliver it at Oakdale Junction.

Sunday night last, in Houston, Texas, Henry Fields, alias George Kain, a negro thief, was shot and killed by E. P. Lockhart, while attempting to enter the latter's residence.

A farmer named George A. Dodd shot and killed a negro named George Sackett, nine miles east of Kosciusko, Mississippi, a few days ago, on learning that the latter had stolen a mule from him.

John Williams, colored, of Humphreys county, Tennessee, was sentenced by the supreme court, at Nashville, last Saturday, to be hanged at Waverly, Tennessee, on Friday, March 11, 1881, for the crime of wife-murder.

The shotgun policy, as a preventive of hydrophobia, finds favor with the people of Giles county, Tennessee, in the neighborhood where Esquire Hannah met such a fearful death. A war of extermination is waged against stray curs.

Arkansas City, Arkansas, has less than one hundred white voters and supports seven or eight saloons. This looks like a good deal of saloon to so little a town, but it is to be taken into consideration that railroad and levee laborers and transient persons do most of the drinking from which these places derive a revenue. It has not transpired that the village has yet erected a church edifice or public schoolhouse. Necessities before luxuries, you know.

Western and Southern States
GEORGE HINES, fifty-five years old, living near Grayson, Cal., went to the home of Lizzie Kuene, a girl of eighteen, and renewed a former proposal of marriage. He met with a firm refusal. The infatuated man then said, "I will kill you," and drew a pistol. Miss Kuene anticipated him by seizing a shotgun conveniently at hand and killing him.

WHILE the people of Lapeer, Mich., were at church, a Mrs. Barnard went to the house of the Rev. E. Curtis, the Baptist pastor, and attacked his wife, an old lady of about sixty-five years. She threw Mrs. Curtis down, poured gasoline oil over her clothing and then set it on fire. The poor woman was so shockingly burned that she lived but a few hours. Mrs. Barnard is the wife of a prominent lumberman, and is believed to be insane.

JOHN SHERMAN was elected to the United States Senate in the Ohio legislature by a combined vote of 84 to 51 for A. G. Thurman.

THE Michigan legislature elected two United States Senators—Congressman O. D. Conger being elected for the full term beginning March 4, while for the unexpired term of the late Senator Chandler, ending March 4, Senator Baldwin, the present incumbent was chosen.

SENATOR COCKRELL has been re-elected to the United States Senate by the Missouri legislature.

NEAR Plain City, Ohio, Mrs. Matilda Scott, a widow, aged about forty, her daughter, age twenty-two, and an adopted son, age fourteen, named Charles Gooce, were found dead upon the floor of their residence, having been beaten to death with a club. Robert Garner colored man who reported this triple murder, was arrested, circumstantial evidence pointing to his guilt.

In a fight between Americans and Mexicans at a ball at Las Mula, N. M., three men—two Americans and one Mexican—were killed and others were wounded.

The captain of an English bark and five other men were drowned by the capsizing of a small boat in Washington harbor, Cal.

GEN. BENJAMIN HARRISON was elected United States Senator by the Indiana legislature, receiving in the house 57 votes to 39 for Gray and 1 for De la Matyr, and in the senate 22 votes to 23 for Gray and 2 for De la Matyr.

S. R. J. McMILLAN has been re-elected United States senator from Minnesota.

Two colored men were arrested for brutally assaulting and then murdering Miss Bessie Werts, a young lady living near Prosperity, S. C. They confessed their guilt and were taken from jail by a crowd of men and lynched.

DAMAGE to the amount of more than $200,-00 has been done by floods in and about Portland, Oregon.

Two persons—a man and a woman—were fatally injured and four others were badly hurt by a train's being thrown from the track near Pend Creek, Ill.

JAMES FRENCH, while dancing a jig on top of a moving freight car at Richmond, Va. neglected to notice a bridge ahead, and was knocked off the train and killed.

The recent extreme and unusually cold weather in Florida caused hundreds of thousands of oranges to drop from the trees. One hundred thousand fell from the branches of one grove at Palatka.

FOUR firemen were fatally injured by a falling wall at a fire in Chicago.

A MORTGAGE for $50,000,000 has been executed by the Wabash, St. Louis and Pacific road to the Central Trust company of New York.

GENERAL CHARLES VAN WYCK, formerly of New York, was elected United States Senator by the Nebraska legislature upon the seventeenth ballot.

MOUNT BAKER in Washington Territory is reported to be in a state of active eruption.

DISPATCHES from various points in the South report heavy snow falls.

On two days recently Apache Indians in the vicinity of San Marial, New Mexico, killed fifteen persons and wounded several more.
brooks-griffey-louisville-1881-01.A32:
James County's Triple Murder.
Sam Mattox and Vance and Wm. Norman, accused of the murder of Griffey and Brooks in James county in January last, after a preliminary hearing before Judge Trewhitt at Ooltewah last week, were each bound over to court in the sum of $5,000, and the bonds were promptly given. All are men of high standing and respectability, the Normans being well-known physicians, and much excitement prevails over the case. Griffey and Brooks were being guarded by the three men above named when killed, and they (Griffey and Brooks), were under arrest for assassinating Henry Yarnell, a respectable farmer. Yarnell, the man first murdered, was a brother-in-law of the Normans, and an uncle of Mattox, and it is alleged that by murdering their prisoners, and claiming that they were shot by unknown parties while under their care, they revenged their kinsman's death.
brooks-griffey-louisville-1881-01.A34:
THE TRIPPLE MURDER CASE
IN JAMES COUNTY.
Further Investigation Before
Judge Trewhitt.
The grand jury have been endeavoring to investigate the case and at the first term of court after the murder, Dr. Priddy was indicted. His case was continued, however, under bond. At the last term of court, indictments were presented against Francis Norman, Wm. Norman, his son and Sam'l Maddox. On the night of the 6th instant, Sheriff Clingan, with a posse of men proceeded to the residence of these parties in the 2nd district, and quietly arrested them. Of course the case was not bailable and their only resource was in a writ of habeas corpus. In the mean time the Chattanooga Times of the 10th inst., contained an article which did the parties great injustice, inasmuch as it purported to "find them guilty" before trial and spoke of "a strong guard" being necessary to prevent "mob violence." It is to the credit of these parties to say that not only was any resistance offered in their arrest, but during the week, that they were awaiting the convenience of the Judge, they virtually remained about town without a guard, and never with more than one.

The case was commenced under the writ before his honor, Judge Trewhitt, last Saturday, Messrs. Clift and McNabb for the State and Shepherd and Parker for the defense, but it was found wholly impossible with the array of witnesses, to get through. Jugde Trewhitt admitted them to bail in a joint bond of $5,000, to appear before him again on Saturday 25th inst. The bond was made and the case remains in that shape. It is certainly to be hoped that the right persons may be found and that although slow, justice will be given them. In the mean time everything seems to be mere conjecture. yours, Ool tewah, June 15th. ANOX.

The James County Murders.
Chattanooga Times
The James County Murders.
Chattanooga Times.
Our readers will recollect the account in the Times of the murder of Henry Yarnell, in James County, in January, 1881, and afterwards the murder of his two supposed assassins. Dr. Priddy, a prominent physician of that vicinity, who had quarrelled with Yarnell, was suspected with being implicated in the crime, and about a year ago an indictment was obtained against him, but as the investigation proceeded the proof became less positive, and when the case came for the Times at Ooltewah, last week, the attorney-general entered a nolle pros. and the matter rests there.

Texas Tragedies.
BRENHAM, TEXAS, June 2.—This morning near Sealey as the work train was switching, a number of cars were cut loose by convicts in an attempt to escape. Two were killed and four wounded—two mortally. One escaped.

JEFFERSON, TEX., June 2.—Last night, in Camp county, four young white men visited the residence of Dennis Brothen, colored, who fired into them, shooting Calvin Cope dead, and mortally wounding Israel Hagrand. The other two men killed the negro and escaped.

The Criminal Calendar.
Dallas, Texas. 3.—Milton and Bakes, notorious burglars and horse thieves, were killed by Hays, county deputy sheriff, while resisting arrest.

San Antonia, 2.—Thomas North, an employee of the Mexican National Railroad, was killed by a policeman at New Loredo, Mexico, and the authorities refuse to give up the corpse over which new excitement is aroused.

Brenham, Texas, 2.—This morning, near Scaly, as the work train was switching, a number of cars were cut loose by convicts in an attempt to escape. Two were killed, four wounded, two mortally, and one escaped.

Jefferson, Texas, 2.—Last night, in Camp County, four young men visited the residence of Dennis Brotemni, colored, who fired on them, shooting Calvin Cope dead, and mortally wounding Israel Lagunde. The other two men killed the negro and escaped.

Chicago, 3.—This morning Thomas Burns shot and killed Charles Bell, his partner, in a saloon at 553 South Clark street. The men came from Dubuque, and are decidedly unsavvy characters. They had passed the night with a French woman who is called Belle Swift. Their quarrel has been chiefly about money matters.

James B. Doyle testified in his own behalf to-day, in an off-hand, unaffected way, showing that he had been a farmer in Bradford, Ill., for about thirty years, and had been a merchant and stockraiser, owning from 400 to 600 acres in Illinois, Colorado and Kansas. He had business relations and ventures with Brockway, the forger and counterfeiter, but had known him only as Spencer, and in the capacity of an honorable man of business.

Monticello, Iowa, specials say James Hogan, on Wednesday night, shot his divorced wife six times, inflicting injuries which are likely to prove fatal, and then with one shot killed himself. She had obtained a divorce because he was a bigamist, and he had threatened to kill her because she refused to marry him.

Tragical Tales.
A boy named Henry Stracke, stabbed his ten-year-old companion, Michael Hilberger to the heart, on the 3d inst., at Lancaster, O.

James Hogan, of Monticello, O., shot his divorced wife six times, inflicting dangerous injuries, and then with one shot killed himself on the 3d inst.

Elijah Sterling, proclaiming himself the son of God, attacked his wife and son with an axe on the 3d inst. at Crisfield, N. Y. The wife is fatally wounded, but young Sterling received only a flesh wound.

At Chicago, on the morning of the 3d inst., Thomas Burns shot and killed Charles Bell, his partner in the saloon business. They quarreled over money matters.

Melton and Baker, notorious horse thieves and burglars, were killed by a sheriff while resisting arrest in Hayes county, Texas, on the 3d.

Peter Morelli was fatally shot by Geo. Melasch, a restaurant keeper at San Francisco, Cal. They quarreled over a mining claim.

John Lynch ambushed and assassinated Charles Lyles about ten miles away from Leadville, Col., on the 1st inst. Cause, a long-standing quarrel over a mining claim.

Daniel McDonald was discharged from a Ludington, Mich., saw mill on the 31st ult., and on the night of the 1st was discovered cutting the belt in the mill by a boy named James Corwin. McDonald turned on his discoverer and kicked him to death.

E. D. Baldwin, of Forest City, Ark., on the 2d inst., by a man named Jones. Baldwin promptly shot his assailant dead and was acquitted by a jury.

A startling discovery was made on the Scofield farm in Woodruff county, Ark., on the 2d, being the mutilated body of a man. The trunk of the body lay in an outhouse, with the heart cut out, and one arm and the head severed. The heart was found in a neighboring field. No clue to the murder.

A number of convicts attempted to escape from a train near Bernham, Texas, on the 2d. Two were killed and four wounded, two mortally. One escaped.

Four young white men meddled with the cabin of Dennis Broteuni, a colored man, near Jefferson, Texas, on the night of the 1st inst. Broteuni opened fire on the party, killing Calvin Cope, and mortally wounding Israel La Grande. The survivors killed the negro and escaped.

At Senatobia, Miss., on the 2d inst., one McCracken engaged in a pistol fight with a barber named Blount. McCracken, who is chancery clerk of Tate county, died of wounds received, and Blount lingers in jail with mortal wounds.

I. J. Stephens brutally murdered an old German at Lake Providence, La., and escaped.

John Thomas, a farmer on the Red river, Texas, got into trouble on the 1st inst., and killed Deputy Sheriffs Krelht and Samuel and Charles Meredith.

A negro field hand named Sebree quarreled with his employer, named Long, near Fayette, Mo., and beat him with fatal effect, using a hoe. Sebree was mortally wounded by Long, before he succumbed.

A negro named Matt Butts crully murdered Maj. W. J. Bethea, in Early county, Ga., was captured near Arlington, on the 1st inst., by a mob of 200 men and hung.

Silas Payne, a Lexington, Ky., negro, was found dead in bed on the 31st ult., having been brutally murdered. Josephine Smith, his housekeeper, is charged with the crime.

Holney Hull was shot and instantly killed at Cynthiana, Ky., on the 31st ult., by his brother-in-law Alex. Odor.

M. Seguin, a correspondent of the Paris Telegraph, was killed by Arabs on the 28th ult., at Beja. The murderers were arrested and promptly shot.

E. L. Stickney, a mining man, entered a boarding house at Denver, Col., on the 31st ult., while the people were at dinner, and opened fire on one of the guests, M. F. Campan, a real estate agent, killing him and a Mrs. Devereaux. It is said Campan was improperly intimate with Stickney's wife. The shooting of Mrs. Devereaux was unintentional.

A quarrel arising from some trivial cause led to a duel with knives between two lads named Trent and Strickland, at Waldron, Ark. The latter will probably die, as the flesh on his arms was cut into shoestrings and portions of his legs were slashed off.

John Enrichs, an ex-policeman at Indianapolis, Ind., whose wife was seeking a divorce, shot his wife and her father on the 30th, and then shot himself. Enrichs is dead, but his wife and her father will probably recover.

In a quarrel about wages at North Middletown, Ky., William Cunningham shot and killed John Alexander.

Billy Meton, a notorious thief, was shot dead by Sheriff Martin, while attempting to escape Nankyles station, Texas, on the 30th.

John P. Nunley, near Charleston, S. C., challenged his nephew, George Nunley, aged 19, and killed him before he had chance to fire a shot. Family difficulties caused the murder.

A tramp named Mehan, stabbed a young man named Wm. Copeland, near Bridgeport, Ala., on the 29th ult., because he annoyed him while he was bathing. Copeiand died almost instantly. While the tramp was in prison, Sam Reese, a cousin of Copeland, stepped up and shot him dead. Reese escaped. Wm. Shock killed his brother-in-law Wm. LYNCHED BY A MOB.

Louisville, Dec. 24.—A Horse Cave special to the Courier-Journal says: "Yesterday morning about daylight Esquire John A. Gardner, who lives about one mile from Rawlett's Station, in Hart County, was called to go to his barn by a negro boy, Sam Campbell, who lived with him, telling him that one of his cows was sick at the barn. Gardner went immediately to the place, and on entering the door was knocked down and robbed by the negro boy. John Campbell, who lived in the neighborhood, a brother to Sand, had stalled all night at Gardner's the night before. News was conveyed to Mrs. Gardner that her husband was lying at the barn with his head mashed. An alarm was given, and in a few hours the whole community was gathered in and Gardner had been carried to his house by negroes and medical aid procured. Upon investigation strong suspicion rested upon the two negroes Sam and John Campbell. They were arrested and searched, and found in possession of a pocketbook and money which was identified by Gardner's wife and others as Gardner's property. They were taken to Manfordville and committed to jail, where they remained until about 12 o'clock last night, when they were called for by a party of seventy-five or one hundred men. The key to the outer door and cell in which they were was demanded of the jailer. The jailer saw that it would be useless to resist, and surrendered the key, requesting that they would not disturb the other prisoners. He was answered that the rest would not be molested. The jail was then entered and the prisoners taken out, and though the streets of the town down a hill side between the town and river, where they were suspended between the earth and sky to a limb of a tree.

It is said that before they were executed the younger one, Sam, confessed his guilt, and said that John had persuaded him into the perpetration of the crime. It is said that John was stubborn, and only said that his people lived in Taylor County, Kentucky.

They were about 20 and 23 years of age, Mr. Gardner is in a very critical condition at this time, and is considered by his physicians as very dangerously ill. His wounds are upon his face and head, and are several in number. His face is severely mangled, and the head swollen.

The negroes had only been in the country a few months.

The Coroner summoned a jury of six men, and held an inquest upon the men, and returned a verdict in accordance with the facts.

CIRCUMSTANTIAL EVIDENCE.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Bosrox, Dec. 24.—The case of Catherine Driscoll, to-day found guilty of the manslaughter of Mary Credon, is one of the most interesting trials in Massachusetts for some years, as the conviction was made entirely on circumstantial evidence. The trial was a very sad one, the prisoner every day being accompanied by her family of little children, the youngest sitting in her lap in the dock. The victim was three years old, was seen to enter Driscoll's house soon after dinner, April 15, and her body was found on the railroad track early the next morning, her dinner not having digested, and her clothing dry, notwithstanding heavy rain had fallen during the night. Soon after the dinner, Mrs. Credon missed her daughter, and, looking into Mrs. Driscoll's, saw her with a child in her arms, and on her apron considerable blood, which the woman said, on being questioned, came from a cut finger of her child. In Mrs. Driscoll's cellar blood found on the walls and floor proved to be that of a human being mingled with that of fowls and cows. In the ground under the stairs the hood of the murdered child was dug up. Near by there was some grass corresponding with a quantity of grass clasped in the hand of the murdered child. The blood was claimed by the defense to be that of an animal's alone, and the prisoner swore that she did not kill the child, who was a loved playmate of her children.

Judge Lord said that there was no substantial difference between circumstantial and positive evidence, and leaned to the opinion that the woman committed the deed in a sudden fit of passion, without intention or thought.

The sentence will be imposed Monday, and will probably be for twenty years.

BOLD ROBBERY.

LAFAYETTE, Ind., Dec. 24.—One of the most audacious robberies was committed about noon yesterday at Williamsport, Warren County. Two men entered the store of the Messner Bros. at that place, only one of the firm being present. They asked the price of several articles, and finally requested to see some handkerchiefs. About the same time one of the strangers asked for tobacco, and while young Messner was in the act of getting it he was dealt a terrible blow with a sandbag. The men then fastened the door and tried to get into the safe. The outer doors were open, and they secured about $00 in money. They were unable to open the inside doors, and, returning to Messner, who had now become partially conscious, demanded to know the combination. He refused to give it, when they beat him nearly to death, and then left the store by the rear door. The Town Marshal happened along about that time, and finding the front door locked and seeing a man lying on the floor, forced his way in, releasing Messner and giving an alarm. A large crowd was soon on the hunt, aided by an accurate description of the villains, but they could not be found.

St. Louis, Dec. 24.—The inquest on the body of the dead infant found on a vacant lot Tuesday, resulted this afternoon in the coroner's jury finding Miss Grover responsible for the death of the child. Her brother-in-law, Frank W. Longly, was discharged, and she is now under police surveillance.

TWO LESS OHIO MEN TO HOLD OFFICE.

Va., Dec. 24.—A dispute arose this evening at the supper table in a boarding house, at New Alexandria, O., near Steubenville, and Dr. Henry, a dentist, attacked Dr. Schooley, a prominent young physician, of Mount Pleasant. A wealthy farmer, named Buckingham, took Henry's part, when Schooley drew a revolver and put a ball through Buckingham's head, inflicting a probably fatal wound. Henry seized a shovel and beat Schooley about the head, wounding him so that he can't recover. All are best citizens of Jefferson county,

NITRO-GLYCERINE EXPLOSION.

BRAFORD, Pa., Dec. 24.—This morning Albert Magee, of Canton, O., and Thomas Perry, went out to torpedo a well one mile east. While Magee was mixing nitro-glycerine in a derrick, Perry, who was in the engine house, turned the steam too rapidly into the frozen compound and an explosion followed which blew the derrick into bits. Perry was driven clear through the engine house, but will recover. Magee was blown into fragments, the only portions of his body recovered being his heart and lungs, which were found on a hillside a hundred yards away, and one leg of his pantaloons.

Bradford, Pa., Dec. 24.—Albert Magie and Thomas Perry, moonlighters, went to the torpedo anvil north of Bradford at an early hour this morning. Nitroglycerine was congealed and Magie placed cans containing thirty-seven pounds in a tub of rain water to liquify it. Just how, no human tongue will ever tell, but at any rate the compound exploded with terrific force. Magie was torn to pieces and his remains scattered about in every direction—an arm, his leg, and lungs, and heart were the largest portion of his body found.

Perry was standing some distance away, but was thrown against the building near by with great violence, his hearing destroyed and body badly bruised. The derrick and engine house was badly reduced to splinters. Concussions broke the windows at a distance of nearly a mile. Magie was aged 25, and has been residing in the oil regions for several years. He is a native of Ohio.

JEWS LEAVING GERMANY.

Berlin, Dec. 24.—Many Jews residing here avoid appearing in public localities. Many Jewish families are preparing to emigrate to Belgium, France and England.

HORSE CAVE, KY., December 24.—Yesterday morning, about 5 o'clock, 'Squire J. A. BROOKLYN, December 25, 1 a.m.—On the 10 h of last month ex-Judge Samuel Morris was brutally assassinated by Deputy Coroner James Dunne, in a saloon, where Judge Morris had been taken by a letter purporting to come from a man who wished to see him on business. CHICAGO, December 25—1 a.m.—The preparation for Christmas this year in Chicago has never been equaled before. The streets have been through for weeks with people buying presents, and yesterday were literally jammed. The railroads and mails have been loaded down with packages. Shipwreck Narrative.

Special Dispatch to The Bec

QUEBEC, December 25—1 a.m.—Cap. Stone, of the bigantine "Pomlico," which has just arrived here, tells a thrilling tale of the rough experiences of himself and crew. They sailed from Quebec on the 17th of November, and on the 20th, when in the gulf of St. Lawrence, they encountered a terrific gale which shattered the ship's rigging, and rendered them helpless. They drifted in the trough of the sea for several days. Most of the crew were badly frozen while on duty, and the captain was disabled by a falling spar. The ship finally grounded on the island of Anticosti, and the men landed safely. After living in a cave for three days, they were finally discovered by the inhabitants and kindly cared for.

HARTFORD, December 19.

To the Editor Inter Ocean:

Your note informing me that Christmas had reached Chicago and has become an inter-oceanic festival, occasions little surprise and no regret, and perhaps I shall not be accused of "giving away" (that is an old sanscrit phrase) the Puritans, from whom I descended, if I admit that while Thanksgiving day was founded on Plymouth rock, Christmas rests upon the rock of ages.

Your sincerely,
CHARLES DUDLEY WARNER.

WASHINGTON, December 21.

At this interesting hour, joyous yet solemn, when the good old year 1880 has nearly filled up the measures of its days, and is soon to take its place among the shadows of the infinite past, and anxious expectation is awaiting the advent of the first day of the first year of the last score of the century, let me congratulate you upon the achievements by which the departing year has been distinguished, and mingle my fervent aspirations with those of the free, progressive and patriotic citizens of the republic for wisdom and justice to guide and control our national councils, and for union, prosperity and peace to all sections of our common country. In bidding good-bye to the old year, I commend to you the old free, progressive north, and in welcoming the new year, with equal fervor I commend to you the prospectively free and progressive new south.

FREDERICK DOUGLASS.

TALLAHASSEE, FLA., February 10.—Colonel W. R. Moore, Colonel of the Second Florida Regiment in the late war, is one of the members of the Assembly from Columbia county. That he bore himself gallantly during the late terrible struggle, the three wounds, received in as many battles, fully testify.

Colonel Moore is of medium size, of rather delicate physique, with a dark complexion, eyes and beard. He was universally beloved by the soldiers in his immediate command, and the people of his county entertain for him genuine respect and esteem. He is modest and unassuming in deportment, upright and honorable in character.

Born in Leon county, he moved when a boy to Madison, and thence in 1842, to Tampa. Another change in 1856 carried him to Columbia, where he engaged in mercantile pursuits. When the war commenced he raised the first company organized in his county, and was sent to Cedar Keys, to take command at that town. He captured there Lieut. Selden, U. S. N., and assisted in making prizes of several vessels.

His company was mustered into the Second Florida Regiment, and reached Virginia in July, 1861.

He received his first wound at Seven Pines and succeeded the lamented George W. Call, killed in that battle, as Major.

At Chancellorsville, in May, 1863, he was again severely wounded.

Returning to his regiment before he was entirely recovered, he rejoined it the day before the battle of Gettysburg, when he received his third wound and was made a prisoner.

He was detained until October, 1864, and then sent through the lines on parole. As soon as he was declared exchanged he again returned to his regiment as its Colonel, and surrendered with General Lee on the 9th of April, 1865.

He was elected Clerk of the County Court and served in that capacity until 1868. In 1874 he was unanimously nominated for the State Senate, but could not accept through circumstances beyond his control.

Last year his friends nominated him for the Assembly. It is needless to say that he discharges his duties with fidelity and honesty.

The present Legislature bears down heavily upon frauds. The following bill is a specimen of their feeling in that direction: "Any person or persons who shall sell or cause to be sold as butter any spurious preparation purporting to be butter, whether known as oleomargarine, or by any other name, shall be
son or persons who shall sell or cause to be sold as butter any spurious preparation purporting to be butter, whether known as oleomargarine, or by any other name, shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and upon conviction shall be fined in a sum not to exceed one hundred dollars, or be imprisoned in the county jail for a period of time not to exceed thirty days, or by both fine and imprisonment, at the discretion of the court.

"Any keeper of any hotel or boarding house who shall supply oleomargarine or any other spurious preparation, purporting to be tutter, for the use of guests, shall be subject to the same pealty."

While their hands are in, the Legislature might as well punish those e.g. gaged in the sale of adulterated sugar, much of which contains a large proportion of glucose. There are other articles of food also that might bear inspection.

Thus far both houses have kept squarely up with the business of the day, leaving nothing undone for the morrow, and leaving no loose ends to bring up. Only nineteen working days remain, and many bills of importance are yet to be subjected to scrutiny.

The Ada Gray troupe has been playing here this week, and have drawn fair audiences. The plays of "Camille," "Lucietia Borgia," and other standard dramas, were well put on the stage, and gave entire satisfaction. Ada Gray is well supported by the company, which contains several actors of sterling merit.

The impending municipal election has brought out the usual horde of greasy, noisy negro politicians, who make as much fuss as if the fate of the world was depending on the result. These are the chaps who go in for whisky and spoils.

A good ticket has been selected by the Conservatives, which, it is thought, will be supported by all the respectable elements of the community. If the people are sensible, they will lend all their energies to the success of this ticket.

It is very important to the interests of a small city, situated as this is, that its municipal affairs should be confided to the charge of responsible and competent civic authorities.

The unfortunate difficulty at Madison, which has resulted in such a melancholy tragedy, and given rise to such great excitement, originated as follows:

Mr. S. Y. Finley, on the part of Gen. Finley, and Gen. Jenkins, on the part of Col. Bisbee, were engaged in taking testimony in the Congressional contest between these gentlemen. A difficulty occurred shortly after between Mr. Patterson and Savage, in which the former charged the latter with having made a false affidavit. Savage branded Mr. Patterson as a liar, and was struck by the latter. Savage at once threw his left arm around the neck of Mr. Patterson, and drawing his head down to his bosom, shot him through the body. After he
at, and was struck by the latter. Savage at once threw his left arm around the neck of Mr. Patterion, and drawing his head down to his bosom, shot him through the body. After he fell, another negro, James, rushed up and discharged his pistol at the prostrate figure, severing one of the thumbs.

There is a rum or that at this crisis Mr. Pennis Eagan cried out, "Kill him!" I have not been able to get definite information on this subject, but, at all events, a warrant was issued for the arrest of Mr. Eagan.

A large number of negroes were outside of the building in which the murder occurred. In a very brief period the Sheriff, one of his deputies and a few men from the Madison Guards arrived, and arrested the two negroes, who were only subdued by the threat of instant death, in the event of resistance.

A great commotion at once arose, the whites threatening to lynch the prisoners, and the negroes declaring they should be protected. The authorities used every effort to preserve order. Early in the night the Governor's Guards, of Tallahassee, under command of Captain Mosely, and the Monticello Guards, in command of Captain Pasco, arrived in a special train.

Meanwhile the Sheriff, with a warrant, had gone to arrest Mr. Eagan, who resides some distance from Madison. He found the house surrounded by a crowd of negroes, resolved not to permit the arrest of Mr. Eagan. After some parley, he was permitted to enter, but could not find the person sought.

United States Marshal Durkee went down last night and his arrival increased the excitement to some extent.

To-day Judge Settle goes down under instructions of Attorney General Devens to open a commission to take testimony in the contest.

It is generally supposed that the Republicans are endeavoring to make all the capital possible out of this difficulty, and that Col. Bisbee will use all his efforts to strengthen his own position.

It is understood that the prisoner will be removed as soon as possible to some other jail for security, and that the troops will then be withdrawn.

An attempt was made in the Senate this morning to reconsider the bill to regulate the sale of spirituous liquors passed yesterday. After discussion the motion failed.

The weather has cleared off most charmingly.

The Governor at once ordered out detachments of the Governor's Guards and Mouticello Rifles, which were transported, at once, by special train to Madison, under the command of Adjutant-General Yonge. On their arrival there, they found a large number of armed and excited negroes collected together from town and country, and the white people of the town greatly disturbed. The arrival of the State troops produced the desired effect, and in a short time entire quiet was restored.

The cause of the trouble was, in brief, as follows, as far as can be learned from the scores of diverse statements which have been in circulation:

On Monday, the evidence of several witnesses was taken in the contested election case of Bisbee vs Finley, at the house of Mr. Dennis Eagan before whom the testimony was taken, as Notary Public. Among the witnesses there examined, was Savage, a violent and unprincipled negro politician, who had been a candidate in the recent election for the office of representative in the Legislature for Madison county. On Monday, the examination was continued at the courthouse, in the course of which Mr. Frank Paterson, a young attorney of the place, who was present, and Savage became in involved in a controversy of words concerning the testimony of Savage and others, given the day before, which culminated in one of the most shocking and cold-blooded murders which has ever occurred in the State, the negro Savage, having caught Patterson with his left arm from behind, and, reaching around his body with his right hand shot him in the front part of the body with a self-cocking pistol. In the subsequent confusion, two other shots were fired at Paterson after he fell, by Savage and much excitement, and imminent danger of a conflict between the officers of the law and the crowd of negroes which had gathered about, were arrested and lodged in jail. Threats were made of rescue of the prisoners, on the part of the blacks, and there was also some talk of lynching them on the part of the whites; but the prompt call for a superior force by the Sheriff, and the Judge of the Circuit, as promptly responded to by the Governor in sending the militia, dispersed the excited mob of blacks, and prevented intemperate action on the part of the whites.

The connection of Eagan with the murder, is as various in statement, as the other facts. It is asserted that proof can be made that he called out to Savage when the difficulty first began, to "shoot him!" also that he had armed many of the negroes and encouraged them on to the point of aggression. However these things may be, and whatever may have been his direct or indirect connection with the crime committed by Savage and James, it is certain that he, or rather his friends for him, as he is understood to assert, felt the liveliest apprehensions for his safety, and having made his escape from the place of the murder, he was guarded at his home by a number of armed negroes for a few hours, and thence escaped into Georgia, and was arrested in Albany, and brought to Tallahassee, where he is now in custody. The detachments of Tallahassee and Monticello troops were, on Friday, relieved by detachments from Jacksonville and Lake City companies, who are now on duty, guarding the prisoners, Savage and James, in Madison jail.—It is probable that arrangements may be made for their removal thence to some other point.—Now that they are in the hands of the law, they will certainly be retained and protected and given a fair trial.

The prompt action of the authorities and the officers of the law and the military have been deservedly commended in all quarters, and meet the hearty approbation of all good citizens, disappointing only those who would rejoice to see Florida and the whole South again deluged in blood, if they could once more regain thereby the power they once enjoyed, and to their last desperate struggle to retain which may be directly traced not only the horrid tragedy in which young Paterson's life was sacrificed, but nearly every ill which yet afflicts an ordinarily patient and long-suffering people.

It is quite evident that the Republicans are endeavoring to make political capital out of this Madison affair. The following telegram from Gen. Jenkins, who was present and witnessed the murder of young Patterson, dispatched to Bisbee in Washington, is the very quintessence of cunning. He said to that embodiment of malignity (Bisbee)—

Intense excitement here. Fight in one precinct and Eagan's life threatened. Have been obliged to stop. One man killed. What shall I do?

To which dispatch, Mr. Bisbee replied as follows:

Call on Judge Settle to take testimony. Continue, unless prevented by force. To abandon Madison will encourage violence elsewhere; but act on your own judgment.

Mark how he withholds the fact that the "one man killed" was a Democrat and was murdered by a Republican negro. Mark also the stress he lays on the so-called fight "in one precinct," when there was no "fight" but a brutal murder by one of Bisbee's swift witnesses. It is plain from Jenkins' telegram and Bisbee's reply, with the comments thereon by the stalwart newspapers, that the impression was intended to create that testimony in the contest between Bisbee against Finley could not be taken in Madison on account of Democratic intimidation and violence, when Jenkins knew that not the slightest opposition to the taking of such testimony had been interposed by any Democrat—that in fact the only violence he had encountered came from his own witnesses. This it was which "obliged him to stop," and not the opposition of the whites. We assert that any person who may be deputed by Judge Settle or any other authority will meet with no opposition in collecting all the testimony wanted, false or true, as the case may be. No better evidence of this is needed than the fact that when this sad occurrence happened, less than half a dozen whites were any where about the court-house, while negroes were in and around in crowds. The whites were quiet, offering no opposition, and this Mr. Jenkins knew. His telegram was an outrageous suppression of facts, and for this he deserves the severest condemnation.

TALLAHASSSE, February 13.—I had a chat yesterday with Captain Mosely, Sheriff of this county, and also the commander of the Governor's Guards, one of the first companies that reached Madison after the late difficulty.

Captain Mosely states that from intelligence previously received, he fully expected, on reaching Madison, to find a large body of armed men. When near Madison a party of, say twenty-five armed negroes, were seen at a railroad crossing.

On reacling the town, the two companies, his own and the Monticello Guards, marched up to the town and stacked arms in front of the jail.

There were small squads of armed negroes loitering about in several directions. No armed whites were visible, except the military. Durag the night pickets were thrown out, and some five negroes were arrested and confined until the morning.

The next morning the Sheriff, with a posse of soldiers and citizens, went to Eagan's house to arrest that individual. The person in charge refused admission. As the officer was about to leave he was invited to enter, and made an ineffectual search. Quite a number of armed negroes were around the premises.

All of the white citizens, as well as the troops, were under the control of the Sheriff, and acted according to his direction.

After Tuesday night there was comparatively little excitement, and very few persons came in from the country.

Thursday Captain Mosely took a squad of men and went to Live Oak, expecting to arrest Eagan. On returning to Madison he found but a very small gathering at the depot.

Captain Mosely very strongly and positively disavows any intention on the part of the people of Madison to interfere with the taking of testimony by the commission. There was no such purpose or desire, and the deplorable murder that broke up the proceedings was altogether unexpected, and originated in a personal altercation between the parties concerned. But for the excitement that temporarily ensued, the examination could have progressed without any interruption.

An acquaintance, who has seen the murderer Savage since his arrest, says that he has entirely lost his arrogance and bravado. He admits that he deserves death, and expresses the hope that he will be allowed reasonable time for repentance.

Mr. Patterson's body was pierced by two balls, both inflicting mortal wounds, a third cutting off the thumb of one of his hands. He lived but a short time after the reception of the injuries.

It is thought now that the two negroes in jail at Madison will be removed to some other prison for security. Should this be done, matters in that town will soon resume their usual serenity.

At present a detachment of fifteen men from the Jacksonville Light Infantry, and a similar force from the Lake City company, are on guard in Madison. Parties from that town this morning represent affairs as perfectly quiet.

Ice formed here this morning, and the weather is clear and delightful.

Some parties are here from the Northern States for the purpose of hunting. Small game is abundant in the vicinity, and a good shot can score a heavy bag of partridges in a morning.

Wild ducks are numerous in the many lakes, while more ambitious Ninrods can find deer, wild turkies, and, perhaps, an occasional bear, at no very remote distance.

Chas. L. Fildes, member of the Assembly from Alachua county, was born in Madison, Fla., in 1856, being not yet twenty-five years of age. He has resided in the State ever since, except a few years spent in Georgia during his early youth. He intuitively took to the printing business, much to the displeasure of his father, who desired that, on reaching the age of maturity, his son should enter one of the professions. It was finally evident, however, that Charles was determined upon being a printer, and at the age of 13, he entered his father's office as an apprentice, faring as other "devils." No favors were shown him, but for the purpose of disgusting him with his chosen vocation, unusually heavy tasks were forced upon him. He bore it manfully, however, and in the course of three years was the foreman in a printing establishment over men who had served at the trade for a quarter of a century. In the natural course of events, with one so infatuated with his vocation, young Fildes soon developed a talent for writing, and before he was eighteen, occupied the position of associate editor of the Monticello Constitution, which place he held three or four years writ-
developed a talent for writing, and before he was eighteen, occupied the position of associate editor of the Monticello Constitution, which place he held three or four years, writing with a vigor and discretion far exceeding his years, and doing valiant service for the cause of Democracy, which at that time lay prostrate under the iron heel of carpetbag Radicalism. Acting upon the axiom, "a prophet is not without honor save in his own country," in the fall of '78 he moved to Ocala, in Marton county, purchasing an interest in the Banner, published at that place. During his residence there he was elected reading clerk of the last Assembly, and as such gave universal satisfaction. Feeling that his abilities merited a broader journalistic field, in the fall of '79 he removed to Gainesville, and established there the Bee. This venture was in opposition to the advice of older and more mature minds, but being a young man "of indomitable energy, and being possessed of a sufficient amount of self-reliance to carry him through the world, he acted on his own judgment and succeeded in establishing a paper which proved very popular and remunerative to the publisher. GRIST FOR THE OUTRAGE MILL
HOW A REPUBLICAN MURDERER SERVED REPUBLICAN ENDS IN FLORIDA.
HOW A REPUBLICAN MURDERER SERVED REPUBLICAN ENDS IN FLORIDA.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 16.—The full particulars of the murder at Madison, Fla., last Tuesday of Frank Patterson a young lawyer, by Charles Savage, a negro bully, have been received here, and they show the entire falsity of the reports of the affair sent out to Republican papers from this city last Wednesday and Thursday. The facts are that testimony in the contested election case between Colonel Horatio Bisbee, Jr., a Republican, now in Congress, and General J. J. Finley, the Democratic candidate, was being taken before Dennis Eagan, United States Internal Revenue Collector of Florida but sitting as a notary public. On Monday the testimony of the man Savage was taken in behalf of Bisbee at a farm several miles from Madison. He swore that he had seen young Patterson near the polls on the day of the election, doubling up two tickets as one and handing them to Democrats to be voted.

The taking of testimony was adjourned to the next day at Madison. Savage, who is a power among the Republican negroes, appeared in Madison the next day and was selected by Eagan to call witnesses as they were needed. The examinations were carried on in the court-house no white men except those engaged in the work, being present. In the room and yard below were over one hundred negroes. During the proceedings Young Patterson came in and examined the testimony Savage had given concerning him. He got up quietly and started to leave, but near the door he met Savage. He donounced the negro's perjury, when Savage, who is very large man, seized him by the coat and drawing a revolver fired twice into his body. As Patterson was falling another negro, Howard James, fired again. Patterson died almost immediately. Eagan, the United States Collector, it is charged, incited Savage to the murder by crying "Kill him," when Patterson first spoke. He fled as soon as the shots were fired. Savage tried to escape, but the Deputy Sheriff, who was present, levelled a pistol at him and he surrendered. James was also arrested.

At the jail a large crowd of negroes threatened to release the prisoners, but Judge Vann and others addressed them with some effect, and in response to despatches the Governor sent his guards and the Jefferson Rifles, of Monticello, to Madison by special train. The demonstration ceased upon the arrival of the militia. A warrant was issued for the arrest of Eagan as an accessory. He had made his escape into Georgia, but was captured at Albany and brought to Tallahassee Friday morning. Congressman Bisbee knows all the parties, that Patterson was a Democrat and that Savage is a Republican, and yet founded on despatches said to have been received by him, the Republican correspondents here last Wednesday and Thursday sent out despatches to make the false impression that a Republican witness was murdered, that the affair was devised to intimidate Colonel Bisbee's witnesses, and that these things and the sending of the militia were a new development of a Southern Democratic conspiracy to suppress Republicanism in the South.

Colonel Bisbee even went to the length of calling upon the Attorney General whom he induced to seek a despatch to United States District Judge Settle, directing him to go to Madison and take the testimony desired. The United States Marshal was also instructed to at envo to protect the Judge. The scheme of Colonel Bisbee and the rest was to make use of the affair before the public should get the details to prejudice the Forty seventh Congress in favor of the Republican contestants of the seats of Southern Democrats elected, and if possible to lay a foundation for investigating committees and other such devices — The strength of General Finley's case was shown in the fact that he agreed to allow the carpet bag Collec or Eagan to preside at the examination of witnesses, knowing that he was prejudiced against him.

THE PATTERSON MURDER TRIAL
Jury Secured-Testimony Being Taken-Evidence of Messrs. Wigginton and Church-Notes.
JASPER, FLA., June 21.—The remaining ten jurors were procured yesterday from the venue of one hundred ordered last Friday. As constituted, it consists of eleven whites and one negro. Thirty-five peremptory challenges were consumed by the defense and nine by the State.

At the opening of court this morning, the indictment was read by the State Solicitor. The witnesses on both sides were placed under the rules and excluded from the court house.

Dr. J. B. Wigginton was the first witness introduced: Am a physician, Knew Frank Patterson. He is dead. He died in Madison, Fl., on the 8th of February, 1881, from a unshot wound, two and a half inches below right nipple, penetrating cavity of the chest. Wound was half inch in diameter. Such a wound is calculated to produce death. I made a post mortem examination. Such a wound is mortal. There was another wound on one of his hands, not serious. I was called shortly after infliction of wound. He lived about an hour after I reached him. When I saw him first he was sinking rapidly, and I considered it unnecessary to administer medicines. Can't say he was aware of his condition.

Charles S. Church sworn: Live in Madison—was living there February 8, 1881, and was Deputy Sheriff. Was in the court house that morning. Saw a disturbance between James, Savage and Mr. Frank Patterson, Savage, James and Messrs Finley, Eagan, Jenkins, Patterson and one or two others were present in the court room. Frank Patterson passed by me and handed me some evidence to read. I heard a souffling at the door and looked over my shoulder to see the cause. Saw Savage with his left arm around Patterson's neck, with his hand on his collar. Just then I saw Savage shoot a pistol, which he held in his right hand. Three shots were fired. Patterson was pushing him off as if to get loose. Savage then fired again. They had got nearly back to a centre post. Patterson jerked loose, Savage falling to his knees. Patterson staggered and nearly fell, but recovered. James then shot at Patterson, who fell to the floor and tried to get up, but could not without assistance. Am positive James shot at Patterson. Was within eight feet of James. No blows were exchanged by the parties. Patterson had nothing in his hands till after he fell and rose, then he reached behind his person and drew a pistol, attempting to cock it, but failed. I suppose he didn't have strength to do so. He was very pale and one of his fingers was wounded. Previous to the difficulty Patterson seemed to be very quiet. Saw prisoners after the shooting and told
strength to do so. He was very pale and one of his fingers was wounded. Previous to the difficulty Patterson seemed to be very quiet. Saw prisoners after the shooting and told them they must submit to arrest. They stood with their pistols cocked and pointed towards me swearing they would die and go to hell before they would be arrested—would be butchered first. I stepped out, locking the door. Was unable to arrest them and went out to summon a posse. Was not present when the prisoners were disarmed.

Cross examination—Patterson walked towards the door when he handed me the evidence spoken of above. Eagan was sitting at the far end of the table, to wards the north, with a pen in his hand. Heard that evidence was being taken in contested election Bisbee vs. Finley. When I entered the room Savage and James were about the middle of the apartment on their way to the door leading out of the building. I think after the third shot I drew my pistol, ordered the firing to cease, and said I would shoot the next man that fired a pistol. My attention was directed generally to Savage and James, because their pistols were pointed to me. Saw nobody else have a pistol at that immed ate time. At this point court adjourned to 3 p.m.

Twenty-seven witnesses have been summoned by the State and twenty by the defense. It is hoped that the testimony will be closed by Thursday or Friday. There was but a small attendance to day. Many of the spectators are negroes. The prisoners preserve a calm and unconcerned demeanor.

It is exceedingly hot and sultry. Crops are suffering severely and rain is greatly needed.

THE MADISON TRAGEDY.
The Patterson Murder Case-Evidence for the State.
JASPER, FLA., June 22.—The testimony has been going on since my last, the court sitting nine hours daily. The State will probably introduce two more witnesses. But little interest appears to be excited in this community, and matters are entirely quiet.

June 21, 3 P. M.—S. M. Hankins sworn: I live in Madison, Fla., was Sheriff of that county February 5th, 1851, and now held that position. On the day just mentioned was in the town of Madison, and saw both the prisoners at the court house. I had a warrant for Savage for perjury. Saw them together that day, between 9 and 11 a.m. I saw Savage have a pistol in his hand as he went up the steps. The pistol was under his coat. The warrant was given to me afterwards. Heard some firing at the court house that day. I was one hundred and twenty-five yards distant. I saw Mr. Thomas, and walked rapidly to speak to him, just after the warrant was handed me. The firing was about half an hour after Savage and James went into the court house. Saw Frank Patterson in Judge Witherspoon's office door. With the assistance of others, I arrested James and Savage in the court room. They were in custody within ten minutes after the firing. An excited crowd was around the lower entrance. My deputy, Church, was standing in the door and told me James and Savage had shot Patterson and he had locked them in the court room. He said they would not be arrested. A posse was summoned. When the men arrived I unlocked the door and went in. Savage and James each had a pistol in their hands when I entered. I said I had a warrant for them and they had better surrender. Savage said he would surrender if I would protect him from being murdered, and handed me his pistol. James refused to give up his pistol, which was taken from him by Mr. Pollard and handed to me—pistols shown—the larger is Savage's. It is the British Bull Dog, a self-cocker, 44 calibre. James' is smaller. Each shoots five times. Savage's had one empty chamber—the chambers of James' were all loaded; one had the appearance of having been snapped. When Pollard handed me James' pistol James said, "You see I haven't fired, my pistol is all loaded." He repeated this two or three times Charley Savage said, "Hush, Howard, you reloaded as I did." He also said, "You'll find my pistol all loaded." I said, "No, there is an empty shell in yours, Charley." He said, "I can't account for it, I intended to reload it." I found one large empty shell and one large loaded cartridge after I went back to the court room. They would fit Savage's pistol. He said that he shoved them out with a penholder. To the best of my recollection he said he used Eagan's penholder. I found cartridges on persons of
They would hit Savage's pistol. He said that he shoved them out with a penholder. To the best of my recollection he said he used Eagan's penholder. I found cartridges on persons of prisoners to fit both pistols, and a needle-rifle, here in court. The rifle cartridges were on James' person. Searched for a rifle adapted to such cartridges, and found it. Got this gun from Edmond Burroughs, a negro, two hours after arrest of prisoners. He came to the jail with it and asked if I had sent for him. I replied "No," and took the gun to examine it.

Saw Mr. Patterson after he was shot, before and after his death. His hand was slender, with small fingers. Third finger of left hand was pierced by a small ball, as if by a buckshot. Think the wound was not inflicted by the large pistol. Think the wound could be produced by a ball from the small pistol.

Cross-examined: Don't know who sued out the warrant for Savage—have never read it. Was handed me by County Judge. One hundred and fifty persons were standing around. Went off as soon as I received it. Did not mention the warrant to Frank Patterson. Don't know where the warrant is. Did not arrest Savage under that warrant.

Neal Coyle sworn: Reside in Madison county. Was at Madison court house 8th February, 1881. Knew Frank Patterson and saw and spoke to him that day. He was in a dying condition, blood running from his mouth, and he said he had been shot. He said he was dying. He did die, perhaps an hour after this conversation. He could not stand, nor utter more than a few words without being choked by the blood. He said Savage shot him twice and James once, the latter in the left hand and Savage in the body. The wound in the hand was produced by a small ball.

C. W. Stevens, sworn: Live in Madison, Fla., and was in Madison court house early in the morning. Knew Frank Patterson, and saw him that day in my office, and also in the court house. Messrs. Finley and Jenkins were taking testimony in contest of Bisbee vs. Finley. While so engaged, Mr. Patterson came in and sat down. I heard a noise in the rear of the room, while I was sitting facing the Judge's stand. Heard the discharges of pistols. Jumped up and ran in direction of the sound. Savage was in a few feet of me, and said: "Don't you come here," pointing his pistol at me. I felt for mine, but did not have it. I said: "Don't shoot me," and he lowered the pistol. Then went to Patterson, who had just risen from where he had fallen. I said, "What's the matter?" He said, "I am shot." "Are you hurt much?" "I am killed." I assisted him, and we passed near Savage. Went down stairs. I smelt cloth burning and saw his shirt on fire. As soon as he laid down I returned to the court room, having in my hand a pistol given me by Patterson as we were going down stairs. It was fully loaded.

JASPER, FLA., June 24.—Several witnesses have been examined by the defense. There seems to be but little prospect of the testimony closing this week. Mr. Dennis Eagan gave his evidence this morning.

Jethro Robinson, colored, sworn: I sell beef in Madison. Was in the court house February 8th, 1881. I saw Savage go in five feet of the door and beckon to James, who went to him. Both were standing, whispering, when Patterson walked up to Savage and struck him. Savage wheeled round and Patterson struck him again. Then Savage grabbed him around the right arm with his left hand and held him. Savage then drew a pistol and they struggled a few seconds and the pistol fired. Savage still held him and put his pistol to him and shot. Then I started out, and as I got to the door I heard the third fire and went out. After the second fire Patterson had a pistol in his hand. Had nothing in his hand when he struck him first.

Cross-examined: Am sure I was in the court room when the difficulty occurred. Got there ten or fifteen minutes before the disturbance, I did not tell Capt. T. H. Willard week before last that I was not in the court house and knew nothing of this matter. Had a chat with Willard after he got back from the Senate. He asked me if I was frightened when the difficulty occurred and if I saw Savage shoot Patterson. I said yes. Did not notice particularly who was in the room. Nobody was talked to me about the evidence I was to give. Just after the firing I did not meet Mr. Hankins, and say to him, "Oh Mr. Hankins, what is the matter?" Witness declined to answer the question if he had ever been convicted of larceny.

The examination of this witness was long and tedious. He has been convicted of larceny, and an appeal has been taken. It is said that he can be successfully impeached.

Dennis Eagan, sworn: Was in Madison court house on the 6th February, 1881, acting as Notary Public in the contest Bisbee va. Finley. The second witness had been called and sworn. I was making a note of the fact when my attention was attracted by a scuffle at the east end of the room. Looking up I saw Patterson and Savage were the parties struggling. Instantly I heard the reports of a pistol. I got up and went near the railing. As I got there the parties had become separated, Patterson stumbling away from Savage and falling upon his side. LATE NEWS ITEMS.
A DISPATCH from the City of Mexico says a train on the Moreles Railway was precipitated into the San Antonio River by the falling of a bridge. Some 200 persons were killed or wounded, mostly soldiers.

TROOPS have been dispatched to a point in San Juan County, Utah, 125 miles west of Durango, where an outbreak is threatened by Pah Ute Indians. A number of battle men have disappeared and are thought to have been killed.

GEORGE WILLIAMS, proprietor of a restaurant at Cleveland, O., was killed on the 25th by William Fritch, of Columbus, who is probably insane. Fritch says he went to the desk to pay for some refreshments, and discovering that he had no money he felt an irresistible impulse to shoot the proprietor.

SEVENTEEN persons were killed and five wounded by an explosion in the Louise Tieffan colliery, Austria.

FRANK BRAGA, Secretary of the Portuguese Protective and Benevolent Society, San Francisco, Cal., has absconded, being a defaulter to the amount of about $100,000.

At Washington, D. C., on the 25th, J. Y. Christmas fatally shot his partner, W. G. Whitney. Whitney was the son of Mrs. General Gaines by her first husband, and Christmas her son-in-law. There had been bad feeling between the two for some time.

WORKMEN on a strike, having attacked the Town Hall at Dramnien, Norway, to release two comrades arrested, were fired upon by troops. One man was killed and several wounded. One officer and some soldiers were injured.

C. P. COYLE shot and mortally wounded Joel A. Phillips, yesterday, at Jasper, Fla. They were both from Madison, attending as witnesses in the trial of Savage and James for the murder of Frank Patterson, in Madison, in February last, during the taking of testimony in the Finley-Bisbee contested election case.
At Paterson, N. J., on the 25th, Edward De Porter, the rejected suitor of Silvia Knockardt, fatally stabbed the father of the girl and made a murderous attack upon Arthur von der Capella, her accepted suitor.
Two sons of Jared Smith, of Eden, Vt., aged 8 and 10, were drowned while playing upon logs, on the 26th. Louis Maurer, Julius Michel and Willie Choupo, all of St. Louis, were drowned while bathing in the Mississippi.
One of the bodies recently found floating in the river at Kansas City proves to be that of Rev. Sidney M. Stray, of Warren County, N. Y., recently pastor of the fashionable church at Lake George, attached to the Troy Presbytery. He supposed he committed suicide in order to escape the vengeance of a brother-in-law, who was after him for shooting his sister some time ago.
charles-savage-madison-1881-02-08.A24:
RIDDLED WITH BULLETS.
TWO FLORIDA MURDERERS KILLED.
Sayage and James Meet their Doom-The Train Bearing Them to Jail Boarded by a Mob and the Prisoners Shot.
JACKSONVILLE, FLA, August 25.—As a train containing the two colored prisoners, Savage and James, reached Madison this morning it was met by about one hundred people, twelve or fifteen of whom rushed into the train and riddled the prisoners with bullets. The agent of the railroad did not suspect any violence until a short time before the arrival of the train, when he attempted to telegraph it back, but found the wires cut, He then ran up the track and signaled the conductor not to stop, but some one had boarded the train and uncoupled the two rear cars.

The prisoners had been convicted of the murder of Frank Patterson, which occurred on the 8th of February, 1881, at Madison, in a room where testimony was being taken in the contested election case of Bisbee vs. Finley. A new trial had been granted by the Supreme Court, and they were being conveyed from Tallahassee to Jasper to undergo that trial when they were murdered as detailed above. There is great excitement in Madison over the affair.
