A PROCLAMATION.
Ex-Emperor Norton Views with Alarm the Dangers Threatening His Late Faithful Subjects in Cherry Creek.
SPIRIT LAND, ETERNAL SUMM

Spirit Land I have devoted most of the time allotted to mundane affairs in correcting the great evils which I behold in the wicked metropolis of Eureka. Until very recently I had no occasion to particularly concern myself about the good people of White Pine's metropolis. But of late I have seen with alarm many things which I fear will destroy the peace and happiness of may late faithful subjects there.

The wood ranches on the hills north and west of Cherry Creek, for a distance of 25 miles, are the sole property of Maurice Fitzgerald, having descended to him in a direct line from Dermod McMurrough, King of Linster, who bartered his kingdom to Henry II. in the eleventh century for these same wood ranches. A claim dating back to such antiquity and bearing the joint seals of two famous monarchs, should not and must be annulled by the greet and avarice of tenderfeet land-jumpers or the edicts of petty courts.

I was also much grieve at that little lynching affair on Star Hill the day after Christmas. It was a bungling job, and for that alone the perpetrators must be punished. No halfway executed business meets my approval. Cruel sport of this kind is never known in Spirit Land. Sentence—$1 fine and one night in the "cooler" each.

But what concerns me more especially and I view with the greatest alarm is the great influx of opium fiends in the midst of my late faithful subjects in Cherry Creek. These fiends are the virus thrown off by Eureka in its late spasmodic efforts to rid itself of the parasites who have long preyed on her people. These newcomers among you are the vilest pests of society. They neither sow nor reap, but revel in the dreamy fumes of the oriental drug. Some of them are young men—no, not men—but vampires, who live and have their being on the thrift and industry of honest workers.

Now, as I look down from my ethereal realms, I wonder how it happens that my late beloved subjects permit these fiends to squat in their midst, eat of their substance and sow the seeds of their vagrancy and their vice broadcast among the rising generation.

I well know that you, my late faithful subjects, are lovers of law and order, and perhaps you dislike to violate the sacred bulwark of liberty in any violent effort to fire out the fiends. I have had recourse to the Law Library in Spirit Land and find a copy of the Nevada Statutes, 1881, in which
ample powers are conferred on you by
the written law to close up the opium
dens and utilize the labor of the fiends
on the new road out to Duck Creek.
And here is my warrant to my late
fai ful subjects for the execution of
the same:

An Act to amend an Act entitled "An Act to
Regulate the Sale or Disposal of Opium, and
to prohibit the Keeping of places of Resort
for smoking or Otherwise Using that Drug."
Approved February 9. 1877; approved
March 4, 1881.

The People of the State of Nevada, repre-
sented in Senate and Assembly, do enact as
follows:

Section 1. From and after the last day of
March, 1881, it shall be unlawful for any per-
son or persons, as principals or agents to have
in his, her or their possession any opium pipe
op part thereof, or to smoke opium, or to sell
or give away for such purpose, or otherwise
dispose of any opium in this State, except
druggists and apoth caries, and they shall
sell it only on the prescription of legally prac-
ticing physicians.

Sec. 2. Any person or persons who shall be
found guilty of violating the provisions of
this Act shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and on conviction thereof shall be punished by a fine not exceeding $500 or by imprisonment in the county jail for a time not exceeding six months, or by both such fines and imprisonment, in the discretion of the Court.

See 3. All Acts and parts of Acts in conflict with this Act are hereby repealed.

Now, therefore, be it known by all to whom these presents shall come, that I have this day given particulars instructions to my worthy mundane bailiffs, Sheriff Raum, Deputy Lyons and Constable Henry, that they immediately, by virtue of this writ, proceed to scoop in the fiends and close the opium dens in Cherry Creek for all time. Let all my late faithful subjects lend their aid and support to my bailiffs in enforcing this our esome decree.

Executed in the third year of our reign in Spirit Land. NORTON I., Late Emperor of America.

The "Lynchers" Discharged.
The hearing of the case against Joseph Bews, Thomas Craig and Tim Rouse, for assault on Charles Tippit, was terminated in Justice Lander's Court at 12 o'clock Wednesday night. The twelve good and true men who were impaneled to try the case, after hearing all the testimony and able discourses of the lawyers pro and con., were unable to agree on a verdict after four hours' deliberation. They stood eight for acquittal to four for conviction. The Court, finding the jury could agree, discharged them, and dismissed the case, which no doubt was the proper course.

WASHINGTON TERRITORY.
A Bad Character Hanged by Masked Men.
Walt Waller March 27th at Alma
WALLA WALLA, March 27th. At Ainsworth yesterday afternoon a rough known as Black Dick, or Dick Osborne, stabbed a gambler named Alonzo Babb in the back, inflicting three deep wounds with a five-inch blade. An opium den had been destroyed by a committee appointed at a recent meeting, Babb being one of the committee. Osborne, an opium fiend, took exception, and afterward stabbed Babb in a dance-house. Osborne was arrested, and last night a party of masked men took Osborne away from the officers and hanged him to a high fence. Osborne was a hard customer, and had had difficulties at Boise City and Walla Walla. Babb is not dead, though the wounds are reported fatal. He was a quiet and peaceable man, and has relatives at Eugene City, Oregon.

Dangerous Illness-Charged Witheducation-The Lynching of Osborne.
PORTLAND, March 28th C. F. Boattie
The Lynching of Osborne.

PORTLAND, March 28th.—C. F. Beattie, Chairman of the Democratic State Committee, is lying at his home in Clackamas county very dangerously ill. No hopes of his recovery are entertained.

William Clark, of Marion county, has been arrested, charged with the seduction, under a promise of marriage, of a young lady named Miss Mollie Musser. Clark had a preliminary examination and was held to await the charge in the sum of $800.

Following are additional particulars just received concerning the stabbing affray at Ainsworth and the lynching of Dick Osborne. Babb, who was stabbed, was merely a spectator of the raid made on the opium den, in which Osborne had an interest, by the committee of citizens organized for that purpose. The raid was made on the den during Friday night. Saturday, while Babb was standing at the door of Hill's dance-house, he was murderously assaulted by Osborne, who, exclaiming "Damn you, I'll kill you," attacked him from behind. He was stabbed a number of times, one thrust of the knife penetrating the lungs, inflicting a wound from which it is thought Babb cannot survive. The citizens of the place were intensely excited over the affair, and strong threats of lynching Osborne were expressed openly. Sunday morning, about 3:15, some fifteen men went to a small building standing back of the dance-house, where the prisoner was confined, and broke down the door. Osborne was pulled out, a rope thrown around his neck, and he was dragged about thirty yards and then strung up to a high pole. Early next morning the lifeless body of Osborne was discovered dangling in mid-air. The act seems to generally meet with public approval.

TELEGRAPHIC.
NEW YORK, March 28.—Thomas J. Eagan, a printer living at 158 East Forty-second street, went out with his wife last night, leaving their neice, Nellie Cunningham, aged 19, alone in the house. Soon after two burglars entered the parlor, and when Miss Cunningham screamed one of them stuffed a handkerchief in her mouth and bound her with a clothes line. Having tied her so that she could not move, they removed the handkerchief, threatening to kill her if she made a noise. They then demanded information as to where Mrs. Eagan's jewels and money were, but Miss Cunningham refused to tell, when one of the ruffians struck her in the face. Still exasperated by her refusal to answer their questions the other burglar stabbed her several times in the arms, face and hands with a pen knife. The young lady became insensible, when the robbers, fearing they had killed her, fled. Miss Cunningham was found in a state of insensibility, and securely bound. To-day she became partly paralyzed and was unable to speak. The police have arrested John R. Camp, and Miss Cunningham recognized him as one of her assailants.

LONDON, March 27.—Advices from Calabar state that a missionary, Mr. Milum, who recently visited Abomey, the capital of Dahomey, found that the custom of making human sacrifices still continues. Several hundred natives were barbarously sacrificed during his stay at Abomey.

WALLA WALLA, W. T., March 28.—A bad character named Dick Osborne, Friday night, fatally stabbed Alonzo Babb in a dance house. Osborne was arrested yesterday afternoon. Last night a party of masked men broke into jail, took him on to the nearest high fence and hung him.

It is reported that a military expedition in three columns is being organized in Mexico for the extermination of the hostile Indians about Santa Rosa in the State of Coahuila.

Seven masked ruffians Thursday entered the house of John Conner, aged 81 years, who lives alone with his wife at Catfish, a place 50 miles from Pittsburg, bound and gagged the couple, compelled the old gentleman to give up the combination of his safe, and took from it $5,000 worth of Government bonds, unregistered coupons, and over $5,000 in cash. MURDER AND HANGING AT AINS-
MURDER AND HANGING AT AINSWORTH. —At Ainsworth on the 26th ult., one Dick Osbourn, a desperado, fatally stabbed in the back, a gambler named Alonzo Babb. Babb is reported to have been a quiet peacable man. He had, with others, endeavored to break up some opium dens in the town which had given offense to Osbourn, and the next day without any warning, he approached Babb from behind and stabbed him in three places. Babb died the next day, Osborn was immediately arrested. The night following ten persons in disguise, demanded Osborn from his keepers and took him and hung him till he was dead. As soon as the hanging became known, several roughs and desperadoes made a few threats of vengeance, upon those who were engaged in the hanging as soon as they could be found out, which induced the orderly citizens of the place to notify about twenty of the gang to leave the place forthwith, and those notified did leave as fast as they could. Capt. Smith tells us that he crossed to the south side of the Snake several of them on his ferry.

Mr. Nicholas Smith, the husband of one of Horace Greeley's daughters, is acknowledged to be the prettiest man in America. It is said he is a love of a fellow, and no mistake.

The Parnell branch of the Irish Land League of Cincinnati passed resolutions severely condemning Irishmen who favor the use of dynamite or other Niblist methods to promote the cause of Ireland.

Jay Cooke has just found out and sent to a private asylum, with orders that she be made comfortable, one Sarah Marshall, who lost her money and reason in the panic to which his failure gave the start.

A wife at Massillon, Ohio, eloped with her husband's brother. The husband followed them to Black river, whipped the brother, got a bullet in return, cursed the pair in the presence of a street crowd, and went home alone.

frank-wright-colorado-1881-02.A1: AN EX-WASHINGTON LAWYER KILLED OUT WEST.—A special dispatch to the Baltimore American from Westminster states that news has been received there of the killing of Frank J. Wright, formerly of that place, aged 27, in Colorado. Mr. Wright, who practiced law in this city for some years, went west last May to attend to some business for one of his clients, and became interested in certain mining claims in Colorado. In order to look into the matter further, he purchased some mules, and having hired a servant, started out for a prospecting tour in the mountains. The mules had been stolen, but Mr. Wright, of course, was not aware of the fact when he purchased them. The real owner, having learned that they were in his possession, started with some friends in pursuit, and coming up with him, the party shot him dead, supposing that he was the thief. Nothing was heard of him by his family from August, 1880, until a day or two ago, when a letter was received from Rev. Dr. David Wilson, formerly of Westminster, but now a chaplain at one of the United States army posts in Colorado. Becoming alarmed at the young man's long absence and silence, the family had written to Dr. Wilson, who, after making an investigation, discovered the facts as given above. Mr. Wright is spoken of as a young man of excellent character.
frank-wright-colorado-1881-02.A3:
ANOTHER BROKER SAYS:
Am Innecent Man Lynched.
A Westminster, Maryland, special gives particulars of the lynching of Frank J. Wright, son of a prominent citizen of that place, in the mountains of Colorado recently by a band of vigilants. The murder was a horrible one and wholly unprovoked. Private advices to his family state that after removing to Colorado he hired a servant and purchased some mules for traveling purposes from a party who, it is said, had stolen them, Mr. Wright being ignorant of the facts. He was, however, pursued by a gang of desperadoes and hanged, with his servant, before he could make an explanation. Mr. Wright was a man of thirty, a member of the Carroll county and Washington, D. C., bars, and well connected socially and of recognized integrity. His object in going to Colorado was to attend to some business for a client and while there he purchased an interest in a mine. His family are overwhelmed with grief at his terrible fate.
frank-wright-colorado-1881-02.A7:
Lynching of a Carroll Countian in Colorado.
In May, 1880, Frank J. Wright, aged thirty-two years, son of Isaac Wright, of this city, left his home in Washington, where he was engaged in the practice of law, for Colorado, to look after some land claims of one of his clients. Whilst in Colorado he purchased an interest in a gold mine. His family heard from him frequently for some weeks, the last letter being received in July. Not hearing any tidings from him for several weeks, the family wrote to a cousin in Washington, and received the information in September that a letter had been received from him, dated Ouray, Colorado, July 30, 1880. He was then on his way to Los Velos, New Mexico, and expected to be in Washington in September. Since then, until Saturday last, nothing had been heard from him. Some time ago, relatives in this county wrote to Rev. Dr. David Wilson, a chaplain in the U. S. Army, stationed in Colorado, and asked him to institute inquiry concerning him. The Doctor complied, and on Saturday last he wrote to relatives in Uniontown, that in August young Wright purchased a couple of mules, and with a servant, started on a prospecting tour in the mountains. The mules Mr. Wright had purchased proved to have been stolen property, a fact of which he was entirely ignorant. He and his servant were overtaken by a vigilance committee, and notwithstanding their protestations of innocence, they were lynched by the vigilantes. They were thus the innocent victims of a mob of outlaws, who hold that the theft of horses, or mules, or other stock, is the worst of crimes, and for which the punishment by law is too slow and uncertain. For the crime of murder, the accused is allowed a trial by due course of law; but for theft of stock, lynching to the nearest tree is the penalty in the western wilds.

The unfortunate young man was born in Uniontown, this county, and was highly esteemed by all who knew him there, and by his friends in this city. Upon reaching his majority, he took up his residence in Washington, subsequently studied law, and established an office at 508 F street N. W. His aged father, now a teacher in a school near Union Mills, and his aged mother, have the sympathy of the entire community in their bereavement.

frank-wright-colorado-1881-02.A25:
Two Innocent Men Hanged.
Mrs. Gowan Spence, the wife of a wealthy jeweler in Newark, New Jersey, has just received the news of the terrible death of her brother, Frank J. Wright, in Colorado. The young man was a lawyer in Washington, and in May last he went to Colorado to attend to a land claim for a client. He was induced to purchase an interest in a gold mine, and after buying some mules, started with a servant on a prospecting tour in the mountains. That was on July 30, and nothing further was heard about him until a few days ago, when the Rev. Dr. Wilson, pastor of a church in Colorado, wrote that young Wright had been hanged by vigilantes. The mules he purchased had, it seems, been stolen before he bought them, but the vigilantes refused to hear his explanation when they found him in the mountains. They hanged him and his servant to the limb of a tree, where their skeletons were afterward found. Wright was only 30 years old.

The above was specially telegraphed to the New York Herald, and has been floating about ever since. We have had it in type for several days, but it has been crowded out. In this morning's dispatches the whole thing is contradicted.
frank-wright-colorado-1881-02.A28:
Bond of His Own Death.
Several weeks ago news reached Westminster, Md., that Mr. Frank Wright, a lawyer, had been hanged in Colorado, the story being that his servant had bought for their use in the mountains some animals that had been stolen, though unknown to them, and that men in pursuit of the animals, finding them in possession of Wright and his companion, hanged as both thieves, refusing to accept their explanations. Mr. Wright's family were almost crazed by the news. They have received from Silver city the following telegram, which has given unspeakable relief:

Read to my horror an account of my death in the New York Herald. Arrived here after perilous adventure.

FRANK.

Active measures have been taken to learn how this false story of death could have originated.
frank-wright-colorado-1881-02.A32:
Not Lynched.
BALTIMORE, March 15.
cstminster, Md. to night

A SPECIAL from Westminster, Md., to-night, says: A few weeks ago news reached Westminster and was reported in the various papers of the death by violence of Mr. Frank Wright, son of Isaac Wright, of this city. Mr. Wright left Washington for Colorado in May, 1880, and until the middle of August wrote regularly twice a month to his family here. Since that time nothing has been heard of him until the sad news of his death at the hands of a so-called Vigilance Committee was communicated to the family by Rev. Dr. David Wilson, formerly pastor of the Methodist Protestant Church here, but now a chaplain in the United States army and stationed in Colorado. Dr. Wilson stated that young Wright had purchased two mules and 1 started to the mining district, that the mules proved to be stolen, and the owners, forming themselves into a Vigilance Committee, had followed him, and, notwithstanding that Mr. Wright assured them he did not know they were stolen when he purchased them, had hung both him and his servant to a tree and left them. The only thing that gave a ray of hope to the family was the fact that a letter had been received from the postmaster at Hancock, Col., in January, stating that Frank Wright was there on the 11th of November, which was after the supposed lynching; that he had sold a part of his mining claim to a man who had accompanied him to Alpine, paid him the money and left him, and that was the last time he was seen alive by any of his friends. The hope that he might have been alive at that time, and that some unknown and unforeseen combination of circumstances had prevented his writing, took definite form in the following telegram received this morning:

"SILVER CITY, N. M., March 14, 1881.

"To Isaac Wright:

"Read to my horror an account of my death in New York Herald. Arrived here after perilous adventure.

FRANK."

When the last letter was written, in August, Mr. Wright walked ten miles to mail it, not waiting for a convenient opportunity, as he did not wish to keep his family in suspense. The family and friends are now awaiting with great anxiety a letter, which they hopefully expect in a few days, and which we trust may satisfactorily explain all things. Active measures have been taken toward securing Government detectives to find out the facts, and, if possible, punish the actors in the crime; but until something further is heard from Mr. Wright, action in the case will be suspended."

The wretch then, leaving the mangled corpse on the ground, turned with redoubled fury in pursuit of

When the unfortunate Henderson returned home he found his wife hacked to pieces, lying murdered in the yard. He looked for his daughter, but she was not there. Some traces of blood showed the direction in which the murderer had gone. The frenzied father followed this crimson trail only to find his daughter further on,

A LIFELESS CORPSE, with brains battered and bleeding. His cries attracted the neighbors, and the sheriff and coroner were sent for.

Henderson having informed the sheriff that he suspected William Farrington of having committed the deed search was made for him immediately, and he was arrested by the sheriff before daylight at his house. When arrested he had blood upon his hands and upon his hat, and it was noticed that one of the heels of his shoes was missing. The missing heel was subsequently found near the murdered woman's body. His clothes, from which he had been endeavoring to wash out the blood, were wet. Farrington was taken to jail at daylight Saturday and put in irons.

Vendredi soir il y eut dans notre paroisse à deux milles d'Abbeville, le meurtre le plus atroce, le plus barbare qui puisse se commettre. Des causes ou motifs qui poussaient au crime nous ne dirons rien, vu que par tout renseignement obtenu. il n'y avait rien qui justifiit un homicide et surtout un homicide marqué d'une cruauté, d'une bestialité sauvage. Mais, bref. Vendredi soir, un nommé William Epperson. quitta le village d'Abbeville, vomissant des imprécations trop sales pour être répétées, et se rendit à la résidence d'un nommé Pine Henderson, homme de couleur très estimé de tout le monde de notre paroisse. L'épouse âgée et une jeune fille de 14 ans, étaient seules à la maison, le père étant à une réunion de l'Eglise Methodiste au village. Le monstre, à forme humaine, s'introduit dans la maison par la fenêtre et veut s'emparer de la fille. la mère saisit une hache pour sauver son enfant, il la lui enleva et d'un premier coup lui fend la tête, mais ce n'est pas assez. la victime est morte, sa brutalité n'est pas satisfaite, de six autres coups de hache il lui sépare le coup par derrière, lui coupe la gorge, lui partage les deux machoires, lui déionce le coffre entre les épaules et pour couronner son œuvre diabolique d'un dernier coup il lui ouvre l'abdomen faisant sortir les entrailles de la bonne vieille femme. En ce qui regue, il est un acteur de accoupli. mais la fille, objet de sa convoitise charnelle et criminelle?—Quelle est son sort? Il la prend dans ses bras, l'emporte au bois voisin et après avoir de force assonvi sa passion déréglée et sans pareil, il la tue; lui aplatissant le craie d'un bâton qu'il avait pris sur une corde de bois qui était à toucher. Pendant ce temps le brave père de famille était resté à l'église; mais quel fut son étonnement à son retour chez lui; aussitôt l'alerte, les officiers sont avertis; avec une diligence qui leur fait honneur, ils se mettent à la recherche et vers sept heures du matin le misérable était logé dans la prison de paroisse. Nos officiers, cette à dire, le shérif G. B Shaw, et son député George E. Lyons l'avaient pris chez lui conché, les taches de sang qui convraient ses vêtements lavés unitilement, elles y étaient encore, tellement il est vrai que le meurtrier ne peut jamais se débarrasser du sang de sa victime, il le tient, le poursuit et est ineffacable. ATROCIOUS MURDER.
On the night of Friday the 12th instant a most atrocious murder was committed about two miles from Abbeville in our Parish. On that night Pine Henderson a worthy colored man of our Parish was attending church in the town and one William Epperson also. Henderson had left his wife and daughter aged about fourteen at home, Epperson more or less under the influence of liquor, it is said, left church long before Henderson, uttering the most vilest imprecations against the whole people, white and black. After church, Henderson returns home, his bed and floor covered with blood, his wife murdered in a most fiendish manner and his daughter upon whom he doted with more than ordinary parental affection missing. The neighbors are notified, the officers of the law likewise. To them the horrid and ghastly sight presents itself of the mother litterally butchered, having received with an axe a first blow that split the cranium and produced instantaneous death ; but not satisfied with this the hellish monster, in human form, had severed the neck from the body, but a small particle of flesh and skin, keeping the two together, chopped off one of the hands, cut the throat from ear to ear and with one last stroke cut open her abdomen exposing the entrails of the aged victim. She is dead, murdered but what has become of the daughter ? owing to the diligent search of our officers she was found in a neighboring wood a corpse, her head crushed, and bearing other marks of fiendish violence. The sheriff and his deputy after further research found the said Epperson in his house, in bed, but his clothes still red with his victims' blood. He was brought to town, by seven in the morning, he confessed his guilt with utter indifference. At about 12 M. a crowd of the most worthy citizens of our Parish, despite the powerless resistance of the officers took charge of the prisoner and in a short time he was launched into eternity. He to the last showed callous indifference, refusing anything like religious consolation showing no sign of repentance, and admitting that he fully deserved the punishment inflicted on him. ATROOIOUS ORIMES.
Besides the recent homicides committed in various parts of Louisiana, as detailed in our columns under the heading of State News Summary, two bloody affairs have occurred in the parishes of Vermilion and Pointe Coupée which call for more than mere passing mention among crimes of comparatively low degree.

The Pointe Coupée Banner reports that on the night of the 13th ult., a party of young ladies and gentlemen gathered at the residence of Mrs. J. B. Garon, on False river, to have a gumbo. A ball was given the same night by colored people in a house adjoining Mrs. Garon's, owned by Mr. David Johnson, and about 11 o'clock a fuss occurred there which disturbed the entire neighborhood. Mr. Johnson, accompanied by Mr. L. T. Chenvert and two or three others walked over to the ball room and informed the occupants that they must either preserve the peace or vacate the premises. As Mr. Johnson and his friends retired they were fired upon by the crowd of colored men who had congregated in front of the building. Mr. Chenvert was shot dead, and young Joseph Garon, who ran from his mother's house with a revolver upon hearing the firing, was severely wounded. Mr. Johnson ran to his house, got a double barreled shotgun and discharged both barrels, loaded with bird shot, at the assassins, who quickly dispersed, several having been wounded by the small shot. The affair created the most profound excitement throughout the parish; business was suspended in the vicinity of the tragedy and an organized pursuit of suspected persons instituted.
isn; business was suspended in the vicinity of the tragedy and an organized pursuit of suspected persons instituted. Sixteen colored men had been arrested when the Banner closed its report, but all save two were discharged by Judge Yoist after preliminary examination. The men held to answer the charge of murder are Val Dorval and Leopold Polite.

The Vermilion crime, the particulars of which we obtain from the Meridional, was still more revolting and atrocious. Friday night, the 12th ult., Wm. Epperson, a drunken, quarrelsome Negro, entered the house of Pine Henderson, one of the worthiest colored citizens of Vermilion, while the latter was absent at church, and murdered Henderson's wife and daughter in a fiendish manner, mutilating their bodies in a way horrible to think of. The mother was killed inside the house, but the body of the daughter, who had evidently fled from the premises and was overtaken by the murderer, was found in a neighboring wood, bearing marks of brutish and lustful violence, her head crushed by a blow as from a heavy stick or some kindred instrument. When Henderson returned home he summoned the Sheriff and a deputy and communicated his suspicion that Epperson had committed the crime. The fiend was arrested at his cabin, his clothing bearing blood-stains, and he confessed his guilt with stolid indifference. He was taken to jail, at Abbeville, about 7 o'clock next morning. At noon a crowd of citizens, white and colored, forced an entrance to the jail, brought the black-hearted murderer forth and hanged him to the nearest tree. The villain acknowledged the justice of his punishment and made no attempt to evade it.

Tragical Tales.
At Houston, Texas, on the 12th inst., Jack Dempsey, a wheelwright, was shot dead by W. A. Phillips, an express messenger, whom Dempsey attempted to kill at Henrietta.

John Taylor, a negro, who had grossly assaulted a white woman, was taken from Greenboro, N. C., jail and hanged on the night of the 12th, during the eclipse of the moon.

A stabbing affray occurred at Louisville, Ky., on the 11th inst., in which Mack Watson (colored) was killed.

Geo. C. Gattling, of San Francisco, stabbed his wife to death at a beer garden on the 10th inst.

Three masked men called J. E. Martin out of his house at Beiknap, Texas, on the 10th, and shot him dead.

Manly Ellis and Wight Newson, of Wilsom, N. C., both being in love with the same girl, quarreled on the 9th inst., when Ellis shot and killed Newson.

George Henderson, of McKeesport, Pa., while walking in the cemetary with a young lady, on the 7th inst., was set upon by a party of roughs and so badly beaten that he has since died.

Barry Corpenter shot and killed his brother, Lee Carpenter, fifteen miles west of New Albany, Ind., on the 9th inst. Barry, who is a low character, had been charged by Lee with seducing his own daughter.

At Soda Springs, five miles west of Leadville, Col., on the 9th inst., Otto Ballainx shot and killed a man named Andrews.

Louis Paxton, aged 19, was found in a field near St. Paul, Neb., on the 8th inst., with a rope around his neck and fastened to a plough handle, a bullet hole behind the right ear and the skull broken. His horses and wagon were gone. Vigilantes are in pursuit of the murderers.

Samuel D. Haines, serving a life sentence for murdering a guard, attempted to escape at Thomaston, Me., on the 8th inst., and was shot dead.

A difficulty occurred on the 8th inst., at Oak Bower, a small place near Fort Smith, Ark., between Thomas Ingraham and Andy Rhea, in the course of which Rhea was fatally wounded in the bowels.

An old man named Hull, living near Locksburg, Ark., was murdered in Sevier county, that state, by three negroes who were captured and hung by citizens. They confessed the deed before the final moment.

Two desperadoes named Knowles and Conners attacked Voorhees' store at Espanola, N. M., and shot the proprietor twice, probably fatally. A lynching party overtook the miscreants, shooting Knowles dead and lynching Conners.

Lewis Sweeden was assassinated while sitting on his porch in Van Buren county, Ark. It is whispered that he knew too much to suit certain "moonshiners."

In Stokes county, N. C., on the night of the 7th inst., Frank Baker, deputy sheriff, was shot and killed by Jesse Smith, for whom he had a warrant of arrest.

Charles D. Kidder, aged 35, traveling salesman for a Boston dry goods firm, was shot dead at Springfield, Mass., on the 6th inst., by his half-brother, D. Wright, aged 17.

A party of roughs attached to a circus attacked a dancing party at the village of Chesaning, Mich., on the night of the 7th. A policeman was pounded to death, and several persons were badly hurt.

A difficulty over a payment of 15 cents caused a man named Lee to stab fatally one Jennings, a negro, at Dolby Springs, Bowie county, Texas, on the 7th. Jenning's wife, who witnessed the fight, ran to her husband's aid, and with a hatchet fearfully mangled Lee. He is not expected to recover.

Wm. Murphy, the divorced husband of Mrs. N. McClarum, shot Mrs. McC. through the back, near Pittsburg, Pa., on the 7th, and then shot himself through the head. Mrs. McClarum will recover.

Capt. Costernaruff, a hero of the Crimean war, was shot and killed in the streets of Sebastapol by a retired colonel of the Russian army.

At a Joplin, Mo., variety theater on the 7th inst., a shooting affray was occasioned by a dispute in regard to terms of sale of the institution. C. F. Thompson, stage manager, and Thomas Carney, an employee, were killed.

Special to the Herald.
Graham, June 10.--J. E. Martin, a prominent merchant of Belknap, was called out of his residence, about 8 o'clock last night, by three unknown men, who led him off about a half mile and shot him to death. The men then proceeded to Mr. Martin's store and robbed it of all they could carry off. A furious storm was raining at the time, under cover of which the villains did their work. Sheriff Melt n, of this place, and several deputies started for Belknap this morning in search of the robbers.

The heaviest storm of the season burst upon us last night about 6 o'clock. It came from the northeast. Hall stones as large as pigeon's eggs fell, breaking a large number of windows. About three inches of rain fell in less than two hours.

leave their homes on account of threatened violence. The trouble originated in the prosecution, by order of Judge Harris, of two delinquent Deputy Sheriffs, Green Myers and James Isham. The Judge and the editor then received written notice through the Post-office to leave the town within fifteen days, under the penalty of death. They left. Judge Harris arrived at Little Rock and had an interview with the Governor, who promises him all the assistance needed to protect the lives of threatened parties and to maintain the law.

ANTHONY W. GARDNER has been elected President of Libería, and Rev. W. F. Russell, Vice-President. They are pledged to the education of the masses and numerous other needed reforms.

A PHILADELPHIA patent-lawyer, Mr. Connelly, is said to have received $250,000 from the Bell Telephone Company for a simple device, of his invention, by which a central telephone office can be done away with.

JOE FLINT, a notorious Chicago thief, received fatal injuries while trying to escape from two detectives at Kansas City, Mo. He was run over by a train which he attempted to board, both legs being severed.

HAYES WHITE, colored, the murderer of Sheriff Beattie, of Crittenden County, Ark., was hanged at Marion on the 10th.

A MAN named Herman and his son were killed by lightning near Baltimore, Md., on the 9th. Another had a thigh broken and several others were stunned by the shock.

A NUMBER of workmen were badly scalded by the explosion of a boiler near Pottsville, Pa., the other day, three of whom can not recover.

GEORGE C. GATLING, of San Francisco, Cal., suspecting his wife of infidelity, decoyed her into a beer garden and stabbed her to the heart.

A HANDSOME female burglar, aged 18 years, and named Frances Merch, has been captured by the Cincinnati police and locked up.

WEST POINT (N. Y.) graduates were addressed by President Garfield, Gen. Sherman, and Secretaries Hunt and Lincoln, on the 10th.

A DISPATCH from Halifax, N. S., says the Norwegian barque Mette Margoethe was wrecked off St. Paul's Island. The captain, first officer, carpenter, two seamen and a boy were drowned.

J. MARTIN, a merchant of Belknap, Tex., was called to the door of his residence by three men, seized and carried a short distance from the house and shot dead. After killing Martin they went to his store and ransacked it.

During the eclipse on the night of the 11th, about 200 men rode up to the Jail at Greensboro, N. C., and demanded the keys. The Jailer refusing to comply with their demands, they broke open the doors and seized John Taylor, a negro confined for an assault upon a white woman, whom they took off a distance of several miles and hanged to a tree.

Two brothers, Rub and Sidney Patrick, living near Golden, Colo., quarreled over the ownership of a dog. Sidney shot and instantly killed his brother. The murderer was arrested.

A BREAK in the Erie Canal, near Albion, N. Y., caused much damage on the 12th. The water flooded all that section, carrying away fences, bridges, etc., and working destruction in general. A woman and two children were saved by getting on a pig-pen, which floated about a mile before they were rescued.

Wm. Henry, Samuel Buckner and Peter Cook were fatally injured at Lafayette, Ind., the other day. They were tearing down the roof of the Court-house, when it fell.

The Italian exploring party which started from Assab Bay, Abyssinia, consisting of a subaltern officer, ten sailors and four soldiers, has been massacred in the interior.

A PASSENGER train on the Ohio & Mississippi Railway, at Vincennes, Ind., dashed into a wagon containing three men. James Bradley was seriously injured and the others badly bruised.

MISS LIZZIE HUTCHINSON and Miss Cox were killed and Mr. and Mrs. Hutchinson injured by lightning while driving near Archer City, Texas.

ANDREW D. ROBESON, nephew of ex-Secretary Robeson, of New Jersey, was killed by lightning near Hunnewell, Kans., on the 12th. His clothes were literally torn from his body, his watch-chained melted, and his face and body much torn.

REIMHEILER, the German who shot and robbed Al Angel, near Irish Grove, Mo., recently, was taken from Rockport Jail on the 10th by some twenty-five men and hanged.

A COLORED boy who was bitten by a spider, at Natchez, Miss., the other day, died soon after in great agony.

At Kingston, N. C., Quincy Gardiner and James Bryan engaged in a cutting affray which proved fatal to the former. They had taken up a quarrel begun by their wives, who were compelled to witness its sanguinary termination.

JOHN SCHSRALM, a prominent business man of Canton, Ohio, died on the 11th from paralysis of the stomach caused by drinking iced seltzer-water.
MR. ALFRED CRISWELL, a farmer residing near Raymond, Ill., was returning with his family from a meeting in town on the night of the 11th, when in crossing the track of the Wabash, St. Louis & Pacific Railroad his wagon was struck by the express train, running at a high rate of speed.

THREE MURDERS.
Under Arrest in a Texas Town and in Danger of Lynching.
GRAHAM, TEXAS, June 27.—Sheriff Milton has arrived and lodged in jail Pete McDonald, D. McDonald and Nick McDonald, who murdered Mr. Martin at Belknap and robbed his store. They were caught while asleep at the house of the father of two of them.

Goods they had with them were recognized as stolen goods and seven head of horses those as stolen in Grayson. A large number of people are here from Belknap and it is feared an attempt will be made to lynch the prisoners. Great excitement prevails.

A MURDERESS · HORRIBLY PUNISHED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., Sept. 10.—Information was received here tonight that Jane Campbell, a colored woman living near Dyko Mills, La., killed two children, aged respectively 10 and 12. The woman beat out their brains with a pino knot for some trivial net of disobedience. After the inquest, and when the cause of death became known, a mob of whites and blacks dragged Mrs. Campbell from her cabin, tied her to a stake, and, despite her screams, literally roasted her allye. The crime and punishment is without parallel in the criminal annual.

END OF A GREAT CASE.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

NEILLSVILLE, Wis., Sept. 10.—The jury in the Cochrane murder case, after being excluded for twenty-four hours, returned a verdict of not guilty. The immense crowd in the court-room received the verdict with voicerous cheers, which there was an effort to suppress, and Cochrane was immediately surrounded by congratulating friends, having to pass through a compact line of handshakers all the way from the court-room to his hotel. The verdict gives universal satisfaction here.

CONVICT RECAPTURED.

PORTLAND, Sept. 16.—This morning Edward Mordaunt, an escaped convict, who was supposed to have leaped overboard from the steamer Columbia below Astoria, was found stowed away in the vessel. Mordaunt, on being discovered, leaped into the river and attempted to swim ashore, was seized with cramps, and shouted for help. He was rescued and brought on board, when it was found that no hand broken off his shackles. He was sent to the Penitentiary at Salem today.

KILLED AT A WEDDING.
KANSAS CITY, Sept. 16.—At a wedding last night, during the dance, a party of roughs intruded. A row ensued, and Deroy Wiltfang, one of the gang, was shot in the head and killed by J. B. Jones, one of the guests. It is claimed that the shooting was done in self-defense. Jones and two others were arrested.

WEAVY BURGLARY.

BAY CITY, Mich., Sept. 10.—A successful gang of burglars have been operating for some time in this city. Last night they went through the storeroom of Busset, Seeds & Co., securing $1,500 worth of silks. There is no clue to the burglars.

THEIR GOWNS BETRAYED THEM.
Jennie Rollins and Jessie Robertson.

Jennie Rollins and Jessie Robertson are two disreputable young women who recently took up their abode in this city, having come from Ottawa, Ill. They were before Justice Wallace yesterday, charged with larceny, and were hold under bonds of $900 cash to the Criminal Court. The complainant against them was Henry Froiberg, of Peoria, a traveling rulesman. While in Ottawa not many weeks ago, he missed several handsome drowses which he was exhibiting as

samples. He had no idea as to where the garments had gone, and had given up all hope of recovering them. Day before yesterday, while walking on State street near Madison, he spied two women dressed in toggery which so nearly resembled that which he had lost, that his suspicions were aroused. "THE QUIET LEVEL."

Some Notable Attributions of President Garfield—Extracts from His Speeches Poculiarly Interesting at This Time.

To the Editor of The Chicago Tribune.

DAVENPORT, Ia., Sept. 14.—"From the quiet level of the deep all hights and depths are measured," said a most eminent citizen a little more than a year ago, and now the lips which uttered those memorable words are trembling with the whisperings of months of pain and sickness. And there are those who remember that the originator of those words has said many things not only worthy of passing notice, but also which offer food for almost an illimitable amount of thought. From the years of life in that lowly log cabin in the Ohio forest, and no doubt from the influences fostered in the young mind by that noble mother, has sprung a mind whose works shall go down in history as worthy of a place beside those of Washington and Lincoln; and how similar to the latter has been the life of James A. Garfield.

The widow Garfield had prayed that bright things might come through her "Jinnle," and had often talked with him about the noble life she wished him to lead, but it seemed almost hopeless when the boy left the little home for a life on the canal; but still the little mother hoped and prayed for her boy. James came near losing his life one night in the canal; he fell overboard, but as luck, or may be it was Providence, would have it, the rope which he held in his hand kinked and caught on the gunwale of the boat, thus saving the life which is now so important a one to all of us. While the boy was in the water he thought in a few seconds of a great deal of his past life, and when he climbed all dripping to the deck something prompted him to try and make the rope kink over the gunwale again; but we will let him tell what followed:

"I have thrown this rope six hundred times; I might have thrown it ten times six hundred without its catching; ten times six hundred are six thousand; so there were six thousand chances against my life. Against such odds Providence alone could have saved it. Providence, therefore, thinks it worth saving; and if that's so I won't throw it away on a canal-boat. I'll go home and got an education, and become a man."

We all know that our country has been better off for the salvation of that life; if in nothing else, it shows the chances which lay before the poorest and most lowly.

How well he made a man of himself he has shown in a thousand ways. It is needless to pass over the years of toll and struggle in obtaining his education, we have all heard of them; but after all the regular courses were passed, and only what schooling the world in the years of his future life could give him lay before him, he wrote one day:

"Again the path
Leads o'er the summit where the sunbeams fall,
And thus in light and shade, sunshine and gloom,
Sorrow and joy, this pathway leads along."

And twenty years after he fell on the "summit" midst the "sunbeams," pierced by the bullet of a wretch. In the midst of his success, at the highest pinnacle which a human being can reach in this world, he fell, and the hearts of fifty millions of people fell with him. No man over stood more in the universal love of the people, and when we look back along his pathway we see the reasons.

A BRUTAL OUTRAGE.

An Unnatural Mother Ruthlessly and Horrifically Dealt With.

LITTLE Rock, September 17.—News has been received of a tragic affair that occurred near Dyke's Mill, Louisiana, not far from the line of Columbia county in this State. A negro woman, named Jane Campbell, lived in the vicinity, supporting herself and two children by washing and cotton-picking. The other day she became angry with the children because they disobeyed her in some trivial matter, and, taking a pine knot, beat out their brains. Coroner Sykes held an inquest over the remains, the jury finding that the children came to their deaths from wounds caused by a club in the hands of an unnatural mother. After the verdict was announced, and the cause of the death of the two children became generally known, a mob, composed of blacks and whites, gathered, seized Mrs. Campbell, tied her to a stake and, despite her screams and cries for mercy, literally roasted her alive. The crime and punishment is without a parallel in the criminal annals of the history of this country.

LONDON EXHIBITION

Of Apparatus of All Kinds Devised to Prevent Smoke.

WASHINGTON, September 17.—The department is in receipt of a communication from the British legation at Washington relative to the exhibition to be held in London of apparatus of all kinds devised to prevent smoke. This exhibition will open October 21. The department has been further informed by the British Charge d'Affaires at Washington that the committee has decided to consider favorably all applications from foreign exhibitors throughout September, and they will as far as possible reserve space for late exhibits, so that none may be excluded up to the close of business.

Election of a Lady Librarian by the Trustees.

At a regular meeting of a the Board of Trustees of the Odd-Fellows Public Library last night considerable interest was manifested. The dues were reduced from five to three dollars for yearly membership, and the salary of the Librarian was fixed at twenty-five dollars per month. Two Odd-Fellows' widows were put in nomination, viz: Mrs. A. J. Wheeler and Mrs. John D. Adams, resulting in the election of the latter, to fill the unexpired term made vacant by the death of Major W. R. McClune. Now that a lady has been selected as Librarian, it is thought that new life will be infused and the library will become a popular resort for the reading public. New books are to be purchased and the library made as attractive as possible. It is earnestly hoped that the people of Memphis will give it a hearty support.

WILL YOU KISS ME?

A Female Asks an Officer This and Then Assaults Him.

Addie Stilker is one of the honest and respectable tenants of the Gayoso House. She is a young married woman, the wife of Joseph Stilker, and was recently run out of her room at the Gayoso by the fall of a part of that celebrated building. Last night Addie got considerably under the influence of liquor and was making herself rather noisy, when Private Policeman Joe Jones told her that she would have to be more quiet. At this she came up to him, and putting out her face, said: "Do you want to kiss me?" She came quite close to him and he pushed her back. At this she became very much enraged and made a quick plunge at Mr. Jones's long whiskers, making things rather uncomfortable for him. She was helped by her husband, and both were arrested on the ground of assault and battery. At the stationhouse, last night, Addie's language would have done credit to the famous women of Billingsgate.

From the Hub. A Horrible Crime.
On last Friday night, two negroes—Jim Taylor and Bob Green, went to the house of Col. Jas. Irwin during his absence and committed a horrible outrage upon the person of Mrs. Irwin. The negroes went to the house for the purpose of outraging a step-daughter of Col. Irwin, but she was absent at Reidsville with her step-father (Col. Irwin), and these two devils assaulted Mrs. Irwin, a lady nearly 50 years of age. Both of the negroes were arrested and carried to Reidsville, and during the trial confessed their guilt, and were committed to jail at Wentworth. A party was organized to lynch the rascals, but Sheriff Johnson took the negro Taylor, the negro who committed the outrage, and hurried to Kernersville, where he took the train and carried him to Greensboro and lodged him in jail at that place. During the night a party went to Wentworth and forced the jail, but when they found that Taylor was gone the left without molesting the other prisoner, and went in pursuit of the Sheriff and Taylor, but unfortunately failed to come up with them.

The victim of this outrage is a neice of our townsman, Maj. Ham Scales, and is also related to Capt. Grogan and Mr. Peter Dalton, and is a lady of great respectability and much loved in the community in which she lives. The courts should not be bothered with her outragers.
john-taylor-wentworth-1881-06-05.A3:
The Horrible Outrage near Reidsville, N. C.
On Friday night last, near the town of Reidsville, Rockingham county, between the hours of 9 and 10 o'clock, two negroes, John Taylor and George Gunn, in the employ of Col. James Irwin, as farm hands, during the absence of their employer and his daughter, went to the house of Col. Irwin and finding Mrs. Irwin alone with her little son, entered the house. From what we are told it was a premeditated affair. The negroes went to Col. Irwin's not to assault or injure Mrs. Irwin, but the young lady who had accompanied her father to Reidsville. Bent on crime, however, Taylor then assaulted Mrs. Irwin. Notwithstanding the resistance made and the cries of the poor, unprotected victim, Taylor accomplished his purpose. Gunn, the other negro, it is said, made no assault upon Mrs. Irwin. He was present, however, and witnessed the hellish act. The negroes then left the premises and went over to Reidsville. Mrs. Irwin immediately went to a neighbor's house.

On Saturday about noon Taylor and Gunn were arrested and taken before a Justice at Reidsville, and during the trial confessed their guilt. The crowd which had assembled, became indignant and at one time lynching was freely talked of. The parties were committed to Jail at Wentworth. No effort was made to lynch them on the way to Jail, but on Saturday evening, it is reported, a number of gentlemen organized a lynching party. It appears that no attempt was made and Taylor and Gunn remained in Jail until Sunday night. During the afternoon of Sunday the Sheriff of Rockingham received information that another party had been organized and that an attempt would be made to take the negroes from the Jail Sunday night and hang them. Anticipating such an event, Sheriff Johnston took charge of John Taylor, the negro who actually committed the horrible deed, and moved off in the direction of Danville, Va. Gunn was left in the Jail at Wentworth. During the night a party of men went to Wentworth, and on reaching the Jail demanded the keys from the Jailor, but were refused. The next thing was to force the Jail doors, which was done, but when it was ascertained that Taylor was gone, the party left and went in pursuit of the fleeing Sheriff and his prisoner. Sheriff Johnston, in order to elude the pursuing party, changed his route and moved in the direction of Kernersville, in Forsythe county. Mr. O. C. Wheeler, the Jailor of Guilford county, met Sheriff Johnston at the depot, took charge of Taylor and conducted him to the county Jail, where he was confined in one of the cells.

Taylor is 22 years of age, weighs about 140 pounds, seems to be in excellent health, and although he is considerably excited, talks freely about the affair. He says, however, that Gunn is the guilty man; that he accompanied him to a point near the residence of Col. Irwin and then stopped. He heard the cries of Mrs. Irwin but was atraid to go to the house. He says that Gunn had frequently threatened to kill him.
but was afraid to go to the house. He says that Gunn had frequently threatened to kill him (Taylor.) He acknowledges the fact that he and Gunn were to go together and commit the crime with which they stand charged.

Mrs. Irwin is suffering considerably from the attack upon her. The good people of Reidsville seemed determined to mete out quick justice upon the guilty wretches. Rockingham Superior Court is now in session and it may be that these devils in human form can be tried this week. The people of this entire section sympathize with Col. Irwin and his estimable wife. No more worthy or highly esteemed citizens live in Rockingham county. Mrs. Irwin is said to be about 40 years of age, and is greatly beloved by the citizens of Reidsville and the immediate neighborhood, for her noble qualities.

In addition to the above the Raleigh Observer says: "A gentleman informs us that on Monday night a large party of armed men rode into Greensboro to take the negro fiend from the jail there, but he was taken away by the Sheriff and escaped death then."

VIRGINIA VIGILANTES
Break Open the Jail at Greensboro, Secure a Negro Prisoner and Hang Him.
DANVILLE, VA., June 12.—During the eclipse of the moon last night, John Taylor, a negro who had grossly assaulted a white woman, was taken from the Greensboro jail and hanged. A large number of persons visited the scene of the lynching to day. The lynchers numbered about two hundred, and upon the refusal of the jailer to deliver the keys of the jail they tore down the fence, broke open the jail doors and overpowering the guard, took the keys and entered. They unshackeled the negro and brought him to the buggy in waiting. The crowd then rode off at a swift gallop, and at a point seven miles south of Reidsville, Rockingham county, N. C., the negro was hanged. The afair was so unexpected and so quietly done that it was not generally known in Greensboro till all was over.

DEAD AND DONE FOR! DECENTLY AND IN ORDER!
Thus be it Unto all of his Kind!
DEAD AND DONE FOR! DECENTLY AND IN ORDER!

Thus be it Unto all of his Kind!

John Taylor, the African brute, who outraged an aged and honorable white lady, near Reidsville, Rockingham county, has been hanged until dead, and dumped into the soil at the foot of his gallows-tree.

It will be remembered that some ten days ago, Col. James Irwin, a well known citizen of Rockingham, carried his daughter, (a former pupil of the B. F. Seminary in Raleigh,) to attend a concert in Reidsville. Two negroes took the coach horses, and galloped back to the Irwin plantation; apparently unaware that Miss Irwin had come to town with her father. At least it is said they went to the house with hellish designs upon the daughter. The mother, a lady of near 50 years of age, suspecting no ill, sat at home until seized by the two villains. When she recovered consciousness she fled across the fields to the nearest neighbors giving the alarm; then fell fainting, and has been at death's door ever since, if not already dead at this writing.

The two brutes, John Taylor and Geo. Gunn, were soon in jail, and as the country aroused the sturdy farmers flocked in with fixed resolve to give that "short thrift" which is the only real deterrent in punishment. There being some doubt in the case of Gunn, he was allowed the benefit of a regular trial, and now lies in Rockingham jail, free from any danger of lynching. This is right. But there was no possibility of mistake in Taylor's case; therefore he should have gone to the gallows within twenty-four hours after his crime.

Unfortunately the Sheriff being a sworn officer, felt it his duty to save the prisoner for the formalities of the law; consequently took Taylor in his buggy, and fled through by-roads to Greensboro, 40 miles distant. Judge Lynch followed him, thither, but failing to find him, dispersed, until Saturday night last.

RETRIBUTION.

About 11 p. m on Saturday a body of 50 or 60 horsemen entered Greensboro, and being refused the jail keys, cut through three heavy doors, and found Taylor chained to the floor. In half an hour, the cavalcade marched out of town, in military order, carrying the mulatto tied to the back of a buggy. The latter realized his doom; but acted in sullen stolidness, as he has done from the first, refusing to affirm or deny his guilt. To a by-stander in Greensboro he said that all he wanted was to go to Heaven! (Every negro murderer adopts the same tune; and really seems to think he will have nothing to do but step off the gallows into the arms of the angels!)

Seven miles from Reidsville, the lynchers received word that Mrs. Irwin was too ill to permit of any commotion passing the house; therefore the procession halted by the road-side; and Taylor was placed upon the back of the horse he had ridden to do his crime. Being asked if he had anything to say,—he responded sullenly—"Get it over quick!" A sharp switch sent the horse from under him and he fell six feet, breaking his neck. This was about 4 a. m. on Sunday morning.

The news had gone abroad, and from far and near, came the country people, white and black, of all ages, to view the dangling ravisher. Towards evening the coroner appeared, and held inquest. Then the corpse was buried where it lay.

We have no regrets for the lynching,—May we commend it in all except two particulars: viz the delay, and the waving of handkerchiefs by women as the lynchers passed. Judge Lynch should always act calmly, quietly, even solemnly, as if fully conscious that he is usurping the office of the law, but not through passion, sudden feeling, or any other impulse than the grave necessity of Nature's Higher Law,—self-preservation. We repeat that we regret the delay, because the real object of Lynch Court is to set the seal of swift and sure retribution on certain foul crimes! Vengeance should follow within one hour after there is no longer a doubt of guilt. The lynchers should organize a jury and if any three or four intelligent gentlemen will assert doubts as to the prisoner's guilt, let him be remanded to jail to await formal trial. But where there is no possibility of mistake, the ravisher, whether white or black (and we should be more merciful to a negro than a white man, because he has fewer moral and educational influences to restrain his brutalusts)—the ravisher, we say, should be strapped, on his knees, to a stake; and the nearest male relative of the injured woman should be called upon to blow out his brains. Then a pile of stones and dirt should be heaped upon the godden corpse, and all men disperse to their homes.

Ah! have you ever thought what a "home" that must be, to which all eyes are turning as the scene of outrageous violence done to a gentle woman!

Conceive, if you can, a fate more horrible for a delicate and pure hearted girl, on the threshold of life, blushing with the rosy tints of maidenhood, per chance of "Love's Young Dream,"—suddenly, in one black hour, struck down and crushed like a trampled lily-lower, trampled and withered, and stained, through no fault of her own; zoomed to drag the lengthening chain of many weary years,—until the grave rings oblivion to the dreadful recollection—ever present, asleep and awake,—of that sudden assault, the vain cries or help, the fainting struggle against brutal strength, the wild alarm, the rocking of cruelly curious crowds, theaggerated details, the columns of newspaper reports, with her name hunted to the four corners of earth! THE SOUTH.
North Carolina.
Hanged by Masked Men—A Woman's Brutal Assailant Punished.
REIDSVILLE, June 15.—Shortly before 11 o'clock Monday night a band of masked men, about sixty in number, silently entered the city of Greensboro, N. C., proceeded to the custodians of the jail and demanded possession of the negro John Taylor, who, on the night of the 3d instant, brutally assaulted the wife of Colonel James Irvine, late State Senator and one of the most prominent citizens of Rockingham county, N. C. Their demands being unheeded they, by means of sledges and other implements, quickly forced an entrance through three strongly bolted doors into th- prisoner's cell, severed the chains that bound him to the floor, and in a few minutes appeared on the street with their guilt-confessed captive securely bound. They then placed him in a suitable conveyance, mounted their horses and silently departed. Yesterday morning at daylight John Taylor's body was hanging from a tree, near troublesome old ironworks, about seven miles south-west of Reidville there to await the coroner's inquest as to the manner of his taking off.
john-taylor-wentworth-1881-06-05.A17:
Speedy Punishment.
The negro man who committed rape upon Mrs. Irwin last week near Reidsville, met with speedy punishment from the hands of the outraged people of Rockingham county. He was taken from the Jail at Greensboro on Saturday night last and hanged in Rockingham county on Sunday morning. The Greensboro "Battle Ground" gives the following short account of the affair:

"Saturday night at 10 o'clock a body of men met at a rendezvous about five miles north of Greensboro, and entered the city about 11 o'clock, and went direct to the city prison and demanded the person of John Taylor, the mulatto, who, about a week ago, outraged Mrs. Irwin, a highly respectable lady near Reidsville, in such a shocking and horrible manner. Mr Wheeler refused the keys, and as they had come prepared, they produced sledges and chisels and cut their way into the prison. They cut through three doors, each door having three heavy and massive locks. Taylor was also chained to the floor. At 11.20 they succeeded in getting into the cell, and he was tied hand and foot, and at 11.30 they emerged from the Jail, bringing him with them. He was placed in a buggy that was waiting at the gate. He was tied to the back of the buggy, and the crowd moved off in the direction of Reidsville. As they prepared to leave the city, the order was given by the leader to form in twos and be prepared for action in case they were fired into. They stated that they would hang him to a telegraph pole in Reidsville, provided they could arrive there before daylight; in case they were delayed, he would be hung to the first tree after they crossed the Guilford line. It was a determined set of men and the negro seemed to know his time had come and said he wanted to go to heaven. [Of course every negro criminal is led to believe that he is going to heaven if he is hanged.] Some one in the crowd told him that he now had a chance to say his last words, he replied that he had no statement to make. It is said that there were over two hundred men in the body.

It was evidently a pre-arranged affair, and must have occupied much of the time of the leaders who organized the movement. We are not prepared to say if any Greensboro men were in the party, but we think the general impression is that they were all citizens of Rockingham county."

When first arrested the negro confessed his guilt. It is stated that the colored people of that section express the opinion that Taylor got his just deserts.

[From the News and Observer.]
TAYLOR, THE NEGRO RAPE
FIEND, LYNCHED.
HANGED BY A BODY OF MASKED MEN—SPEEDY LETTIBUTION.

The notorious criminal, John Taylor, the negro who last week so brutally outraged Mrs Irwin, an elderly lady of Reidsville, on Sunday paid the penalty of his horrible crime, being hanged by a great party of lynchers, who took him from the jail at Greensboro Saturday night.

About fifty or sixty persons left Greensboro with Taylor, while a dozen ladies waved their handkerchiefs from the windows as the procession passed by. At 4 o'clock Sunday morning the party reached a point seven miles from Reidsville, when they stopped and swung up the prisoner to an oak limb. He (Taylor) was stubborn and sullen to the last, and he said little or nothing.

All day long the body swung there, until, the rope relaxing somewhat, the feet touched the ground. The scene was visited by very large and curious crowds of excursionists, both white and colored. These came from far and near, in every imaginable kind of vehicle, and on foot.

Late in the evening the coroner made his appearance and had the body cut down. A jury was empaneled and at once rendered a verdict that the deceased, John Taylor, had been hanged by unknown parties. The body was not molested. Taylor was hanged just as the law hangs criminals. He was assisted up to the limb of the tree by being mounted on the back of the same gray horse which he had ridden from Reidsville to the home of the lady, to commit the rape.

Jupe Billard, colored, was secured to inter the body, and placed it in a grave right at the foot of the oak on which it had swung. The county paid $4 for the interment. The county people agree that the lynching was right. T. C. E.

The San Francisco Board of Trade have adopted the report of its Committee on Immigration, and passed resolutions asking California's Representative in Congress "to urge the survey of all unsurveyed lands in the State, and to obtain the passage of a Chinese restriction law, and of the act providing for civil government in Alaska. “Governor’s Day” at the Atlanta exposition brought a great crowd to the grounds. The visiting governors were formally welcomed to the exposition at 2 o’clock. The contractors who are constructing the New-York, Ontario and Western Railroad are endeavoring to lessen the expense by securing cheaper labor than that of the Irishmen and Italians now employed. It is said that on the Middletown Branch, which covers a section of twenty-five miles, 300 negroes are now employed at $1.25 a day. It was rumored yesterday among the white laborers on other sections that a large force of negroes was on the way from Maryland and the District of Columbia to replace them. It has been resolved to hold a meeting at Middletown to protest against the action of the contractors.

middletown-middletown-1881-08-05.A3:
NEGRO LABORERS.
NEW YORK, Aug. 5.—The announcement that a large number of negroes are on their way from the South to work on the New York, Ontario & Western Railroad has created great excitement among the men now employed by the contractors in the different sections. Thus far none have been engaged for Section No. 1, which commences at the west end of the new tunnel at Guttenberg and extends twenty-five miles, but on the Middletown branch, which embraces five sections, a distance of twenty-five miles, over 300 negroes are employed. They are employed in the gravel banks and rock cuts of the highlands and work at the low rate of $1.25 a day. One contractor, who holds a sub-contract from Douglass for building five miles of the Middletown section, has refused to employ any negroes, and has engaged only Irish and Italians. Another contractor on Section No. 1 announces his determination to bring on the colored men at all hazards, justifying his action on the ground that he can obtain a uniform rate of $1.25 a day, and that he can obtain 1,000 or more negroes, whereas the white laborers refuse to work at such a low rate.

THE NEGROES NOW EMPLOYED came mostly from Maryland and the District of Columbia, from which district another contingent is expected to arrive next week. The reports in regard to the number expected seems to have been so exaggerated that a meeting of the white laborers has been called for next Sunday, at Middletown, to protest against further importations. If a leaf ear be turned to their protest by the contractors a strike will certainly result, and serious trouble is expected. The contractors do not seem to be deterred by these threats, however, and what the end will be it is difficult to foresee.
middletown-middletown-1881-08-05.A4:
LABOR TROUBLES AT MIDDLETOWN.
The excitement among the white laborers of the
The excitement among the white laborers of the New-York, Ontario and Western Railroad over the proposed action of the contractors to substitute colored men at $1 25 a day in the places of the Irishmen and Italians now employed at $1 60 a day, continues, and the feeling of the men has become intense. The negroes who, it is said, are on their way from the South to be put to work on section No. 1, have not yet arrived, and the laborers on that part of the road expect that at the meeting to-day in Middletown the action of the white men will be decided upon. The 300 negroes now employed on the Middletown branch do not intend to be frightened by the threats of the white men, for they claim that they have rights which they will contend for in any emergency that may occur.

It is expected that the action taken at the meeting at Middletown to-day will determine the course of the men in case the threatened invasion of negroes takes place.

In conversation with a TRIBUNE reporter, one of the laborers on section No. 1 said that the men proposed to wait patiently until the meeting at Middletown to-day was held, unless the colored men should arrive in the meantime. What action will be taken is not now definitely known; much depends upon circumstances. Many of the men are in favor of sending a petition to Mr. Tilden, who is a large stockholder in the road, asking him to interest himself in their cause. There is one thing certain, the men say, and that is that they will not remain at work as the Middletown men have done, if the negroes are brought there; the whole matter is a scheme to reduce their wages to $1 25 a day.
middletown-middletown-1881-08-05.A5:
No Strike on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad. MIDDLETOWN, N. Y., Aug. 6.—The rumor that a strike of white laborers at work on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad, near this city, is imminent, on account of the employment of gangs of colored laborers from Maryland and the District of Columbia, was exaggerated by the reports in yesterday's newspapers. The negroes are at work, about a hundred in number, near Cornwall-on-the-Hudson, at $1.25 a day. Near this city are about sixty white men working for $1.50 a day, while a gang of Italians are at work between Cornwall and this city at $1 and a loaf of bread a day. The rumor that there would be a strike arose from the change of sub-contractors on a section of the road nearest to the city. The new sub-contractor, Mr. King, came from building the Shenandoah Valley Railroad, where negroes are employed. There is to be no indignation of white laborers here to-morrow, as has been rumored. KINGSTON, N. Y., Aug. 6.—A short time ago William Gillander of Quaker Hill, Delaware County, sued James Williamson for abducting his daughter, claiming damages in the sum of $2,000. middletown-middletown-1881-08-05.A6:
Competitive Labor in New York.
New York, Aug. 6.—The white laborers employed in the construction of the New York, Ontario and Western railroad, are much excited over the rumor that the contractors intend to bring from the south a large number of negro laborers, who can be obtained for $1.25 per day, while the white men have been receiving $1.60. Three hundred negroes are already at work on the Middleton branch. They are from Maryland and the District of Columbia, and have formed a curious colony by themselves. They all mess together, and it is said that their board, washing and mending never exceeds $10 a month per man. They live on ham and bacon, with fresh meat once a week. Their evenings are spent in singing and dancing, and every Sunday a regular religious revival is held, which attracts large crowds from the surrounding country. The white laborers say their whole object is to gradually cut down the wages to $1.25 a day, the amount for which the negroes are willing to work; that it was bad enough to be ground down to the level of Italian laborers, but this new move is something too much for patient endurance.
