middletown-middletown-1881-08-05.A8:
THE LABORERS AT MIDDLETOWN. The condition of the laborers, on the New-Yo
The condition of the laborers on the New-York, Ontario and Western Railroad, is now much quieter than was anticipated from the reports which reached this city from Middletown, of intended violence in case negroes from the South were put to work in the places of the Irish and Italians now employed. On the first twenty-five-mile division, which includes five sections, no negroes are employed; on the extreme western part of the division native laborers from Middletown are doing the work and on the rest of the division five or six hundred Italians are employed. They are paid $1.25 a day, while the Irishmen receive $1.50 a day. On the next division, this side of Cornwall-on-the-Hudson, a gang of about forty negroes is employed by the contractors, McLaughlin and Riley, who brought 130 negroes from Baltimore and Washington June 1, most of whom have since returned to the South. Donglass and Graves, the contractors of the Middletown division, say that they are now working five or six hundred men, nearly all Italians, and will today have two hundred and fifty more. They will procure white labor if they can, but if they cannot, an effort will be made to get negroes, who, they say, can do more work than the Italians. No white men will be discharged to make room for the negroes. The colored laborers at Cornwall receive $1.25 a day in gravel, and $1.50 a day in rock work. Whether the contractors on the eastern divisions contemplate bringing negroes from the South could not be learned yesterday. Most of them speak highly of them as laborers, and say that if they cannot get white labor they will send for negroes.
middletown-middletown-1881-08-05.A9:
COLORED RAILROAD HANDS. MEN OF VARIOUS RACES PEACEFULLY WORKING IN ORANGE COUNTY.
Colored Men from the South brought on to Supply an Unfilled Demand on a Branch of the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad.

MIDDLETOWN, N. Y., Aug. 7.—Further investigation to-day of the rumors that a strike was intended by laborers near here on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad, because negro laborers in large numbers have been brought from the South, and more are coming, proves beyond a doubt that not only is there no strike, but also that none is anticipated. The reason why no disturbance is looked for is that the contractors are engaging all the workmen they can get in this vicinity, and also have agents in New York city who hire men and send them to work on the railroad between this city and the Hudson River. Even after these efforts to get help, the contractors lament that they no not have laborers enough. This raking and scraping the whole country round about us for day laborers has resulted in bringing together several races. In fact, Orange County was never so cosmopolitan as this summer.

The work on the projected railroads is in such a condition that the different races are brought closer together than they will probably be when the roadbed is graded. They do not, however, come into actual daily and social contact, but they live each in their own neighborhoods. The two large railroad enterprises to connect New York city with the West, by way of Buffalo and Lake Ontario, were begun in June last, and the most active operations are being carried on in this vicinity. One is the New York, Lake Shore and Buffalo Railroad, and the other the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad. The former is to run from Weehawken nearly to Albany, and then across the State to Buffalo. The New York, Ontario and Western is to run from Jersey City to Ontario, N. Y., and the two roads approach within twenty-five miles of each other at this point. They are to be connected by a branch railroad from Cornwall to this city, and it is on this branch that it was rumored that the strike was threatened.

The contractors for this 25-mile branch are Messrs. W. A. Douglas and Graves, and their headquarters are at Cornwall. Both Mr. Douglas and Mr. Graves said to your correspondent to-day that there was nothing but harmony among the workmen. Mr. Graves went on to explain that nearly 600 Italians are at work on the Cornwall end of the branch, while less than a hundred laborers, mostly Irishmen and residents of this section, were at work on the western end of the road. The section of five miles next to this city, Mr. Graves continued, was sublet last week to Contractors Evans and Ackerman of Binghamton. Mr. D'Arcy has been the contractor up to the present time, and the change of contractors may have aroused the fears of some of the Middletown laborers that the whole work is hereafter to be done by negro labor brought from the South. "The fact is," said Mr. Graves, "I asked Messrs. Evans and Ackerman what workmen they were to employ, and they said positively that Italians were to be brought to work. They are now using Italian labor in Binghamton.

"The negroes are at work on another part of the work from the Italians, Irish, and Yankees," continued the contractor. "They are blasting in the solid rock on the river front at Cornwall, on the projected main line from Weehawken. Good workmen they are, too. They are quicker in accomplishing work than white men, and far superior to the Italians. I account for it by their singing at their work. They work under Contractors McLaughlin and Riley, and they receive the same wages that the white men do. In removing earth they get $1.25 a day, but when they handle rock they get $1.50 a day. Very shrewd they are, too. When they are digging earth sometimes the grading has to be done through deep cuts. All about this hilly country the earth is full of stones as big as your hat, or much larger.

"Well, Pomp." I will sometimes say to one, 'how does it go?' He will straighten himself up and say, with a twinkle in his eyes:

"Well 'nuf, boss, on'y a dolla' 'n a qua'tah ain't 'nuf for dis yer kin' o' wuk. Luk o dat dar rock now,' kicking one over with his foot. 'doan you tink we's a wukin' in rock wuk; a dolla' 'n a 'af ain't none too much for rockwuk."

"You see, down South the negroes don't know anything about stones. Rocks is the term by which all kinds and sizes of stones go. About 160 negroes were first brought here from Washington and Baltimore in June. About half of these have deserted and gone to work on farms hereabouts. After work they go about in groups and sing Southern plantation songs and pick up coppers. No; I do not know that they have any camp meeting services or preaching on Sunday or any of the other characteristic goings on of their race. They like to lie out in the sun and sleep when off duty or on Sundays."

The Italians live in shanties along the line of the branch railroad and in two or three frame houses on the main line north of Cornwall, while the negroes live in houses in Cornwall and work south of that place. The Italians are supplied with rye bread by Louis Canterbury, who has a bakery looking out on the Hudson River. Louis is the Italian who transported a large force of Italians to Cape Cod not long ago to dig a canal, and was forced to bring them back to New York at a loss. Yesterday Louis said that he lost $5,000 by the operation, as he had to pay the men their wages. The banks of the river were made picturesque yesterday by half a dozen Italian women with their skirts tucked about them, red handkerchiefs on their heads, and standing with the water half way up to their brown knees, while they pounded and scrubbed their consorts' linen on the rocks.
middletown-middletown-1881-08-05.A10:
TROUBLE ENDED FOR THE PRESENT.
It is now thought that if the contractors on th
It is now thought that if the contractors on the New-York, Ontario and Western Railroad had decided to bring negroes from the South to replace the white laborers in grading the road, they have abandoned the scheme on account of the hostility of the Irishmen and Italians to the colored men. The contractors now disclaim any intention of putting negroes to work at present; when cold weather comes, said one of them yesterday, the Italians will doubtless quit work; then we shall have to get colored laborers to fill their places. middletown-middletown-1881-08-05.A11:
COLORED LABORERS.
EXCITEMENT OVER THEIR EMPLOYMENT AS RAILROAD LABORERS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

New York, Aug. 11.—The excitement in regard to the employment of cheap colored labor by the contractors on the New York, Ontario & Western Railroad has not only not abated, but work has been actually suspended on some sections of the line north of Cornwall. Supplies which were ordered from this city for the use of the workmen have been countermanded. On the sections south of Cornwall the colored men are progressing steadily with their work at the fixed rate of $1.25 per day. The contractors show no disposition to yield to the

PROTESTS OF THE WHITE LABORERS, and the Directors of the railroad company have refused to interfere on the ground that the contractors are bound in heavy securities for the completion of their work and are not responsible to the Company for the means they may employ in constructing the road, provided the work be properly done. The action of the white laborers has had the effect of preventing the importation of colored men to the sections between Guttonberg and the terminus of the fifth section, but on the Middletown Branch, embracing five sections, a distance of twenty-five miles, the negroes are still retained.

LONGVIEW, October 17—We are permitted to condense the following from a special report sent to the Longview Democrat: The most horrible crime ever committed in this part of Texas was perpetrated last Wednesday, near Breckville, by a family of negroes named White. A family named Sloan had recently moved into the neighborhood to pick cotton on the farm of a Mr. Hill. A dispute between the Sloans, and a negro, Lum White, because of an accusation made by Lum that the Sloon children had been grabbing peanuts from the hills of Lum's patch. Lum went to the house of Sloan on Tuesday, and wanted to whip the children, but was prevented by Mrs. Sloan and her daughter, about fifteen years of age. For this he swore revenge, and next morning upon the plea that he would show her where some fine muscadines were the wife of Lum enticed the girl to a deep ravine, a secluded spot, where Lum was in waiting. While his wife held the girl Lum outraged her, and then using his pocket-knife, cut her bowels open both lengthways and crosswise, deliberately cutting off pieces of the entrails as they protuded, and scattered the fragments far and near. He then cut the girl's throat from ear to ear and left her body. When found at the inquest the woman confessed to all of the revolting details, when a young man named Hart, incesed at this cool recital of fendish brutality, shot the negro dead. The wife of Lum and an old negro who lived with them were started on their way to Carthage, but a crowd of men met the escort and took the prisoners and shot them.

LONGVIEW, TEXAS, October 19.—The most horrible crime ever committed in Texas was perpetrated last Wednesday, near Brockville, by a family of negroes named White. A family named Sloan had recently moved into the neighborhood to pick cotton on the farm of Mr. Hill. A dispute arose between the Sloans and a negro, Lum White, because of an accusation made by Lum that the Sloan children had been grabbling peanuts from Lum's patch. Lum went to the house of Sloan on Tuesday, and wanted to whip the children, but was prevented by Mrs. Sloan and her daughter, about fifteen years of age. For this he swore revenge, and next morning, upon the plea that she would show her where some fine muscadines were, the wife of Lum enticed the girl to a deep ravine, where Lum was in waiting. While his wife held the girl, Lum outraged her, and then using his pocketknife cut her bowels open, both lengthwise and crosswise, deliberately cutting off pieces of the entrails as they protruded, and scattered the fragments far and near. He then cut the girl's throat and left the body where it was found. At the inquest the woman confessed to all the revolting details, when a young man named Hart, incensed at the recital of fiendish brutality, shot the negro man dead. MET HIS DEATH

While Resisting an Officer—An Alleged Alabama Murderer.

Yesterday's Press contained a short report of the killing of one Burrell Poole, in Lincoln county. From Deputy-Sheriff Victor Waldstein, who has been actively engaged for some months in working up this case, we learn the following additional particulars: In 1870, in Pickens county, Alabama, Burrell Poole waylaid and killed the Tax Collector of that county, whose name was Mustin, while the latter was riding in a buggy attending to his official dutier, and it is believed, robbed the dead body of $3000 in money. It is known that Poole could have had no other incentive for the crime than that of robbery. W. S. Mustin, a son of the murdered man, who now resides at Columbus, Mississippi, tracked the murderer of his father to Louisiana, and from there into southeast Arkansas. Poole, in the meantime, had located in Lincoln county, and from some cause took sudden alarm and fled, leaving his wife and children, and his whereabouts until very recently was unknown. Upon losing all trace of Poole, the son of the murdered man turned the matter over to Mr. Victor Waldstein, furnishing him with a description of Poole and a requisition from the Governor of Alabama for the arrest of the murderer. For several months, after patiently watching the house where Poole's family lived, Mr. Cunningham, who was authorized by Deputy-Sheriff Waldstein to watch Poole, came to town and reported that Poole was loitering about in the neighborhood of Palmyra. Waldstein gave Cunningham orders to watch and spot Poole until he could get there. By some means Cunningham found out that Poole was fixing to leave the vicinity, and he deputized a man named Felley, who was intimate with and enjoyed the full confidence of Poole. Last Thursday morning Felley approached Poole in the corn crib, while Cunningham secreted himself near by, and Poole being some distance from his shot-gun and pistol, which he always carried, Felley went up very close and spoke in a friendly tone. Seeing that Poole was off his guard and unarmed, Felley pointed his shot-gun at Poole and said: "Mr. Poole, you are my prisoner; I arrest you for murder committed in Alabama." Whereupon Poole instantly sprang at Felley and attempted to wrench the gun fr in his grasp, saying: "I'll be d—d if I surrender. I will die before I'll go back to Alabama." The Worst Crime Yet Told—Indiscriminate Lynching. [Special to the Galveston News.]
Longview, Oct. 17.—We are permitted to condense the following from a special report sent to the Longview Democrat: The most horrible crime ever committed in this part of Texas was perpetrated last Wednesday near Lueckville, by a family of negroes named Lum. A white family named Sloan had recently moved into the neighborhood to pick cotton on the farm of a Mr. Hill. A dispute arose between the Sloans and the negroes Lum, because of an accusation made by Lum that the Sloan children had been grubbing peanuts from the hills of Lum's patch. Lum went to the house of Sloan on Tuesday and wanted to whip the children, but was prevented by Mrs. Sloan and her daughter, about fifteen years of age. For this he swore revenge, and next morning, upon the plea that she would show her where some fine muscadines were, the wife of Lum enticed the girl to a deep ravine, a secluded spot, where Lum was in waiting, and while his wife held the girl Lum outraged her, and then, using his pocket knife, cut her bowels open, both lengthwise and crosswise, deliberately cutting off pieces of the entrails as they prowled, and scattered the fragments far and near. He then cut the girl's throat from ear to ear, and left the body where found. At the inquest the woman confessed to all these revolting details, when a young man named Hart, incensed at the cool recitation of fiendish brutality, shot the negro dead. The wife and an old negro who lived with them were started on their way to Courney, but a crowd of men met the escort, took the prisoners and shot them.

Tom Herbert, a discharged employee, was arrested and charged with the murder. On the night of the 18th inst., Deputy Sheriff Ben Mitchell was killed while defending Herbert from a mob. A man supposed to be Tim Carby, was mortally wounded.

Near Breckner, Texas, on the 12th, a horrible outrage was committed by a family of negroes, who were visited with swift and terrible vengeance by an enraged community. It seems that a quarrel has existed between a family named Sloan and a negro named Lum. On the 12th inst., Mrs. Lum enticed Miss Sloan, aged 15, to a deep ravine where her husband was in waiting. MAGISTATE COMINGS' COURT.

GONE OFF WITH A HANDSOME MAN Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. MILWAUKEE, Wis., June 13.—A farmer named P. Peckhard, resesiding in Milwaukee County, came into the city to-day and reported to the police that his wife had deserted him and cloped with an unknown party. She is about 50 years of age, has been married to Peckhard twenty-six years, and is the mother of a large family. Before departing with her paramour she took an ax, chopped open a trunk, and took therefrom $2,130, which she safely stowed about her person before departing. No trace of the guilty old woman can be found. A NEGRO 'LYNCHED. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., June 13.—Late last night Charles Diddell, a negro, was lynched at Weston, in Platte County, for a nameless crime committed upon Nancy Stillwell, a white woman, aged 19. Diddell left the girl for dead with a crushed skull, and when arrested admitted the crime. At a late hour a mob took him from the Sheriff to a high bridge, and tied one end of a rope around his neck and the other to the end of a stringer. A brother of the young girl then pushed him into eternity, and this morning his body was cut down by the Coroner.

RECAPTURED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Boone, In., June 13.—An exciting hunt took place last evening, Henry Mays, the escaped convict, having been seen in the afternoon. Hundreds of men were out after him, and howas captured and brought to town about dusk by Frederick Pollard and Charles B. Webb, who marched him through the streets with a pistol at his head. Mays is a desperate of the worst stripe, and the officer from whom he escaped intended that he be shot. If he made the least resistance. The officer started with him for the Auburn Penitentiary this afternoon.

HOMICIDE AT CINCINNATI.

HOMICIDE AT CINCINNATI.

CINCINNATI, O., June 13.—James McDonough, formerly a private watchman at the city stables, was the man who shot Pat Malloy shortly after midnight this morning. He was arrested about 5 o'clock this morning. He and Malloy had been drinking together and went to Malloy's house, where Malloy fell asleep. On awakening he found McDonough and his (Malloy's) wife in a suspicious position, and he and McDonough began a fight in the house. It was ended in the street, where McDonough shot and killed Malloy.

"AN OLD FEUD."

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ATLANTA, Ga., June 13.—In Polk County, a day or two since, Joe Thomas was killed by a man named Shilley. The cause was the reopening of an old feud. Thomas, after cursing Shilley, advanced upon him with a pistol, and was killed by Shilley, who split his head open with an ax with which he was cutting wood.

A SELF-CONFESSED MURDERER.

A SELF-CONFESSED MURDERER
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

OMAHA, Neb., June 13.—Sheriff Crem, of Howard County, to-day arrested Henry Tedrapen for murdering Lon Paxton, while the latter was plowing on his farm in that county. He has made a confession, and the murdered man's friends talk of lynching him.

CUTTING AFFRAY.
Louisville, Ky., June 13.—A cutting affray took place yesterday near Lagrange between John Basler and Willis Downing, in which Basler was mortally wounded. Both are young men in good circumstances. The fight was the result of a drunken quarrel. Downing escaped.

CAPTURE OF A SNEAK-THIEF.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LANSING, Mich., June 13.—A. B. Carrl, notorious sneak-thief and crook, was captured in this city to-night by Detective Abellis. He was wanted for robbing St. Luke's Church in Kalamazoo. He made a determined effort to escape after he was arrested.

A PUMP-FACTORY BURGLARIZED. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. JACKSON, Mich., June 13.—Bedford's pump-factory was burglarized last night. The thief stole a suit of clothes he found in the shop, and a few other articles.

STABBING AFFRAY. BUFFALO, June 13.—Hank Hermann, a saloonkeeper, was probably fatally stabbed tonight by Max Albrecht in the saloon where Albrecht played a piano.

"A privileged person—One who is so much a savage when thwarted that civilized persons avoid thwarting him."

"A liberal-minded man—One who disclaims to prefer right to wrong."

"Liberals—Men who dutter radicals."

"Conservatives—Men who give give way to radicals."

"A domestic Woman—A woman like a domestic."

"Humor—Thinking in fun while we feel in earnest."

Richmond Democrat. THURSDAY EVENING. JUNE 16 1881.
The damage by the cyclone, in Dekalb county, last Sunday, is estimated at $200,000.

Jerry Hollihan, a well known tailor, of St. Joseph, was run over and killed, by the cars, last Tuesday.

Gov. Crittenden has gone to New York to arrange about accepting the three million dollars the Hannibal and St. Joe Railroad owes the State, and Bob. Campbell is now Governor.

The situation at Albany, New York, is practically unchanged, and apparently there is no prospect that successors to Conkling and Platt will be chosen at an early day. We can't form the remotest idea of what the final result will be, but we still hope the Democats will be profited by the situation.

The people of southern Illinois are becoming disheartened over the crop prospects. Army worms are said to be destroying the meadows, the chinch bugs are devouring the wheat, and locust are playing sad hovoc with the young fruit.

When Congress reassembles, the fact that Democratic Missouri has borrowed money at three per cent. will illuminate some of the dark spots in Windom,s refunding game. The United States can certainly do as well as Missouri, and while Windom,s unauthorized three and half per cent refunding is well enough as far as it goes, it does not go far enough by one half of one per cent.

Calico Charlie Foster has been nominated by the Republicans of Ohio, for a re-election to the position of governor. Foster belongs to the Administration wing of the Republican party and if we can trust the prophecies of the Globe-Democrat, the leading Republican paper in Missouri, will be called upon to take a trip up Salt river in October next. The Republican majority in Ohio is not large and the stalwart wing has received a direct slap in the face, in the shape of a resolution endorseing Garfield's administration, which will not make them very enthusiastic in support of the ticket. Secretary Sherman or rather Senator Sherman, as he is now, was a conspicuous figure in the convention and what he had to say, will not add much to the love Conklings friends have for the president. The situation in Ohio ought to be satisfactory to the Democrats.

Col. Fred Conkling, a brother to Lord Roscoe, says that some member of the Ways and Means committee, of the Lower house of Congress received $100,000, last Congress from the New York sugar ring, to influence his vote in favor of such a tariff on sugar as the ring wanted. Of the members who compose that committee but one Democrat voted as the ring wished, and that was Fernando Wood, now dead, and the natural conclusion reached, is that Col. Fred has lied or that the $100,000 went to a Republican. The truth of the matter is that there is a general rumpus among the Republicans in New York and that the frauds and peculations of that party are likely to come to the front at any time. Look at Albany a moment, if you want to be convinced that the Republican party is rotten to the core. An effort was made to buy a vote for Deprew, the railroad lawyer for the sum of $2,500, and the money actually paid. This is the kind of tactics the monopoly Republicans are advocating and it is time the people were being awakened to the rascalities of the men they have placed in power.

A mulatto negro, named Charles Didell, raped and cut the throat of Miss Annie Stillwater, aged sixteen years, near Weston, in Platte County Mo, on Sunday evening last. She was walking in the woods near her father's house when the brute came upon her and accomplished his purpose, and because she would not agree not to tell of the awful crime, he attempted to murder her by cutting her throat and mashing her head with a club. He was captured and taken to Weston, but about 8 o'clock Sunday evening a party of armed men took him out and hung him to the Railroad bridge. The girl was handsome and bore an excellent reputation, was alive at last accounts but not expected to live. The brute met a just fate and retribution was none too soon in following the crime.

GENERAL NEWS.
Yesterday's ballots in joint convention of the New York Legislature were as follows: For the short term—Jacobs, 51; Wheeler, 38; Conkling, 32; Cornell, 11; Lapham, 12; scattering, 12. For the long term—Depew, 54; Kernan, 52; Platt, 27; Cornell, 12; Crowley, 5; scattering, 5.

The Democratic State Convention of Iowa m t yesterday in Des Moines. Colonel E. D. Fenn, of Story county, was chosen temporary chairman. W. A. Shaw, of Fremont, was chosen permanent chairman, and a ticket was nominated headed by L. G. Kinne, of Tama county, for Governor.

J. A. Bentley, Commissioner of Pensions, has resigned, and W. W. Dudley, at present U. S. Marshal for Indiana, has been appointed his successor. Judge N. C. Farland, of Kausas, has been appointed Commissioner of the General Land Office to succeed Williamson, resigned.

It is stated "authoritatively" by a Washington evening paper that Custodian Pitney, of the Treasury Department, will retire at the close of this month and be succeeded by General E. W. Whittaker. The latter was chief of staff to General Custer during the war, and is now a real estate during agent in Washington.

The President yesterday appointed Henry Cox to be Pension Agent at San Francisco, in place of William H. Payne.
The correspondent of the Times at Dublin says:—"The desire to emigrate continues. The South Dublin Guardians have resolved to send away thirty-seven able-bodied paupers who desire to emigrate to America. They have been in the Workhouse from three to twenty-five years."

It is said that the twenty young men who yesterday graduated at the Reusselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, N. Y., have all been offered lucrative professional situations in various parts of the country. There is a demand for educated engineers.

A colored man named Ruse, charged with feloniously assaulting awhite girl, was taken from the jail at Weston, Missouri, on Tuesday night and lynched. After being hanged his head was cut off and thrown into the Missouri river. Juan Monterea, a murderer, was lynched by a mob in Taus county, New Mexico, on Saturday night.

A man named Larkin, was shot dead by his cousin, George S. Larkin, a Deputy U. S. marshal, while resisting arrest for a violation of the revenue laws, near Rogersville, Tennessee, on Wednesday afternoon. Geo. S. Larkin was arrested and lodged in the Rogersville jail. As threats of lynching were made the Governor ordered a guard for the jail.

According to the census reports, there were engaged in the fisheries of California, Oregon, Washington Territory and Alaska, during 1880, 16,745 persons, and 5,547 vessels and boats; valued at $583,145. The total capital invested in the fisheries was $2,748,883, and the total value of the product was $9,548,277.

John Cummings. of Licking county, Ohio, was yesterday fined $25 and costs for having punished his child by "putting a split stick, with a tack in it, on its tongue."

The Adame White Lead Company's Works, near Baltimore were destroyed yesterday by fire. Loss $75,000. The fire is attributed to the spontaneous combustion of lusseed oil. Papineau's mills near Monntreal, were burned yesterday. Loss $30,000. Fifteen houses and 4000 cords of wood at Kingsley's Falls, Quebec, belonging to the Grand Trunk Railway, were burned yesterday.

It is reported from Tuscan, Arizona, that seventy cowboys, well armed and equipped, have left Wilson, in that Territory, to attack Frintares, in Chihuahau, in revenge for the killing of several of their comrades in that village about three weeks ago. The Mexican authorities have been warned and will resist the expected assault.

The suit of the wife of Elkins, a well-known artist in Chicago, against a saloon keeper, named Oudney, for $20,000 for selling her husband liquor and assisting in ending his career in an inebriate asylum, resulted yesterday in the discharge of the jury for failure to agree. The trial lasted ten days. It was in evidence that the work of Elkins' brush, when he was sober, was worth about $80 per day.

At noon yesterday, John Griscom the Chicago faster, wieghed 171 pounds, a loss of ¼ of a pound during twenty-four hours, in which he drank 32 ounces of water. His pulse was 60, respiration 13, temperature 98 2-5.

The first annual examination of the pupils of the Indian Training School, at Carlsle, Penna, took place yesterday. A surprising progress was shown by the Indian children.

Tragical Tales.
Near Mt. Vernon, Ky., on the 18th inst., James Hart shot Andrew Baker dead. They were both drunk, and Hart claims that the shooting was accidental.

Johu McCombe, a prominent Colorado politician shot and probably fatally wounded James McDonald, an actor, at Leadville, Col., on the 17. Cause, misunderstanding in regard to the use of a buggy.

Robert B. Cyphert, a leading citizen of Marion county, Arkansas, was shot by an assassin while standing in his doorway.

A crazy man shot and severely wounded Miss Fannie Walker at Elizabethtown, N. J., on the 17th inst., and then killed himself.

Thos. Meyer, of Rantowles, S. C., crazed by religion, shot his 13-year-old boy as a sacrifice on the 13th. He failed in the attempt to murder two more of his children. The murderous father persuaded his little son to walk ahead of him on the road, and then deliberately shot him down.

A printers' strike at Pittsburgh, Pa., resulted in a tragedy on the 16th inst. One of the displaced men named Michael Corcoran, assaulted a "rat" and was shot dead.

At a saw-mill fifteen miles from Hot Springs, Ark., on the 15th inst., R. L. Justice was shot with a rifle by a man named Gregg, who had also recently killed a negro.

Juan Monterea, of Toas, New Mexico, killed Lem Gallagher with a hoe, for interfering in a fight with his mother. A lynching party swung Mouterea from the court house railing on the same evening.

Geo. L. Larkin, deputy United States marshal, killed his cousin, also named Larkin, at Rogerville, Tenn., on the 15th inst. The deceased had violated the laws and was resisting arrest when shot down.

Clay Wilson, a notorious gambler, was shot dead at Denver, Col., on the 16th, by James Moor, another of the gentry.

At Bedford, Ind., Wm. Brannan was shot by a concealed assassin and instantly killed.

Robert Martin shot his wife and child, a girl three years old, at Newark, N. J., on the 15th inst. The woman was instantly killed and his child mortally wounded.

Freeman Alvoirs, a lunatic, was murdered by Byron L. Day, a fellow unfortunate at Wauwatosa, Milwaukee county, Wis., on the 13th inst.

Two neck-tie sociables on the 13th inst.—one at Denver, Ark., and the other at Weston, Neb. At the former place Emory, a murderer, was taken from jail and hung; and at the latter village Charles Diddell, a negro rapist, had his neck stretched by an angry populace.

Timothy Mahoney, a policeman, was shot dead by burglars at Chicago, on the night of the 12th inst.

Wm. Gordon and Peter Magnus quarrelled at Chicago on the 12th, when Magnus kicked Gordon in the neck, causing instant death.

Patrick Mallory was shot and killed by James McDonough at Cincinnati, on the night of the 12th.

savannah-savannah-1881-08-26.A1:
An Escaping Prisoner Shot.
An Escaping Prisoner Shot.
Yesterday evening about half-past 6 o'clock an officer was carrying a negro to jail, when his prisoner made a sudden jump, and, clearing himself of the officer's grasp, darted down the street. A shot was sent after him from a Smith & Wesson, which took the fugitive darkey in the thigh, and compelled him to stop. He was then easily captured, and was returned to the jail. It was impossible to learn any further particulars beyond the fact that the negro had been shot.

sergeant-h-h-harvey-wounded-white-savann.A1:
Yesterday morning about half-past seven o'clock the negro laborers employed in loading the steamship Gate City at the Central Railroad wharves made a demand upon Mr. H. M. Branch, who is in charge, for an increase of wages from $1 50 to $2, declaring that they would not work longer at the present rates. The demand was rather unexpected, as there had been no previous indications of such a course, the men appearing to be perfectly satisfied, though it seems that the strike had been decided upon at a secret meeting. Mr. Branch informed the negroes that he could not respond to their demand until he had seen the agent and laid the matter before him, and advised them to continue work. Their course, however, had been determined, and they all knocked off work and left the wharf. The steamer is only partially loaded, and is advertised to sail to-day, hence this cessation of work occasioned considerable temporary inconvenience.

After leaving the wharf the men collected on the vacant lots east of the canal, at the foot of the railroad bridge, where their numbers were largely augmented, crowds of females from Cooper Shop lane and the surrounding precincts having gathered quickly on the announcement of the strike. These females played a very conspicuous part in the subsequent demonstration, and were exceedingly boisterous, vindictive and violent in their manner. During the forenoon, however, there was no active demonstration, and the negroes, who were engaged under the Messrs. Dixon Bros. in discharging the steamship Dessoug, lying at the adjoining wharf to the Gate City, continued their work without interruption. They had also made a demand for an increase of wages, but were induced, by the promise of Mr. Dixon that they should receive the same compensation as the others obtained, to continue at work. At one o'clock they knocked off for dinner, and returned to their labors shortly after two o'clock. They had well patronized the

At one o'clock they knocked off for dinner,
and returned to their labors shortly after
two o'clock. They had well patronized the
barrooms in the locality during their dinner
hour, and were more or less under the influence
of liquor, quarrelsome, and so careless
in their work that Mr. Dixon considered it
advisable to let them go, and they marched
off in a boisterous manner, but made a de-
tour, not going by the bridge where the
strikers of the morning had gathered, and
who, after stopping work, had been stimul-
ating themselves with whisky. Under the
influence of the liquor, and aroused by the
inflammatory talk of the negro women these
parties, about 2:30 o'clock, took possession of
the railroad bridge and refused to allow
any one to pass to or from the wharves.
The street was blockaded with the drays
loaded with cotton, and traffic was entirely
obstructed. Message was sent by private
telephone from the warehouse of Messrs.
W. W. Gordon & Co., on River street, near
the bridge, to their office on the Bay, con-
veying information of the riot, and asking
that the police barracks be notified.
The message was at once communicated
to the barracks, and Sergeant Harvey gall-
oped his horse to the scene, two other policemen following. On reaching the bridge
Sergeant Harvey found it blocked up with
negro men and women. He at once rode
forward and ordered them to disperse. The
crowd pressed around him, and showed but
little signs of obeying. He forced his way
forward, however, when a negro woman
struck him a terrible blow with a stick
across the knee, and a rush was then made
to bear him from his horse. He reached
over in his saddle to seize the woman who
had struck him, but was unable to do so on
account of the crowd pressing up and sur-
rounding her. He then jumped from his
horse with the determination to capture
her, but had hardly touched the bridge
when some villain in the crowd fired
a pistol, the ball striking the Sergeant a little to the rear of the left side, passing about
an inch below the heart and coursing up-
wards towards the right lung, where it
lodged. He drew his pistol after he was
shot and fired, and one of the other two policemen who had come up also fired, but
with what result is not known, as, if there were any negroes wounded, they succeeded in getting off.

Sergeant Harvey was at first removed to Gordon's warehouse, where he was seen by Dr. McFarland, but was subsequently, and as soon as possible, conveyed to his residence, corner of State and Jefferson streets, where he was attended by Dr. McFarland and Dr. J. B. Read. His wound is considered very serious and dangerous, but the ball, evidently being a small one, there is hope it will not prove fatal. His condition, however, is regarded with the gravest apprehension, though he has the best attention. Sergeant Harvey is one of the bravest and most popular officers on the police force, and it was generally regretted that he should have received so serious a wound at the hands of some worthless negro, who has thus far escaped.

The news of the trouble soon reached up town, and General Anderson, Chief of Police, was quickly in the saddle, and ordered out a squad of fifteen men with muskets, under Sergeant Killougrhy. The policemen took the street car at the barracks and rode to the corner of West Broad and Broughton streets, where they disembarked and double quicked to the bridge. The crowd seeing the policemen coming with fixed bayonets dispersed rapidly, many getting off into the swamp, and the bridge was at once opened to traffic.

The police remained on duty at the bridge and in the vicinity until about six o'clock, when a patrol was thrown out and the remainder of the squad returned to the barracks. The situation was then quiet, but as a matter of precaution the patrol in that locality was increased last night. It is understood there was a meeting at some place on Fahm street, at which the strikers determined not to work to-day without the increase.

There were sixty negroes engaged during the morning discharging and loading the steamship Saragossa for Baltimore, under Mr. Merritt W. Dixon, and no trouble was experienced with them up to six o'clock. As the steamer has to get off to-day they were notified to return to work for the night.

About seven o'clock some thirty put in an appearance and went to work. A crowd, numbering probably one hundred and fifty, collected at the bluff foot of Lincoln street, near where the steamer is lying, evidently with the intention of interfering with the hands, though no demonstration was made, as several policemen suddenly appeared, and the crowd soon dispersed along River street.
sergeant-h-h-harvey-wounded-white-savann.A2:
Riotous Stevedores in Savannah-A Policeman Mortally Wounded.
SAVANNAH, GA., September 19.—This morning the hands engaged in coaling the steamship Gate City struck for two dollars per day, and, on being refused, quit work. Those on the steamship Desoug continued to work till dinner. When they came back nearly all of them were drunk and would not work nor allow others to do so. They took possession of River street, leading to the Ocean Steamship Company's wharf, and stopped all business in that direction. A telephone was scat to police headquarters, and Sergeant Harvey and two men were dispatched to the scene of the difficulty. The officer, being mounted, arrived before the others, and was at once attacked by a crowd of negroes. In the miliee one of the mob shot the officer, inflicting what is supposed to be a mortal wound. Reforemements of the police arrived and dispersed the rioters, though they gathered several times afterwards and made demonstrations to interfere with the men at work. The ships are being loaded to-night under the protection of the police. It is feared there will be further trouble to-morrow.
sergeant-h-h-harvey-wounded-white-savann.A3:
A STRIKE IN SAVANNAH.
Riotous Conduct of Negro Laborers-A Police Sergeant Mortally Wounded Bloody Work Feared To-Day.
Riotous Conduct of Negro Laborers. A Police Sergeant Mortally Wounded—Bloody Work Feared To-Day.

SAVANNAH, September 19.—This afternoon the hands loading the New York steamer at the Central Railroad wharf without warning stopped work, and immediately interviewed the dramshops in the vicinity. At 3 o'clock they assembled in large force at the canal bridge leading to the wharves and obstructed the passage of drays and trucks, swearing that no work should be permitted on the wharves until their demand for two dollars per day, an advance of fifty cents, was allowed. The police barracks was telephoned and Sergt. H. H. Harvey, with two policemen, mounted, proceeded to the place. Sergt. Harvey rode upon the bridge and ordered the crowd to disperse, and there was a disposition on the part of the men to obey, but the violent and incendiary conduct of the women who encouraged them to resistance induced them to stand. The sergeant then rode into the crowd, when a negro woman dealt him a fearful blow with a large stick on the leg. He jumped from his horse to grab her, when some one in the crowd fired upon him, striking him in the breast an inch below the heart, inflicting what is thought a mortal wound, his condition to-night being considered hopeless. After being shot Harvey fired two shots into the crowd and it is thought wounded some one. The other policemen opened fire and the ringleaders dispersed.

Meanwhile a detail of twenty policemen, armed with muskets, double-quicked to the scene and the negroes abandoned their position and fled to the swamps. Large crowds, however, principally negro women, remained in the vicinity and were very defiant. The police remained at the bridge until dark, when the situation became quiet and they retired.

To-night a full force is out and the city is under guard. Meetings of the negroes were held, and it is rumored an attempt will be made to stop work on all vessels at 7 o'clock to-morrow morning. The authorities have been advised and arrangements made accordingly, and if any interference is attempted there will be bloody work. There is intense excitement in certain negro localities, and the streets are filled with drunken men. The steainship agents refuse to accede to the demand and telegrams have been sent to the country for negroes who are expected by the early train to-morrow. There are apprehensions of serious trouble.

A Fatal Accident.

This morning Samuel Davis, colored, aged 10 years, while fooling with an old musket accidentally discharged it, the contents lodging in the head of his sister Priscilla, aged 7 years, killing her instantly. This occurred on the Ogeechee road, eleven miles from the city.

Anderson, Chief of Police, with a detail of fifteen men, armed with muskets, proceeded rapidly to the scene, and before any trouble occurred were upon the ground. The appearance of the police thus armed had a mollifying effect upon the crowd, which divided into groups and stood around talking among themselves in a sullen manner.

ARREST OF A RINGLEADER.

General Anderson's attention was attracted to a muscular looking mulatto of repulsive men who was making himself rather conspicuous by passing from one group to another and talking in whispers to them, apparently encouraging them to maintain their ground and counseling resistance. He was evidently a ringleader in the troubles, and Gen. Anderson sent a policeman to him with a message that he wished to see him. The fellow, with an independent swagger and impudent air, walked over to where General Anderson was sitting on his horse, when the General inquired his name. The negro replied defiantly that he had no business to ask his name, and declined to give it. The Chief informed him who he was, when the negro responded most insolently, and said if any one wanted to know his name they could find it out, that he wouldn't tell. The Chief thereupon ordered Policeman Smith, with another officer, to arrest him and carry him to the barracks. This action seemed to take the crowd by surprise, and there was some commotion among them. Thinking possibly that the crowd might attempt the rescue of the prisoner, Gen. Anderson, in a tone sufficiently loud for all to hear him, ordered the policemen to proceed at once to the barracks with their prisoner, and if they were obstructed and interfered with, or an attempt was made to rescue the rescue of the p
In consequence of the excited feeling existing in the community and the ugly aspect of affairs, the Mayor, who had determined to preserve the peace of the city and put down, in the most summary manner, any general disturbance, about nine o'clock requested the commanders of the Savannah Volunteer Guards to have the members of their battalion assemble at the arsenal and be in readiness for any call that might be made upon them to assist the police. The Chatham Artillery were also summoned to their armory and to have two guns in readiness to be brought into action without delay. They were provided with canister, and it was distinctly understood and made known that in the event their services were called into requisition there would be work, as no blank cartridges were issued.

One thousand rounds of ball cartridges were also procured and deposited at one of the armories, where they could be easily procured and issued.

The Chathams were at their armory from one o'clock until nightfall, and the Guards, to the number of over eighty men, assembled at their arsenal at five o'clock in the afternoon and remained on duty until eight o'clock, when a detail was left in charge and a signal agreed upon which would call them together in a short time. The Georgia Hussars were also notified to be in readiness, and would have turned out fifty men.

It was decided only to use the military in case of grave emergency, and to assist the police force should they be found unable to quell any riot that might occur. These precautions were well taken, and the moral effect was good. The negroes who were thus threatening the peace of the city were by this movement put on notice that should they carry their riotous demonstrations too far that there would be no tampering with them, and that any riot would be speedily and summarily nipped in the bud. We are glad the occasion did not arise for calling into use the military, and the day passed off without serious disturbance. The arrangements that were made would have enabled the authorities to have suppressed any riotous proceedings.

ON THE WHARVES.

Whilst the centre of the excitement was in the vicinity of the Central Railroad bridge, there was a disquieting feeling all along the river front, and some timid draymen for certain business houses were afraid to go to the steamers to get freight. We heard of one case where a merchant was exceedingly anxious to obtain some goods without delay, but was unable to do so, as his colored drayman said he was afraid of being hurt by the discontented laborers. This was an exceptional case, though there were other firms that were inconvenienced by the delay in obtaining their goods. At the Baltimore wharf the hands under Messrs. Dixon Bros., who had been engaged unloading the steamship Saragossa, which was appointed to sail at four o'clock, resolutely refused to resume work unless their demand for an increase of wages was acceded to. As it was necessary, on account of some through freight to Europe, that the steamer should leave at the time appointed, the agents, Messrs. James B. West & Co., consented to pay the increase, but this concession is no index of their future action.

The Philadelphia and Boston steamers were subjected to like inconvenience, but the emergency not being so great with them the demands of the strikers were not granted. The steamship Gate City, which was taking on her freight when the strike commenced, was also appointed to sail in the afternoon. Her crew were brought into requisition and she finished loading and sailed on schedule time. The City of Macon came in yesterday, but in consequence of the interruption of work her cargo was not touched. She will be unloaded to-day, as arrangements have been perfected for securing sufficient force.

There was no interference with work at any of the presses or on any of the ships in the port, and with the exception of the wharves noted there was no visible excitement.

THE SITUATION SERENE.

Towards dark the crowds of negroes who had gathered in various parts of the city, and particularly the large crowd at the railroad bridge, among which were hundreds of negro women, who as usual were blatant and violent, began to slowly disperse. Many of these negroes, we understand, live five and six miles out on the road, and have been in the habit of coming into the city every day to work. They are more inclined to rioting than those who live in the city, but after a disturbance commences are the first to levant. After dark there were no persons in the neighborhood, though Fahm and Indian streets were filled, dotted with groups of men and women discussing the situation.

TO-DAY.

There was some apprehension expressed last night that the troubles would be increased to-day, but this belief is not general, as the preparations that have been made for the preservation of order will undoubtedly have a salutary effect upon the riotously inclined. We trust such may be the case, and the community relieved of the excitement and turmoil which have disturbed all classes for the past two days.

The Wounded Sergeant.
The Wounded Sergeant.

There was general inquiry yesterday among all classes of our citizens in regard to the condition of Sergeant Harvey, who was shot on the railroad bridge Monday afternoon while endeavoring to quell the riot. A number of citizens expressed a willingness to subscribe liberally to a fund as a reward for the apprehension of the rascal who fired at him. We are glad to state that at twelve o'clock last night his condition was somewhat favorable, though he was suffering much pain at intervals.

He was warned to leave, but refused to go, and became very insolent. Mr. John M. Harden, one of the clerks at the wharf, started to arrest him, when he broke into a run. He was ordered to halt, but paid no attention, when Mr. Harden fired at him, hitting him in the chin. Three shots were fired, and it is understood all took effect, judging from the traces of blood left by Calvin in his run. Colonel Wadley was present on the wharf, where Calvin was cavorting around among the laborers, endeavoring to foment trouble, and ordered his arrest. When the fellow was seen running, some of the negroes, not knowing the cause or recognizing him, threw rocks at him as he passed in their vicinity.

Colonel Wadley remained at the wharf the entire day, and staid on one of the steamers last night. He had made arrangements for feeding the new hands at the wharves, as it was thought they might be injured by some of the strikers should they get beyond the protection of the police.

They were put to work without delay, and although not able to make as rapid headway in loading and discharging the ships as the old hands, got along very well. These were protected throughout the day and continued working up to ten clock last night. There will be one hundred more men here to day, and, although work has been greatly retarded by these troubles, yet with the force now secured, it will not be long ere "the blockade is raised."

There was no other trouble at the wharves, and towards the afternoon the crowd had almost entirely disappeared, and at dark the situation at the bridge was perfectly serene.

During the morning and afternoon circulars of an incendiary character were distributed about the streets, and some were posted at the market and other public places. They were unsigned, and were evidently issued by some of the ringleaders who are anxious to keep up the troubles.

EFFORTS TO EFFECT AN ADJUSTMENT.

The serious aspect of affairs, and the certainty that a continuance of riotous demonstrations could have but one result, induced Lieutenant Colonel Woodhouse, Major De-
The serious aspect of affairs, and the certainty that a continuance of riotous demonstrations could have but one result, induced Lieutenant Colonel Woodhouse, Major Deveaux and Adjutant Toomer, of the colored battalion, three well known representative colored men, at the suggestion of some citizens, to go among the strikers and endeavor to check the spirit of insubordination and disorder which was so manifest. They made very conservative speeches, and advised the men, for their own sakes, to refrain from any acts of violence, and to take the peaceable method of petition for the adjustment of their troubles. The men listened with attention, and showed a disposition to act on the advice given, and it was decided to ask a committee of citizens to confer with Col. Wadley and ascertain what arrangements could be made. Captain John Flannery, Colonel J. H. Estill and L. H. DeMontmollin, Esq., consented to act as mediators, and at once proceeded to the railroad wharf, where they had an interview with Col. Wadley, who, after hearing the proposition of the strikers, replied that he was perfectly willing for the men to return to work at once, and then after this affair had quieted down, if they had any petition to make he would give it consideration, but under no circumstances would he make any promises as to his future course. Meanwhile a communication had been addressed by the Chairman of the strikers to a number of prominent Bay street merchants, requesting them to intercede with the employers with the view of effecting a satisfactory adjustment of the difficulty, which they agreed to do.

In the afternoon at 5 o'clock, an immense mass meeting of colored men was held at the foot of Bryan street, which was addressed by the colored officers above mentioned in the same style as in the morning, and afterwards by Mr. DeMontmollin, who stated the result of the interview with Colonel Wadley. The men seemed inclined favorably to take the course suggested—return to work at the old rates, and petition for an increase in a proper manner, but, after some discussion, it was decided to wait until 12 o'clock this morning to ascertain what had been accomplished by the other committee. The indications are that the negotiations will be successful, and that the troubles will be ended to-day, as the laborers will perceive that the only possible way to succeed in securing an advance in their wages is to adopt the course referred to, return quietly to their work and then make a respectful presentation of their claims for an increase. The more sensible among them are awakening to this fact, and as stated, there is good reason to anticipate an adjustment to-day.

PEACE MUST BE PRESERVED.

The proclamations of the Governor of the State and the Mayor of the city, which will be found elsewhere, will, we believe, have the effect of preventing any further disorder, and the excitement which has so seriously affected business the past three days will be allayed. The strong arm of the law will be exerted to preserve the peace and maintain order, and the turbulently inclined will find that they consult their own interest by realizing this fact.

THE SAVANNAH, FLORIDA AND WESTERN RAILWAY.

The following communication in reference to the condition of affairs at the above named railway, concerning which there were so many startling rumors, will be read with satisfaction;

SAVANNAH, FLORIDA AND WESTERN RAILWAY, OFFICE GENERAL MANAGER, SAVANNAH, September 22 — Editor Morning News: My attention having been attracted to an article in the Times of this evening that the strike had extended to the laborers in the cotton yard of the Savananh, Florida and Western Railway this morning, in justice to the employees of our freight department I beg to say that there has not been even a ripple of excitement among them. They are attending to their duties as if there were no discordant element in the city. A Strike in Savannah.
On Monday morning, the 19th inst., the negro laborers loading the steamship Gate City at Savannah, struck for $2 per day, and on being refused quit work. Those on the steamship Dessong continued until 1 p. m. When they came back nearly all of them were drunk and wouldn't work or allow others to do so. They took possession of River street, leading to the Ocean Steamship Company's wharf and stopped all business in that direction. A telephone message was sent to police headquarters, and Sergeant Harvey and two men were dispatched to the scene of the difficulty. The officer, being mounted, arrived before the others, and was at once attacked by a crowd of negroes. In the melee one of the mob shot the officer, inflicting, what is supposed to be, a mortal wound. A reinforcement of police arrived and dispersed the rioters, though they gathered several times afterwards and made demonstrations to interfere with the men at work. The ships were loaded under the protection of the police. The employers manifested a determination to resist the demands of the strikers to the bitter end, and employed new hands. The trouble continued from time to time during the whole of last week, the strikers making several demonstrations. On Thursday a skirmish took place between the police and the rioters, resulting in several casualties, and the temporary dispersal of the rioters. Later an attempt was made to harmonize matters by a committee of old citizens, acting at the request of the strikers, but it failed, as the strikers would not agree to the terms adopted by said committee.

Needed Improvements.

As has been before intimated in these columns, and as is well known to the better element in the community, Burrillville is in need of improvements in various directions. Improvement implies reform, and just how it is to be effected under the present unfavorable conditions is a conundrum which is difficult of solution. With a Town Council who utterly fail to appreciate the simplest needs of the people, and who fail, whether from lack of ability or for political reasons is not known, probably a combination of both, to enforce existing laws, or pass ordinances which have a tendency to prevent indecent exhibitions of the rowdyism elements in the town, it is perhaps, idle to expect any reform or improvement, but it would certainly be more agreeable to all peaceable citizens, and better for the reputation of Burrillville if our "executive department" could devise some way in which they can insure their re-election, and at the same time prevent the open and shameless disregard of all law; see that the amount appropriated for highways is expended in a sensible manner, even though thoroughness is impossible, and from the experience of other towns put some better interpretation upon the liquor law than at present, namely, "that all saloons within 400 feet of a school-house shall not pay a license." Perhaps that is not exactly the way the Council worded their interpretation of the law, but that is practically their verdict. And further, why is it that there is no attempt to enforce the law against the desecration of the Sabbath? Or, in fact, any other law, unless it happens that some citizen, from personal motives, causes the arrest and punishment of a violater of the statutes. Now, the plea of the Council is, so far as we have heard it, that they have appointed officers to enforce town and State ordinances, and can do no more. This is a foolish plea, and no one can blame an officer for neglecting to arrest guilty parties when he knows it will not be pleasant to the powers that made him an officer, and that the only result would be that he would secure an enemy and probably be deprived of his office, from which he may perhaps be deriving some income. The question is, who is to blame for the present disgraceful condition of things? It is the people who have put men into power who do not believe in correcting these abuses. There is no doubt that a majority of the voters could, if they would attend to their duties as citizens, and use their influence in favor of needed reforms, revolutionize this misgoverned town, and put men into office who have some weightier interest in the public good than is

evinced by the present administration. No doubt there may be members of the Council who are, passively, opposed to the present reckless disregard of what is right and proper, but the Council as a whole, needs regeneration and we hardly think their sins of omission will be condoned in the future as they have been in the past. SERGEANT HARVEY DEAD.
The Work of a Lawless Assassin Brought to a Close Yesterday Morning—The Funeral Ceremonies to Take Place To-Day—Measures Proposed for the Relief of His Family.
At five o'clock yesterday morning Sergeant H. H. Harvey, of the Savannah police, who was shot during the labor riots, which were inaugurated on the 19th of September last by the negro laborers employed on the Central Railroad wharf, died after a lingering period of suffering of one month. Everything which the affection of his family, the earnest regard of his many friends and the unceasing attention of his watchful and skillful physicians—Drs. Read and McFarland—could do was done to save a valuable life, endangered in the active and fearless discharge of duty, but all in vain. Yesterday morning his soul passed away into the presence of its Maker, and to-day all that is mortal of one of the truest men which Savannah has ever been able to count upon, either as a citizen or as a defender of her laws, will be consigned to the dust.

Sergeant Harvey was born in Bryan county on the 24th day of November, 1850, and was therefore, at the time of his decease, nearly thirty-one years of age. He came to this city in 1871, and on the 16th day of August of that year was appointed a member of the Savannah police force. Almost from the very day of his joining the force he showed himself to be honest in the extreme, fearless in any danger which he was called upon to confront, active in the discharge of every duty, and in all respects thoroughly reliable. Many were the notable instances in which these characteristics were displayed, and in this connection we may mention one which is still vivid in the minds of our citizens.

It will be remembered that on the 31st of May, 1876, Mr. Alexander Irving, when returning from an excursion of the Knights of Pythias with his little son, lost his footing and fell from the boat into the river. Mr. Harvey, who was on the boat at the time, saw him fall over and, without hesitation, and impelled solely by a desire to save a fellow man from death, plunged in after him. Owing to the darkness, his effort was unsuccessful, and both Mr. Irving and his child perished. The Knights, however, recognized the unselfish bravery of the noble deed, and, in token of their appreciation thereof, presented Mr. Harvey with a gold medal, which his widow still has and prizes most highly. We merely record this incident as illustrative of the true character of the gallant officer and brave soul, whose very bravery and gallantry led to his untimely end.

During his long and painful illness Sergeant Harvey bore himself unmurmuringly and with unfinching fortitude. To the last he retained all his faculties and would converse coolly and sensibly with friends about his bedside regarding his approaching end. Never was there a more striking instance of one being perfectly reconciled to leave the world. Convinced that his life had been square and true, and marked with fidelity to all trusts, he did not in the least dread to meet the grim messenger. To the contrary, as the last solemn moment approahed, feeling that earthly friends were powerless to aid him longer, he unhesitatingly put his whole trust in God, and knowing that his faith was well founded, and both feared no danger. Calmly and serenely he awaited the time in patience when he should receive the welcome summons "Well done good and faithful servant; enter thou into the joy of thy Lord."

After his decease, Coroner Sheftall having received due notification, proceeded to where his body lay and held an inquest over the remains. Doctors Read and McFarland and Messrs. John S. Higgins and James G. Bennett were all examined under oath, and gave in testimony establishing the facts already detailed as to the cause of his death. The jury have not yet rendered a verdict, having adjourned until four o'clock to-day to further consider the evidence. Doctors Read, Charlton, McFarland, Duncan, Myers, Sanders and Stone made an autopsy in hopes of discovering the ball which had produced the blood poisoning which caused the wound to result fatally, but it could not be found. It was a very small bullet, and, in the opinion of the physicians, had become imbedded somewhere in the spinal column.

Sergeant Harvey leaves a wife and one child, who are in straitened circumstances. It is the universal opinion, as far as we have heard it expressed, that the citizens of Savannah owe it to him who gave his life in their defense that these should be provided for. To this end several of his friends yesterday held a meeting, and, after the consideration, concluded to request the following named gentlemen to meet at Armory Hall to-day at 12 o'clock, to decide upon the best means for carrying out the object proposed: Messrs. S. P. Hamilton, R. H. Anderson, R. R. Richards, Thomas Ballantyne, Joseph A. Roberts, Felix Prendergast, Jacob Paulsen, Jacob Einstein, B. H. Levy, Daniel O'Connor, E. L. Neldlinger, E. Moran, W. B. Mell, W. G. Waller, D. B. Lester, J. L. Warren, R. N. Reed, James E. Walters, F. M. Hull, R. McIntyre, P. M. Russell, Sr., S. B. Adams, P. H. Ward, Jordan F. Brooks, J. J. Dale, Osceola Butler, John Flannery, S. Guckenheimer, Marmaduke Hamilton, P. W. Meldrim, E. A. Well, W. W. Gordon, H. M. Comer, George A. Hudson, R. H. Lewis, W. H. Turner, W. M. Sneed and J. Stern.

We feel assured that it will only be necessary to mention the subject to insure a hearty and generous response. The people of Savannah owe it to themselves to see that the wife and child of the man who fell a martyr to his duty, while protecting their lives and property, should be raised above all possibility of want.

The funeral will take place this afternoon at three o'clock, at Trinity Methodist Church, St. James square. The Masonic fraternity, of which he was a practical and zealous member, the Knights of Pythias and a detachment of police will attend, and we doubt not a large number of our citizens will avail themselves of this opportunity to pay their tribute to a brave, guileless, true man, and show their appreciation of his fidelity and worth.
sergeant-h-h-harvey-wounded-white-savann.A15:
SERGEANT HARVEY'S WIDOW.
Action Taken Yesterday to Save Herself and Child from Want-The Young Men's Historical Society and the John T. Ford Dramatic Association to the Front.
In accordance with the request of certain friends of the late Sergeant Harvey, as announced in these columns yesterday morning, a meeting of citizens was held at Armory Hall at 12:30 p.m. yesterday to devise ways and means for raising a fund to save the widow and child of the gallant deceased from present want and to provide for their future necessities. On motion Mr. S. P. Hamilton was unanimously elected Chairman of the meeting and Mr. Samuel B. Adams Secretary.

On being called to order the Chairman stated briefly the objects of the meeting, and Mr. P. M. Russell, Sr., made a motion that a committee of five be appointed to decide upon such matters as would be appropriate for the consideration of the meeting. This motion was unanimously adopted, and in accordance therewith the Chair appointed the following gentlemen as such committee: Messrs. P. M. Russell, Sr., Chairman; Thos. Ballantyne, S. Guckenheimer, D. B. Lester and D. O'Connor.

The committee then retired, and after due deliberation reported that it had been agreed to assign certain portions of the city to different committees to be canvassed for subscriptions, as follows:

Bay Street—F. M. Hull, Thos. Ballantyne, H. M. Comer, John Flannery, W. W. Gordon.

Savannah, Florida and Western Railway—Gen. R. H. Anderson, Felix Prendergast.

Bryan Street—E. L. Neidlinger, M. J. Doyle.

Congress Street—W. B. Mell, B. H. Levy.

Broughton Street—E. A. Well, John Lyons.

Public and Attorneys' Offices—S. B. Adams, P. M. Russell, J. J. McGowan.

River Street and all west of Jefferson—Daniel O'Connor, Jacob Paulsen.

Barnard to Bull, south of Bay—D. B. Lester, W. G. Waller.

Drayton, east and south of Bay—E. Moran, M. Lavin, John Schwarz.

South of Hall—John Sullivan, J. R. Hamlet.

Special Committee for Banks—S. P. Hamilton, S. Guckenhelmer.
Central Railroad—Edw. McIntire, B. J. Cubbedge, D. D. Arden, R. Barthelmess.
The committee also proposed that subscription lists be left at the various newspaper offices in the city, so that any person desiring to contribute might have the opportunity to leave their names at such offices, together with the amount of their subscriptions. This report was adopted without a dissenting voice.
A motion, offered by Mr. Neidlinger, that the secretary make out lists of the various committees, stating the territory assigned to them, and furnish the same to the chairmen of such committees, was adopted, as was also a motion offered by Mr. S. B. Adams, to the effect that whatever sums are collected be turned over to Mr. S. P. Hamilton as treasurer, and that when the collections were all in, that gentleman, as chairman, be authorized to reconvene the meeting for the purpose of deciding how the fund shall be invested for the benefit of Mrs. Harvey. In the meantime, however, he is to use his discretion in sending to her whatever sums he might ascertain to be required by her to meet her present necessities. He, as chairman, was also authorized to fill any vacancies in the existing committees which might accrue from any member being unable to serve, or from any other cause.
There being no further business to be considered at this time, on motion of Mr. Ballantyne, the meeting then adjourned subject to the call of the chairman.
The various committees enumerated above will begin to-day their work of canvassing. It is needless to commend their efforts to the generous consideration of our people of all classes. Sergeant Harvey met his death in the active and zealous discharge of his duties, and while gallantly exerting himself to protect the lives and property of our citizens. His widow and fatherless child have lost their mainstay and sole reliance for support, and are in need. We feel assured that it is merely enough to mention these facts to secure from the citizens of Savannah a hearty recognition of their duty in the premises, and a liberal response to the appeals which will be made to them for this most praiseworthy and charitable object.
Last evening the Young Men's Historical Association assembled at their hall, in response to a call from their President, Mr. S. S. Guckenheimer, to consider the subject of giving an entertainment for the benefit of the widow and child of the deceased. A good attendance was present, and, after Mr. Guckenheimer had stated the object of the meeting, a motion, made by Mr. P. Lewis, to the effect that an entertainment consisting of literary and humorous readings and a concert by the musical friends of the association, be given at the Theatre within two weeks, and on a date to be hereafter announced, was unanimously adopted. It was also agreed, without a single vote in the negative, that a committee of three members be appointed to take full charge of the entertainment, and that twelve citizens of Savannah be requested to act in co-operation with such committee; further, it was decided to place tickets for the entertainment in the hands of these gentlemen, and also in those of General R. H. Anderson and each member of the police force for sale. In obedience to this resolution the following committees were selected: Of the active members of the association—Messrs. H. G. Appel, J. CHICAGO. May 13th.—Journalistic enter-
Revised Bible.

CHICAGO, May 13th.—Journalistic enterprise in Chicago led to a lively struggle for copies of the revised Bible. It had been rumored for some days that the Tribune had sent its New York correspondent across the Atlantic to secure the first copies of the first edition. The Times this morning contains a large number of sample changes from both the Old and New Testaments, transmitted over the cable in some 5,000 words. For instance, the term "Jehovah" has been substituted in the New Testament for Lord, God or King. "Babe in the manger" now reads "the babe" in Matthew alone. Over 200 words incorrectly employed are changed. "Art thou a master in Israel?" now reads, "Art thou a teacher of Israel?" In Genesis the original is, "And the Lord set a mark upon Cain; that any finding him should kill him." The revisers make it read, "And the Lord gave a sign and assurance to Cain that those finding him would kill him." In dealing with the Lord's prayer the revisers have stricken out the benediction, "For Thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever, amen."

BAKERSFIELD (Cal.), Oct. 20.—Charles Zeigler and Scodie are partners in a mine at Piute Mountain. Tom Herbert, an employee, and Zeigler worked the mine. Scodie lived at home on the South Fork. Zeigler and Herbert quarreled last Thursday, and the former went to Scodie's house, got money, came back and paid Herbert off, and said he did not want him any longer. The above facts were witnessed by a Frenchman, who since the mystery has disappeared. The next morning Herbert appeared at a neighbors and said Zeigler was dead. He thought heart disease was the cause of his death, but had not examined him. Zeigler was found with three bullet holes in him. One ball entered the neck to the left and a little below the chin, and lodged in his teeth on the opposite side. Another entered his back and passed through the lungs. Justice Goodale of Havilah was sent for, and, acting as Coroner, summoned a jury and held an inquest. Herbert, the only witness, testified that Zeigler came home in the evening and had been drinking. He brought a bottle of whisky, and they drank together a number of times. Herbert went to bed. Zeigler went to his room and came back later with whisky and asked Herbert to drink, which he declined, but finally drank. Zeigler went off and came back with a bottle and cup, and asked Herbert to take another drink. Herbert said he had enough, and wouldn't drink any more. After considerable talk they finally drank. Herbert went to sleep and in the morning found Zeigler on the floor, near the bed, dead. He did not examine him, and did not know what killed him. He heard no noise during the night. He went to the neighbors and told them that Zeigler was dead. Herbert's pants and boots had blood on them. The Judge asked for an explanation. Herbert said he found Zeigler lying across his pants and boots when he got up and pulled them from under him. The Judge returned to Kernville, and a Constable went up and arrested Herbert and lodged him in jail at Kernville. Night before last a mob of 15 or 20 started for the jail to hang the prisoner. A majority of the mob were drunk, and were interrupted 100 yards from the jail by Deputy Sheriff Ben. Mitchell. The mob fired on Mitchell, who exclaimed, "I'm hit!" The officer discharged his gun, loaded with buckshot, mortally wounding Jim Cochran, and then fell dead. Cochran is said to be the man who shot the officer. Cochran is alive. At the last report the mob had dispersed without getting their man. The Sheriff and posse left for Kernville last night.

OTTAWA. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

OTTAWA, Oct. 20.—Referring to his Excellency's departure for England, it is semi-officially stated that there is no foundation whatever for the rumor that he will not return to Canada. His Excellency is only absent to leave, his full intention being to return early in January, and he will open the next session of Parliament, whenever that may be, in person. The Cabinet are understood to be considering the somewhat difficult question of appointing an Administrator of the Government to hold office during his absence. The practice has been during the temporary absence of the Governor-General from the capital, but within the Dominion, that a Deputy-Governor-General should be made to assume his functions for the time, as Chief-Justice Richle was during the recent Vice-Regal trip to the Northwest; but in the case of absence of the Governor-General beyond the bounds of the Dominion an Administrator is appointed. This duty has always hitherto been assigned to the commander of the forces at Halifax. It so happens just now that Sir Patrick McDougall is also absent on the other side of the Atlantic and not available for the important duty. It is thought probable that, pending Sir Patrick's return, Chief-Justice Richle may be appointed Administrator.

Hitherto the telegraph lines owned by the Dominion Government have been under divided management, the lines in the Northwest being under the Public Works Department, and those in the Gulf under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. An order has just been passed in council transferring the management of the latter to the Public Works Department, and placing all Government telegraphs under one control. It is said the Government have under contemplation the laying of a cable under Lake Superior to Thunder Bay to give through telegraphic communication with the Northwest on Canadian soil.
