SENATOBIA, MISSISSIPPI.
Man Charged with Murder Taken
Out of Jail And Shot.
Special to the LEDGER.]
Special to the LEDGER.]
SENATOBIA, Miss, September 10.—
J. W. Gillenwaters, arrested for the murder of Thomas Eason, at Arkabutla, Miss. a few weeks ago, was taken from from the jail by a masked mob last night about 10 o'clock and shot. He is not dead yet, but is not expected to live.
w-gillenwaters-senatobia-1881-09-09.A6: J. W. GLLENWATERS, the man lynched at Senatobia, Miss., last Friday night, but not killed outright, was charged with and undoubtedly guilty of a most atrocious murder committed about three weeks ago solely for the purpose of robbery. Eason, the man killed, was his friend and associate. He crept into Eason's room in a store at night and cut his throat from ear to ear. After that he tried the money drawer and safe unsuccessfully and made his escape on horseback. When found there was blood and bruises on his person and other evidence of his guilt. The settled conviction of the community is that he killed Eason, and this was expressed by friends of the deceased last night. It is said that he recognized those who took him out, which perhaps makes no great difference with them.
w-gillenwaters-senatobia-1881-09-09.A7:
MOB LAW At Arkabutla, Tate County, Miss. — A Man Named Gillenwaters Conflined in Jail for the Murder of S. G. Eason Taken by a Masked Party and Shot, as they Supposed, to Death—His Rescue—Arrest of the Lynchers.
SENATOBIA, Miss., September 11, 1881.
To the Editors of the Memphis Appeal.

On the night of the 9th instant, S. T. Eason, of Arkabutla, in Tate county, Mississippi, was murdered in the back room of his store. About 3 o'clock in the morning a noise was heard in that room by a mechanic who was employed by Messrs. Eason to build a room to the west side of their store, and who was sleeping in the unfinished room as the weather was warm. Fitner, the mechanic, went to the back window to see what was the matter, when some one pulled to the blinds. He then went to a neighboring store, waked the clerk and they returned to Eason's store, when some one got out of the back door, mounted a horse forty or fifty yards in the rear and ran off southward. Jeff D. Gillenwaters having been seen with the deceased late at night, and it having been supposed that he went to bed with him, was suspected, and his arrest was made in a few hours. A shirt was found covered with blood in the room and identified as Gillenwaters's; other signs pointed to him, in the shape of visiting cards of his, also sleeve buttons and studs. Pursuit of him developed traces of blood along his route, and when found his condition betokened the truth of former conjecture. He was after trial committed by the magistrate without bail. Excitement was high and many seemed willing to lynch him, but better and cooler counsels prevailed. Eason was a very popular young man, and his friends were greatly enraged. Gillenwaters is also of good connections, but, since this event, is said to have been somewhat off the line of good conduct which generally marked his family. He and his brothers were frequently about the store, always welcomed, and frequently slept there with Eason, between whom and there there was considerable friendship. Eason was found with his throat cut all around, terribly gashed, and his head badly contused by a sledge hammer lying near, or some heavy instrument. A razor was lying near with all the edge broken off and covered with blood by the cutting. It was a most shocking murder, and great indignation prevailed throughout this section. On last Saturday morning about 1 o'clock the jailer was resting quietly in his bed, unsuspicious of any harm to himself or prisoners, when he was awakened by a noise made for admission at the back door. He went to the door and opened it a little way, saw several shining revolvers pointed at him, and not liking appearances slammed the door and locked it. Seeing that a rescue was imminent, he threw the prison keys through a hole in the floor of his bedroom, while the unwel-
not liking appearances slammed the door and locked it. Seeing that a rescue was imminent, he threw the prison keys through a hole in the floor of his bedroom, while the unwelcome visitors broke down the back door with a sledge hammer. They entered his room, and with the usual demonstrations demanded the keys. The jailer delayed them as well as he could, the females of his family screamed, and one of his daughters continued to scream at the risk of her life, and even blew a loud blast or two on a large conk-shell, which aroused many citizens. Still no help came, as most people thought the noise was occasioned by boys playing in the courthouse yard, the night being very bright and pleasant. At length the keys were produced by the jailer's wife in order to save her husband's life, and the mob went up-stairs, got Gillenwaters, bade the jailer good-bye, and went westward. Just then some one rang the courthouse bell, and in a short time a crowd of citizens were on the ground, but too late to prevent escape or effect anything, unarmed and half dressed. They first thought the alarm was of fire, but not seeing any came on to ascertain the trouble. The two Deputy Sheriffs in town, with the Town Marshal and one or two others, did not lose a moment in pursuing the raiders. After a little shots were heard, and Gillenwaters was beyond doubt dead, but the crowd of raiders, doubtless, alarmed by the ringing of the bell and signs of stirring in town, did not remain to see the result of their work. Gillenwaters walked one hundred and Gillenwaters two hundred yards to the gate in front of a negro cabin, about a mile and a half from town, where he was overtaken by the deputies and others. Dr. French soon followed and pronounced his wounds mortal. The District Attorney, Ira D. Oglesby, was on the ground to hear the dying words of Gillenwaters, if he had not been killed outright; indeed, every possible step was taken to find out who might be engaged in the raid, and to provide for Gillenwaters's safety and comfort. He was brought back to town and lodged in the house of his uncle, D. J. Sherrod, where he now lies almost at the point of death, under a strong guard. The four worst wounds received by Gillenwaters were from behind, one was in the face, and two or three others on the arm and shoulder. He says he fell on his face at the first fire. Two balls entered below the left shoulder-blade and came out below and near the nipple, two others entered below the left and came out between the navel and side. His life is despaired of. Lynchers Who Made a Mistake.
Memphis, Tenn., September 12.—Information has just reached this city of a horrible affair transpiring in the neighborhood of Senatobia, Mississippi, on Friday night. A young man named Gillenwaters was in jail at that plape supposed to be the assassin of a young merchant named Easton, of Arkabutia, Tate county, some time ago. The evidence against him was only circumstantial and he was only being held until the matter could be further investigated. On Friday night an armed and disguised mob, all apparently young men, suddenly appeared in Senatobia and made their way direct to the jail. They came upon the jailer unawares and forced him to open the prison doors. Gillenwaters was taken by this mob some distance from town, where he was fired into, the first shots took effect in his face, and he fell to the ground face downward. Several other shots were fired into his prostrate body, when he was left for dead.

Marvellous to state the shots did not take effect in vital parts of the body and he soon recovered strength enough to return to town and identify six of the mob, who proved to be citizens of Arkabutla. They were promptly arrested and are now in jail. It is thought the entire crowd will be discovered and identified by young Gillenwaters, who was still alive when the gentleman giving the information left Senatobia. Every effort seems to have been made to smother the affair up, evidently for the purpose of discovering the perpetrators.

LYNCH LAW.
A mob of twenty or thirty men broke into the jail at Senatobia Saturday morning and took out Jeff Gillenwaters, charged with the murder of J. T. Eason, and conveyed him a mile and a half from town, fired seven pistol balls into his body and left him for dead. It was their intention to hang the wretched prisoner, but the citizens of Senatobia rang the bells, raised a rescuing party, which pursued and so frightened the lynchers that it frustrated their purpose. Gillenwaters recognized several of the lynchers and six of them have been arrested and confined in jail. Strict and stern justice should be meted out to these masked nightriders, regardless of the crime charged against their victim. Lynch law is no law at all. It is destructive of law, order and justice, and cannot be tolerated in civilized and law-abiding communities. No matter what the offense, or who the victim may be, under our laws, a criminal is entitled to a fair and impartial trial, and all good citizens will gladly join, from a sense of duty alike to the country and themselves, in guaranteeing that this great right shall be preserved and enforced at all hazards in all cases. This is the first instance in a long while that the bloody and merciless Judge Lynch has dared enforce an edict in our section. As we prize the good name and fair fame of our State, let us banish him forever from our borders, as the arch enemy of law, justice, civilization and christianity. We are glad to know that the citizens of our neighboring town of Senatobia had no part or lot in this lawless act. The lynchers came from Arkabutla, several miles in the country, the scene of Eason's brutal and cowardy murder. We commend the people of Senatobia for their promptness and vigilance in doing all they could to bring the offenders to justice; but we deem it our duty as a public journalist to speak out in no uncertain tone in condemnation of this crime against the State, her people her laws and her best interests.

Has Gone Free.
The man Gillenwaters, who some time ago was arrested for the supposed killing of a young store keeper in Tunica county, Mississippi, with whom he was sleeping, has escaped from custody. It will be remembered that Gillenwaters was taken out by a mob and shot nine times and left at the roadside for dead. One of the mob rode over the man's body as it lay on the ground and deliberately shot into his breast, the bullet passing through his body into the ground. While in the hands of the mob Gillenwaters recognized a number of his assailants, and making what was supposed to be a dying statement, he revealed their names. This statement is in the hands of the authorities of Tunica, and six men have been put in jail to answer for the part they are charged with having taken. Meanwhile Gillenwaters with his nine bullet holes, is well advanced toward recovery, and now it is hinted that friends of the murdered man and others interested have connived to let Gillenwaters get away.

WRETCHES WHO SHOULD BE HUNG WHEN CAUGHT.
GREENSBORO, N. C., June 24.—The lynching of the two men a few days since in Stokes County for rape, and the lynching of another one two weeks ago, does not seem to have had the effect looked for by the lynchers. This morning as Lizzie Fluch, a little 10-year-old daughter of Mrs. Jennie Fluch, living near Hillsboro, was on her way to the spring, she was accosted by William Gauch, a negro of bad character. The second made an infamous proposal to the girl, who, frightened by the look in his eyes, attempted to run away. He caught her and committed a rape upon her person. He at once died, and the child now lies in a precarious condition. Citizens of the county are looking for him.

Intelligence has reached here also of an infamous offense of a similar nature at Martinsville yesterday evening. Charles Gilmor, a negro, actually went into the house of Mr. Prince Winchester, white he and his wife were absent. The sole occupant of the house at the time was Miss Winchester. Knowing Gilmor, she asked him what he wanted, and suspecting that he had crept into the house for the purpose of robbery, she ordered him out. The negro, glaring boldly at her, told her he had no idea of leaving yet, and then went on to tell her to keep quiet on pain of death. At once guessing his horrible design, the young woman began to scream for help. Gilmor attempted to commit his devilish design upon her person, and despite her great struggles would have accomplished his purpose had he not been frightened off by the sound of footsteps of neighbors attracted by the girl's screams. He barely had time to leap from the rear window before they entered the house. Posses of citizens have been hunting him all day. This is the third offense of this character committed by Gilmor. Once he was convicted of an attempt at rape and sentenced to nine years in the Penitentiary, but his counsel succeeded in having his sentence shortened. He was a few years after convicted of rape and sentenced to twenty years in the Penitentiary, but after serving nine years he was released.

A Chapter of Violent Deaths.

Thomas P. Dolmer, 70 years old, committed suicide at his residence in Brooklyn, N. Y., Saturday, by hanging himself to a bed-post.

Two boys, Wm. Smith and Jacob Schmederer, aged 11 and 14 years respectively, were found drowned in Rondout creek, N. Y., Saturday.

The body of Jennie Cramer, aged 20, of New Haven, Conn., was found in the water off West Haven, Saturday morning. There are suspicions of foul play.

George Harrington, aged 67 years, died at Stephentown, N. Y., Saturday, from injuries inflicted during an altercation with Michael Ward, a neighbor.

Samuel Miller has been arrested at Williamsport, Pa., for poisoning his father, aged 74. The accused held an insurance policy of $2,000 on his father's life.

W. J. Logle, of Jefferson County, West Virginia, a candidate for cadet engineer at the Naval Academy, was accidentally drowned near Annapolis yesterday afternoon.

Mary Kenny, of Philadelphia, was found lying dead in bed in a room in the Wall House, Brooklyn, New York, yesterday. Investigation showed that she had ended her life by taking Paris green. She was apparently about forty-five years of age.
At Buffalo, N. Y., last night, George Leonard Smith took hold of two of the brushes of the commentator of the generating machine of the Brush Electric Light Company in such a manner as to unite the current and was instantly killed.

A special dispatch from Boonville, Mo., says that in a difficulty between Phineas Silby, first mate of the steamer Mattie Bell, and a negro deckhand, name unknown, at Rockport, Friday, the latter killed the former by stabbing him to the heart. The negro was arrested.

J. T. Noakes was taken from the jail at Orville, Cal., yesterday, by a body of masked and armed men, conveyed a short distance from the town, and hanged to a tree. Noakes had murdered an old man named A. J. Crum, at Chico, three weeks ago by kicking him to death.

James Ross, white, shot and killed Wm. Jones, colored, at Nashville, Tenn., yesterday. Ross had hit a colored boy in the back with a stone. Jones subsequently went to Ross' house and desired to know why he had acted so toward the boy. Ross asked him what he had to do with it, and ran into his house, got a pistol and shot Jones dead.

While sitting in one of the coaches on the Wabash Railroad, near Glasgow, Mo., yesterday, George Wright, a passenger, was approached from behind by two men, one of whom buried a hatchet in his skull and the other fired a pistol-ball into his head. The murderers then rushed from the car and escaped into the woods.

Additional particulars of the catastrophe by lightning in Darlington County, S. C., have been received, showing that a party of twenty white men, laborers, on Friday, stopped under an oak tree to rest and shelter themselves from the sun. Clouds were visible at a distance, and rain was falling some miles away, but in that locality the sun was shining. One of the men stepped off a few yards, when suddenly a terrific crash startled him, and, turning, he beheld his companions, some dead, some paralyzed, and others wounded and struggling in the throes of death. J. M. Mazzingo, Rufus Mazzingo, Willie Waters, and John B. Gatlin were killed outright. These were all young men and recently married. Twelve others were struck and more or less stunned and mutilated, some of them being seriously if not fatally injured. After the clouds had gathered, an hour later, there was a heavy fall of rain. The tools with which the men had been at work may have attracted the electricity.

The wheat crop in Guadalupe county, Texas, is said to be the finest ever raised there.

It has rained nearly every day in Colorado county, Texas, for sometime past, and nearly every cotton plantation in the county has a crop of worms.

For sale cheap, a large quantity of sewer pipe, slightly damaged, suitable for drainage and waste-water pipe, etc. T. J. Graham, South Court, near Second street.

A revenue officer named Brayton was killed a few days since, while on duty near Central, South Carolina, by a man named McDow, whose illicit still had been raided. McDow is still at large.

The Friars Point Gazette states that "Governor Alcorn has been lying seriously ill at his residence at Jonestown, and his case required the most careful attention, but we are happy to learn that he is convalescing."

In a drunken row at Petersburg, Virginia, Friday last, between John W. Green, a commission merchant, and W. F. Green, a prominent citizen, both were killed. The former's throat was cut and the latter shot through the heart. The row began about the payment for a drink.

James Ross, a white man, shot and killed William Jones, colored, in Nashville, Sunday. The altercation occurred about Ross's chastising some colored children for committing nuisances in the vicinity of a spring on his premises. Jones took up the difficulty on the part of the children, went to Ross's house, and after a war of words assaulted Ross with a stone, Ross "getting the drop" on Jones with his pistol.

Tragical Tales.
John Taylor, a wealthy farmer, was killed near Sacramento, Cal., on the 7th inst., by his son-in-law, John Poblitz. The murderer's wife had left him and returned to her father on account of cruel treatment; this so enraged Poblitz that he committed the crime.

J. T. Noakes, who was sojourning in the Oroville, Cal., jail, awaiting his trial for the murder of an old man named Crum, was taken from the jail by a mob on the morning of the 7th inst. and hung.

A blacksmith named Payne shot and killed a young man named Wood at Sipse Springs, Texas, on the 7th inst. A woman in the case.

Crow Dog, captain of the police at the Rosebud agency, shot and instantly killed the Indian chief Spotted Tail on the 5th inst.

In a row at Tracy City, Tenn., on the night of the 6th, Thomas McGou was killed and Taylor Street dangerously wounded. Several other participants received slight wounds.

James Ross (white) shot and killed a colored man named William Jones at Nashville, Tenn., on the 7th inst.

In Washington County, Oregon, on the 6th inst., Geo. Algercheim, in a fit of rage, shot his daughter, inflicting a dangerous wound, and then fled to the woods, where he suicided.

William Watts, city marshal of Tamoroa, Ill., was instantly killed on the 5th inst., by James Vaughn, a coal miner, whom he was trying to arrest.

A brutal murder committed at Lawrenceburg, Ky., on the 16th of July, has just come to light. Arthur Ingram, 60 years of age, was mauled to death with a rock by W. T. Grunt. Whisky caused the murder.

Several prisoners broke jail at Folsom, Cal., on the 4th inst., and were pursued by the guards. George Walker was shot dead, and George Lupton was drowned in endeavoring to swim a stream. One prisoner escaped.

James Baker, a farmer living fifteen miles south of Fort Wayne, Ind., shot Wm. Howell, one of his farm hands, dead, on the 4th inst. Howell had been engaged by Baker's wife to stack wheat, but for some reason Baker objected to Howell's working, and because he refused to leave the premises, shot him dead.

Frank Cheney and Bill Comer, colored, fought a duel with pistols at Atlanta, Ga., which resulted in the death of Cheney.

william-jones-nashville-1881-08-07.A13:
CRIME.
JAMES Ross, of Nashville, Tenn., killed a negro named William Jones for interfering in a quarrel.

A DISPATCH from Rosebud agency announces the killing of Spotted Tail by Crow Dog, captain of the Indian police.

A BAND of fifty horsemen have left McKeesport, Pa., on information as to the whereabouts of the McClure's murderers, in the hope of lynching them.

The police of Toledo have arrested John Cavanaugh and William Harrison on suspicion of having murdered Ira M. Kelsey, whose body was found in Swan creek.

SPECULATIVE insurance caused the murder of Joseph Miller, an old man of Montgomery, Pa., by his son Samuel. The policies on his life aggregated $40,000.

At the exposition grounds in Indianapolis, John and Thomas Carney were killed by a street-car driver named William H. Collier, on the ground that they attempted to rob him. Collier surrendered himself.

A KING, ex-Marshal of Marion, Ala., while entering his gate, had six shots fired at him. His body was riddled with the bullets. His death was instantaneous. Six negroes were arrested.

The Mescalero Apaches who left their reservation have crossed the Rio Grande near San Jose. They killed two herders and a miner near San Marcial, and fired upon a party of thirty-six Mexicans and Americans who went in pursuit of them.

In Lafayette township, Indiana, James Baker killed his neighbor, William Howell. Baker was found on Sunday morning in a hay-mow, at the spot where the murder was committed, and claims that he has not been off his farm since the shooting.

At McKeesport, Pa., in an attempt to recover some stolen goods, Mr. McClure a hardware merchant, was shot dead by the thieves, an officer was fatally wounded, and two others seriously. About a hundred persons are in pursuit of the murderers.
